BL-247.design:
DESIGNED 2026-07-31 (Ben, same session as the BL-214 fold-model revision — see that item's supersession note).

## What this is, precisely

A small, closed-by-default affordance attached to every chart/visual: a toggle reading 'Why this chart', which reveals exactly two lines:

- **Answers:** <the question this specific chart, here, answers> — phrased as a real question a player would ask, not a chart caption.
- **Because:** <why this particular evidence justifies that answer> — one sentence, plain, no hedging.

It is co-located with the chart it describes (not a separate panel, not a global FAQ), closed by default (so the folded/narrow reading this whole design arc has been chasing stays narrow), and revealed by an explicit click — never shown automatically, never animated into view unprompted.

## What this explicitly is NOT (the correction)

Ben's original phrase 'asking interesting questions' was read, in the first pass of this design session, as a Q&A-driven navigation model — a list of pre-written questions ('Why is my Iron Ore extractor losing money?') that the game answers on the player's behalf when clicked (prototyped as build_UI_example_4). Ben corrected this directly: a tutorial, or any in-game help surface, must never tell the player what they should be asking or answering — only how to navigate the information that is already there. build_UI_example_4's Q&A list is therefore NOT carried into implementation as the drill-through mechanism; it remains on disk as a discarded exploration, not a reference design. The chart question log is a different, narrower thing: it documents what a chart that already exists is FOR, after the fact, on request - it does not curate a path through the game or pre-digest which questions matter.

## The dual audience

1. **Player-facing**, lightly: a player who wonders why a particular chart is even here can find out without it being forced on them, and without the game pretending to know what THEY specifically want to ask next.
2. **Design-facing, for Ben**: authoring the Answers/Because pair for a new chart is itself a check - a chart that cannot state a real question and a real justification in one sentence each probably does not earn its place. Reading the log across an existing view is also how Ben means to navigate the UI himself when looking for the next interesting question to add, or when deciding a candidate question is too large to answer in a single visual and needs to be split or deferred.

## Relationship to BL-214's Study-tier derivation captions

This is a distinct axis from BL-214's (now-superseded, but conceptually still relevant) derivation captions and threshold labels. A derivation caption answers 'how was this number computed' (e.g. 'base 23.6/tick × 0.78 hazard factor'). The chart question log answers 'why does this chart exist at all, and what is it for' (e.g. 'is this tile worth extracting Iron Ore from, compared to the best tiles I've surveyed'). A chart can have one without the other, but most will want both — the derivation is evidence, the question/justification is intent. Implementers should not conflate the two into one blob of text; they answer different questions and a reader may want one without the other.

BL-249.design:
FILED 2026-07-31. Promotes ROADMAP § v0.1.0 "Audit instruments" bullet 1 into a buildable item.

## Why it needed filing

The three audit instruments are a **cut gate** — ROADMAP § v0.1.0 lists them between the terrain
strand and "the Cut" — but none of the three existed as a backlog item, so nothing owned them and
the done-definition could not be checked off. This files the first.

## The spec (verbatim from ROADMAP)

"Frame budget. Frame-time HUD: last / avg / max ms + 1% lows. Targets: avg < 8 ms, max < 16.7 ms
panning the full Kepler tile grid (15,120 tiles). If max spikes the HUD says why — GPU present,
draw-call volume, or allocation churn."

## Shape

A self-contained `src/ui/frame_stats.{hpp,cpp}`: a ring buffer of recent frame times plus the
derived last / avg / max / 1%-low, and the HUD draw. Wired from the `app.cpp` frame loop, which
carries NO frame instrumentation today (one `SDL_GetTicks` call at app.cpp:3136, unrelated).

**Off by default and toggleable** — it is an audit instrument, not shipped chrome — and therefore
subject to the standing toggle rule (clicking an active control undoes it).

## The honesty constraint on "says why"

The ROADMAP names three spike causes: GPU present, draw-call volume, allocation churn. Only report
the ones actually measurable from inside the frame loop — time in the render/present call, and
ImGui's own draw-list vertex/command counts. **Do not fabricate an allocation-churn figure that is
not really being measured**; an instrument that invents its own numbers is worse than no
instrument, because the audit then rests on it. If a named cause cannot be measured, the item
records that rather than papering over it.

## Not in scope

Optimisation. This measures; acting on what it finds is separate work.
BL-249.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-07-31. src/ui/frame_stats.{hpp,cpp} plus F11, off by default.

Reports last / avg / max / 1% low against the ROADMAP targets (avg < 8 ms, max < 16.7 ms), colouring a breached figure. On a spike it breaks the worst frame down into build / submit / present / other, with ImGui's own vertex and draw-command counts.

HONEST ABOUT ITS LIMITS, which was the constraint set on it: the ROADMAP named "allocation churn" as a spike cause, and the HUD prints "allocation churn: not instrumented" rather than inventing a figure. The other/build/submit/present split is real, and on the verification capture it correctly attributed a 196 ms frame to "event pump + simulation step" (other 185.78 ms) rather than to rendering — the instrument diagnosing correctly on its first real spike.

OFF BY DEFAULT and verified so: scripts/verify/frame_budget_hud.lua capture 1 is an ordinary frame with no HUD present, which is what keeps every other golden in the suite unaffected by this instrument existing. Toggle rule honoured — F11 while open puts it away.

Drawn on both frame paths (the pre-play early-return branch and in-game), which are mutually exclusive, so it is not double-drawn.

INTEGRATION WIRING added in the main session: the show_panel("frame_hud", open) verify binding the slice assumed but did not add, without which the HUD could not be captured at all.

The absolute frame numbers under --verify are meaningless (offscreen driver, no vsync, no real present) and the verify script says so in its header. The 8 ms / 16.7 ms targets remain a human-in-the-loop measurement against the real app panning the full Kepler grid.

BL-250.design:
FILED 2026-07-31. Promotes ROADMAP § v0.1.0 "Audit instruments" bullet 2 into a buildable item.

## The spec (verbatim from ROADMAP)

"Econ-tick scaling. Extend `econ_stability` to print tick time. Target: well under 1 ms for the
prototype world; confirm it does not grow faster than linearly in bodies x corps."

## Shape

Extends the EXISTING `tools/verify/econ_stability.cpp` rather than adding a harness — the loop it
already drives (run_economy_step -> clear_markets -> apply_budget over 100 ticks) is exactly the
thing being timed, and a second harness would duplicate its world setup.

Three additions: per-tick wall clock reported as mean / max / p95; a sweep across several
bodies x corps sizes with the growth ratio between successive sizes; and an assertion that the
prototype-scale tick sits well under 1 ms.

## The flakiness constraint

An absolute-time assertion on a shared or loaded machine is a false-failure generator. So the
**shape** is the real check — the growth ratio, which is machine-independent — and the absolute
bound is set generously enough to catch an order-of-magnitude regression without tripping on a
busy CI box. The harness states its own tolerance in its output rather than hiding it in a
constant.

Timing must be strictly additive: every existing assertion and every line of existing output
survives unchanged. Measurement must never become a behaviour change.
BL-250.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-07-31. tools/verify/econ_stability.cpp gained per-tick timing and a bodies x corps scaling sweep; every pre-existing assertion (R1-R4) survives unchanged.

Prototype scale: mean 0.0018 ms, p95 0.0021 ms, max 0.0409 ms per tick — 555x headroom against the 1 ms ROADMAP target.

The sweep runs six rungs from 1 body / 8 corps to 8 bodies / 256 corps and reads growth off the MIN per-tick time, not the mean: preemption can only ever ADD time, so the fastest tick is the cleanest estimate of true cost and the ladder's shape survives a loaded machine. That design choice is what makes the check non-flaky, which was the binding constraint.

Result: 32x size -> 83.1x time, i.e. time ~ size^1.28, against a tolerance of size^1.5 (linear 1.0, quadratic 2.0). The largest swept world, 128x prototype, still ticks under 1 ms.

IT FOUND SOMETHING, which is the point of an instrument. The exponent sits above 1.0 because run_corp_strategic_step rescans every tile for every due corp — an O(corps x tiles) term, a rounding error to ~64 corps and about half the tick by 256. Filed as BL-253 rather than fixed here; the sweep now asserts the exponent stays under 1.5, so a regression trips a test.

BL-251.design:
FILED 2026-07-31. Promotes ROADMAP § v0.1.0 "Audit instruments" bullet 3 into a buildable item.

## The spec (verbatim from ROADMAP)

"Data creep. Entity/pool/market/convoy counters + RSS memory readout run long (100 -> 1000+ ticks):
counts and memory must plateau, not climb. A steady climb on an idle run names the unbounded
structure."

## Shape

A NEW `tools/verify/data_creep_harness.cpp` over the REAL generated world
(`make_hard_coded_world()`), not a toy — an unbounded structure is a property of the real data
model, and a hand-built world would not exhibit it. Samples at 100 / 250 / 500 / 1000+ ticks:
entity count, every component-store size, pool count, market and order-book sizes, convoy count,
trade-route count, and RSS (via /proc/self/statm, guarded so a non-Linux build still compiles and
reports RSS unavailable).

"Plateau" is defined numerically in the harness output — the 1000-tick value within a stated
tolerance of the 500-tick value — rather than left to the reader.

## The point is the NAMING

A bare "something grew" is not actionable. When a counter climbs the harness must say WHICH
store/collection and by how much; that is the whole instrument, and the reason it is worth more
than eyeballing RSS.

## Expected to find something

This is the first instrument ever pointed at data growth, so a genuine unbounded structure is a
plausible outcome. If one is found: **report it, do not weaken the assertion to go green, and do
not fix the growth inside this item** — the instrument's job is to name it. The fix is separate,
itemised work, sized once the finding is real.
BL-251.resolution:

Result: every exercised counter is flat from tick 500 to 1500 — entities 34769, tiles 34440, buildings/stockpiles 259, markets 6, nations 30, pools 8, tile_to_nation 6216 — and RSS plateaus at 13980 KiB. No unbounded structure among them. Runtime 7.4 s (world gen 0.15 s + 1500 ticks at 4.8 ms/tick).

IT REPORTED ITS OWN BLIND SPOT rather than passing quietly, which is the behaviour worth preserving: no convoy was dispatched anywhere in the run, so world.convoys, world.trade_routes and world.body_last_glimpse_tick sat at 0 throughout and their plateau assertions passed VACUOUSLY. BL-252.design:
FOUND 2026-07-31, on the first run of the whole suite on Linux/GCC (the cloud session that
closed the v0.1.0 cut set). Filed rather than fixed — the fix is a policy call, not a code change.

## The observation, stated precisely

**Headless.** `ai_skill_harness` fails 8 golden-band assertions. Critically, its own determinism
tier passes completely:

- R0: state_hash identical at every sampled tick across two same-seed runs — PASS
- R0: net-worth curve byte-identical across two same-seed runs — PASS
- R0: action-verb tallies identical — PASS

So determinism WITHIN this platform is intact. What differs is the value against bands blessed on
Windows/MSVC. Seed 0 passes; seeds 1-4 drift, some well outside the band (seed 1 final net worth
211,116 against a band of 250,000-560,000).

**Visual.** Every `--verify` script diffs against its golden: 9.5% on hover_freeze, 21.6% on
building_management_panel, 43-57% on the selection/visibility captures. Font rasterisation alone
would explain a few percent; these are larger.

## The two candidate causes — NOT yet distinguished

1. **Cross-platform float divergence, amplified.** 300 ticks of a feedback-coupled economy is a
   chaotic system; a last-bit difference in one price compounds. This would explain why seed 0
   survives and others do not — divergence is seed-dependent, not uniform.
2. **Stale goldens.** The bands were blessed 2026-07-31 from "a first pass of this exact harness";
   if anything landed after that pass, they are simply out of date.

Distinguishing them is cheap and is the item's first task: re-run the harness on Windows at the
same commit. Identical-to-band means platform; drifted-there-too means stale. **Do not re-bless
before knowing which** — re-blessing a platform divergence would just move the redness to the
other machine.

## Why it matters now, not later

The v0.1.0 done-definition requires "headless harnesses green". With platform-dependent goldens
that phrase has no single truth value, and the quality audit (BL-249/250/251) is measured on
whichever machine happens to run it. This is a cut blocker in effect, which is why it is rated A.

## The policy question to settle

Whether goldens are (a) platform-pinned — one blessed set per toolchain, selected at runtime;
(b) widened until platform-independent, accepting weaker regression detection; or (c) declared
Windows-authoritative, with the Linux suite running only the platform-independent tiers (R0
determinism, the structural harnesses) — which is what actually holds today, undocumented.

The visual goldens likely answer differently from the headless bands: pixel output depends on
font rasterisation and GPU/driver, so (c) may be right for visual while (a) or (b) fits headless.

## Not in scope

Making the numbers match across platforms. Bit-identical floating point across MSVC and GCC is not
a goal this prototype should adopt — the standing determinism invariant is same-seed, same-build
reproducibility, which is intact.
BL-252.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-08-01. The item asked for a diagnostic first and a policy call second; both were done, and the diagnostic changed the answer.

DIAGNOSTIC — the two candidate causes are BOTH real and independent, not one or the other.
  (1) STALE. Re-running the harness on Windows/MSVC at the same commit FAILED 5 assertions — on the very platform the bands were blessed on. The bands were authored from the first run of the harness, in the commit that ADDED it (8542e4b); BL-203 (Corp AI stage B: strategy layer, priority buckets, predictive spending), BL-221 (pre-national ladder) and BL-233 (terrain combat modifiers) all landed afterwards. The AI was substantially rewritten after its own goldens were set, and BL-221/BL-233 reshape the political map every seed generates. So the Windows drift was fully EXPLAINED, and re-blessing there was the sanctioned action, not a judgement call.
  (2) PLATFORM. Cross-platform divergence is also real and large. Same commit, Linux/GCC -O2 vs Windows/MSVC: seed 0 final 395143.0 vs 206245.2, seed 4 182745.5 vs 392148.4 — up to ~2x. Each platform is perfectly deterministic within itself (R0 passes on both).
  CONFOUND REMOVED: optimisation level is NOT the variable. MSVC /O2 reproduces MSVC Debug value for value, byte for byte. The toolchain is.

POLICY — settled by Ben 2026-08-01, and the two golden families answer DIFFERENTLY.
  Headless bands: PINNED PER TOOLCHAIN. ai_skill_harness now carries one blessed set per compiler behind #if defined(_MSC_VER) / #elif defined(__GNUC__), with an #error for any third toolchain so it cannot silently inherit another set. Both platforms now report ALL PASS (0 failures). Option (b) — widen until platform-independent — was measured and REJECTED, not assumed: a band holding both platforms would span roughly +/-100% and would detect no plausible regression.
  Visual goldens: WINDOWS-AUTHORITATIVE. Blessed and diffed on Windows only; on Linux, captures are inspected by eye and not golden-diffed. Pixel output depends on font rasterisation and GPU/driver as well as the toolchain, so a per-platform pin would mean re-blessing on every driver update for no detection gain.

NOT A DETERMINISM FAILURE. The standing invariant is same-seed, same-BUILD reproducibility, and it holds on each platform independently — R0 (state hash, net-worth curve, action tallies byte-identical across two same-seed runs) passes on both. Bit-identical FP across MSVC and GCC remains explicitly out of scope, as the item said.

Policy recorded in docs/development/DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md (new section: Cross-platform goldens), including the re-blessing rule (change only the set for the platform you ran on) and the corollary that a long-unblessed band reading red is usually staleness, not regression.

THE OWED RE-BLESS IS DONE (2026-08-01, same session). The four tile_build_ledger goldens were inspected, then re-blessed on Windows; all now pass at 0.0000%. Worth recording what the inspection found, because it changes what the number meant: tile_build_ledger_land_select — which has NO ledger open — diffed 21.69%, against 22.04% for the capture that does. So only ~0.35% of that diff was BL-162 row anatomy; ~21.7% was whole-canvas world-generation drift from BL-221/BL-233, the same drift that staled the ai_skill bands. A visual golden captures the entire 1280x720 window, so any world-gen change staleens every capture of the canvas at once — the shared-chrome staleness already documented in DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES, one layer down.

BL-253.design:
FOUND 2026-07-31 by BL-250's scaling sweep, on its first run.

## The measurement

    bodies  corps   min ms    growth
    1       8       0.0035      -- baseline
    2       16      0.0080    2.28x for 2.0x size
    2       32      0.0161    2.00x for 2.0x size
    4       64      0.0393    2.45x for 2.0x size
    4       128     0.0924    2.35x for 2.0x size
    8       256     0.2932    3.17x for 2.0x size

    end to end: 32x size -> 83.1x time  =>  time ~ size^1.28

## The cause

`run_corp_strategic_step` (src/world/corp_ai.cpp, landed with BL-202/BL-203) scans the
full tile set for every corp whose strategic cadence is due. That is an O(corps x tiles)
term sitting inside a loop that is otherwise roughly O(corps). At 8 corps it is invisible;
by 256 corps it is about half the tick.

## Why this is NOT a v0.1.0 blocker

At prototype scale the tick is 0.0018 ms mean — 555x under the 1 ms ROADMAP target — and
the largest world in the sweep (128x prototype) still ticks under 1 ms. Nothing is slow.
The curve simply bends, and the ROADMAP's own wording ("confirm it does not grow faster
than linearly in bodies x corps") makes the bend worth naming rather than shrugging at.

## Shape of the fix, when it is wanted

The scan is recomputing a mostly-static thing per corp. The obvious options, cheapest
first: cache the candidate set per body and invalidate on construction/depletion; or
restrict each corp's scan to tiles on bodies where it has presence; or precompute a
per-body ranked candidate list once per tick and let every due corp read it.

Do NOT do this speculatively. It is filed because the instrument found it, and it should
be actioned when corp counts actually rise — which is a v0.2.0+ concern, not a prototype
one. The sweep now asserts the exponent stays under 1.5, so a regression that makes this
worse trips a test.

## 2026-08-10 - re-goaled C/v0.2.0 -> A/v0.1.13 as BL-365's hard prerequisite

Pulled forward by the living-world pivot (BL-365, background industry replaces the abstract
substrate). The arithmetic that forces it: this term is linear in corp count, and BL-365 multiplies
corp count by roughly an order of magnitude. Measured 2026-08-10 on the real generated world, the
econ tick costs ~3.5 ms with 8 corps - against BL-250's 0.0018 ms/tick on the small synthetic sweep
world, i.e. the real world is ~2000x the per-tick cost. With `pre_game_ticks` now 80, that warm
start runs before the first frame of every new game, so a 10x corp count against an un-fixed
O(corps x tiles) scan turns ~280 ms of startup into tens of seconds.

BL-347 (stack pre-pass tick cost, complete) already records BL-193's restructure roughly doubling
the econ tick with the 128x sweep rung breaching 1 ms. BL-365 pushes the same path much harder.
This must land first, not alongside.
BL-253.resolution: 2026-08-11 — complete. rank_extraction_sites() hoists the O(tiles) build-candidate scan out of run_corp_strategic_step's per-corp loop; computed once per tick, read by every due corp. Verified behaviour-preserving (bit-identical ai_skill_harness output vs unmodified main) and measured improving: econ_stability's BL-250 scaling-sweep exponent 1.28 -> 1.18, worst 2x-size-step growth 3.17x -> 3.01x. determinism_harness, order_book_harness, world_audit, ProjectIo build all green. requirements.json § strategic-scan-tile-cost (R0-R3, all complete). Unblocks BL-365.

BL-254.design:
FOUND 2026-07-31, self-reported by the BL-251 harness in its COVERAGE section:

    NOTE: no convoy was dispatched anywhere in this run, so the convoy /
          trade-route / glimpse-stamp plateaus above are VACUOUS — those
          structures were never exercised. `world.trade_routes` in
          particular is documented as never-erased (components.hpp §
          trade_route), i.e. accumulating by construction; this rollout
          does not bound it. A convoy-exercising scenario is owed.

## Why this matters more than the other counters

Everything the harness DOES exercise plateaus cleanly — entities, tiles, buildings,
stockpiles, markets, nations, pools, RSS, all flat from tick 500 to 1500. The three
structures it does not exercise are the three with the most reason to grow:

- **`world.trade_routes`** is documented as never erased. A route is upserted on convoy
  completion and never removed, so it accumulates monotonically in the number of distinct
  body-pairs traded. Bounded by pairs (small) rather than by ticks — probably fine, but
  "probably fine by argument" is exactly what an instrument is supposed to replace.
- **`world.convoys`** should drain as convoys arrive; a leak here is a live-object leak.
- **`world.body_last_glimpse_tick`** gains an entry per glimpsed body.

## The work

Drive convoy traffic in the rollout so all three are non-zero and repeatedly cycled — the
harness already has `seed_convoy`-style helpers available in the supply layer (see
scripts/verify/proximity_glimpse.lua and tools/verify/trade_routes_harness.cpp for how
existing checks manufacture convoy activity). Then let the plateau assertions bind, and
report what they find.

Rated v0.1.0 because it closes a hole in a v0.1.0 cut gate: the data-creep instrument is
one of the three audit instruments, and it currently cannot see the structure most likely
to creep.

## Credit where due

The harness FOUND AND REPORTED THIS ITSELF rather than passing quietly. That is the
behaviour to preserve in any future instrument — a vacuous pass reported as vacuous is
worth more than a green tick.
BL-254.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-08-01. tools/verify/data_creep_harness.cpp now drives convoy traffic through the rollout, so the three plateaus that were vacuous now bind. No src/world change: convoys are manufactured as convoy_component records and handed to the real advance_convoys / credit_arrived_convoys pair — the same pattern tools/verify/trade_routes_harness.cpp and app.cpp verify.seed_convoy already use. The schedule is a pure function of the tick (pair, corp and cargo all rotate), so nothing about it is random or clock-dependent.

RESULT — all three plateau, and the plateau now means something.
  world.convoys                steady 4 at every mark; 1500 seeded, 1496 credited + retired, 4 in flight at the end. It drains; no live-object leak.
  world.trade_routes           18 at every mark. The schedule cycles the entire (corp x body-pair) key space every 36 ticks; the store reached 18 of a structural bound of 18 (3 corps x C(4,2) = 6 unordered pairs), last grew at tick 36, and stayed flat for the remaining 1464 ticks — and for 3964 ticks in a 4000-tick run. So the never-erased store is bounded by distinct pairs, not by ticks. That was previously an argument; it is now a measurement.
  world.body_last_glimpse_tick 2 -> 3 by tick 500, then flat. Stamps are overwritten in place by the player lanes, not appended; bounded by bodies.
Every other counter and RSS stayed flat, as before. GROWTH FINDINGS: none.

SECOND FINDING, surfaced by doing the work: the generated world seeds all six markets on the single tiled body (Kepler), so it holds NO inter-body market pair and CANNOT record a trade route however long it runs. That is a cause of the BL-254 blind spot independent of the launchpad gate, and it is printed in-output. The plan authors three stub markets once, pre-run, to give the lanes endpoints (the verify.seed_convoy pattern); world.markets carries that constant offset (6 -> 9) and it is not a per-tick allocation. Whether non-home bodies should have markets at campaign start is a design question this item does not settle.

COVERAGE HONESTY PRESERVED. The vacuity note is not deleted — it is now conditional on the convoy count actually being zero, and reads as a diagnostic that the schedule itself is broken. A new STILL UNEXERCISED block names what the rollout still does not touch: dispatch_convoys auto-dispatch never fires (inter-body lanes are launchpad-gated and the generated world places no launchpad; the intra-body branch also never fired), so what is under test is the credit + upsert + retire path, not the dispatch decision. A new asserted R4 fails the run if the three structures are ever un-exercised again, so the vacuous green pass cannot come back silently.

BL-255.design:
FOUND 2026-08-01 by the verifier-review barrier over the v0.1.0 audit batch.

## Two coupled hazards

**1. No default build type.** CMakeLists.txt never sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. For a multi-config generator (MSVC) that is fine - check.bat passes --config Release. For a single-config generator (Ninja, Unix Makefiles - i.e. every Linux and cloud session) an unspecified build type means NO optimisation flags at all, and --config is silently ignored.

That matters now in a way it did not before, because BL-250 added assertions with real margins:
  - largest swept rung 0.2932 ms against a 1 ms bound (3.4x headroom)
  - growth exponent 1.28 against a 1.5 tolerance
  - worst single doubling 3.17x against a 4.0x ceiling

A -O0 build is routinely 5-10x slower. The 1 ms bound would fail, and the exponent could shift, for reasons that have nothing to do with the economy loop.

Fix: set a default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE (Release, or RelWithDebInfo) when the generator is single-config and the user has not chosen one. Standard three-line idiom.

**2. No test timeouts.** No set_tests_properties(... TIMEOUT ...) exists anywhere. The suite now contains two genuinely long tests (data_creep_harness ~7 s, econ_stability's sweep, corp_terrain_matrix ~9 s). A harness that hangs - an infinite loop in a future economy change is exactly the class - blocks CI on the default 1500 s ctest timeout rather than failing fast.

## Not urgent, but cheap

Neither has bitten yet: the Linux build in the session that found this was configured with an explicit -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, which is why the numbers came out clean. It is filed so the next person configuring without that flag gets a comprehensible failure instead of a mysterious one.
BL-255.completion_note: COMPLETE 2026-08-01. CMakeLists.txt now sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release via the standard GENERATOR_IS_MULTI_CONFIG guard, CACHE STRING, only when the generator is single-config and unset - MSVC/multi-config (check.bat's --config Release) untouched, and an explicit user choice (including Debug) is never overridden. Every ctest test now carries a TIMEOUT: 60s default, 120s for the three named structurally-long harnesses (corp_terrain_matrix, econ_stability, data_creep_harness), applied uniformly in the tools/verify/*.cpp glob loop that registers every add_test call. Verified on WSL2/Ubuntu+Ninja (the single-config case this item is about; MSVC was never affected). Real measurements: default-configure resolved to Release automatically (confirmed via CMakeCache.txt); an explicit -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug configure was preserved unchanged; 33/33 tests carry a TIMEOUT; the suite ran clean at 32/33 pass on both a Release and a from-scratch Debug build (only ai_skill_harness fails, on golden bands - BL-252, pre-existing, out of scope). Slowest Debug/-O0 runtimes measured: corp_terrain_matrix 20.16s (its 120s TIMEOUT is the tightest margin at ~6x), ai_skill_harness 11.00s, history_ladder_harness 8.18s, planetology_harness 7.45s, road_generation_harness 5.80s - all comfortably inside their tier. STALE-BASE GAP, RECONCILED ON MERGE 2026-08-01: the agent worktree was cut from a base predating BL-250 s econ_stability timing sweep and containing neither data_creep_harness.cpp nor font_glyph_harness.cpp, so it could not build or measure them and said so. The integrated tree has all three. Verified post-merge: tools/verify/ contains corp_terrain_matrix.cpp, econ_stability.cpp (with the BL-250 sweep), data_creep_harness.cpp and font_glyph_harness.cpp, and the tools/verify/*.cpp glob loop assigns each a TIMEOUT, so the three named long-runners inherit the 120s tier as intended. Their runtimes under the integrated tree have not been re-measured against those bounds; the integrating ctest run covers that.

BL-256.design:
REWRITTEN 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A, resolving NR-005). Supersedes the original 2026-08-01 filing, which framed the globe as a ~200 px sketch beside the charts with interaction explicitly out of scope. The projection design in that version was sound and is kept; what changes is the globe's STATUS on the screen, and the addition of panning and a pre-world view.

## What Ben asked for

"I just think it would be cool to see the world forming as a 3d shape with pan features. E.g. can't go above north pole or below south pole. For pre-world steps, we can show the solar system shape. That way, the expanded details are interesting mathematical extras on top of an immediate view of what the world will look like."

Three changes fall out of that, and the third is the one that reorders the screen:

1. **Pan**, clamped in latitude so the camera never passes either pole. No roll.
2. **A pre-world view.** Early rounds have no body to draw; show the solar system's shape instead, so the screen is never empty and the player always sees the thing being decided.
3. **The globe is the PRIMARY view; the charts are extras.** This is the real change. The wizard today is charts with prose; it becomes a world you look at, with the derivation available on top. The disclosure spine (BL-214) already supplies the fold idiom for exactly that relationship.

## Ben asked to be told if this is hard. Here is the honest read.

### It is not a 3D pipeline, and it must not become an argument for one

The app is ImGui over SDL_Renderer's 2D path — no depth buffer, no shaders — and TECH_FOUNDATIONS forbids swapping that out. None of this needs it, because the globe is drawn as a **per-pixel inverse projection into a texture**, not as projected geometry:

- For each pixel of an NxN disc, invert the orthographic projection to a (lat, lon) on the sphere; skip pixels outside the disc.
- Sample the source field at (lat, lon), shade, write RGBA. Upload once per frame and draw through ImGui's image path.

This is worth stating because the obvious alternative — projecting each tile as a polygon — is the one that breaks. That approach would put ~7,500 front-facing hexes at 6 vertices each against ImGui's 16-bit draw indices (65,535), which works at 90x42 and falls over at 180x84; and it would render polar rows as degenerate slivers, because a row-offset hex grid has no tile that IS the pole. Per-pixel sampling has no vertex budget at all, and the poles merely OVERSAMPLE the top row (smearing) instead of shattering. Do not "optimise" this into geometry.

### Risk 1 — how the poles actually look (the one that cannot be settled on paper)

The source is an equirectangular grid, 180 columns x 84 rows on the home body. Wrapped to a sphere, longitude compresses toward the poles, so the top and bottom rows smear across the cap. Ben's own pan constraint hides the worst of it — a camera that cannot pass the pole never looks straight down at it — but it is visible at high latitude and no amount of design settles whether it reads as "a planet" or "a texture bug".

Possible treatments, none chosen: a shaded ice cap drawn over the top few degrees (cheap, and physically plausible since those rows are polar anyway); latitude-weighted sampling; or simply accepting it.

### Risk 2 — CPU cost, which the ORIGINAL item got backwards

The first version warned that the continents pass was "the expensive half" and might not be affordable per control move. Reading the code says otherwise: `continents.cpp` is 231 lines of O(width x height x plates) work — roughly 180 x 84 x ~12 integer operations for the home body. That is sub-millisecond territory. **The generation half is probably not the cost; the DRAWING half might be.**

A 200 px sketch is ~31k lit pixels per frame. A primary view at 600 px is ~283k, each needing an inverse projection (asin/atan2 or equivalent) plus a sample and a shade. At 60 fps that is the frame's dominant cost and could plausibly run into milliseconds.

The fix is structural rather than clever, and should be designed in from the start: **the pixel -> (lat, lon) mapping depends only on the disc size and the camera LATITUDE**. Rotation is a longitude ADD. So cache a lookup table of per-pixel (lat, lon0) and rebuild it only when the size or the pan latitude changes — spinning then costs one addition and one sample per pixel, and panning costs a rebuild only while the drag is happening.

Measure before assuming either way. The point of stating this is that the cost lives somewhere the first version did not look.

### Risk 3 — the pre-world view is a different object

`solar_system_canvas` exists, but it is a 2D top-down diagram of orbits, not a 3D scene. Dropping it in for the early rounds gives the screen two visual languages: a diagram, then a globe. That may be fine — they genuinely are different things, and a system IS better read from above — but it is a deliberate call, not an oversight, and STARTUP.md should say which it is.

### What is genuinely cheap

- **Pan with a latitude clamp.** Two floats and a clamp; the projection already takes a camera basis.
- **"The world forming."** The per-pass intermediates already exist — `generate_body_tiles` takes an optional `generation_record`, which is the same data GENERATION_LEDGER.md is built on. Showing height, then ocean, then bands, then composition is a matter of choosing which field to sample, not of new generation work.

## Sequencing — the prototype comes first, and not in the wizard

**Task 1: prove the projection against the ALREADY-GENERATED world.** Draw the globe from a live `world`, in a throwaway debug window, on a machine Ben can look at. This puts the pole artifact and the real frame cost in front of him in an afternoon, using data that already exists.

Everything else is contingent on that. If the poles read badly the whole direction changes shape, and any wizard integration built first is wasted. Do not start at the startup flow.

**Task 2 onward** (only after task 1 is seen): the wizard preview chain, the field-per-stage progression, the pan clamp, the solar-system view for pre-world rounds, and the layout inversion that demotes the charts.

## The tier question, revised

The original item proposed two fidelities — a characterisation globe from planetology scalars (Tier 1) and a real-landmass globe that also runs continents plus tile Pass 1 (Tier 2) — and recommended building both. Ben's framing wants the real planet as the immediate view, so **Tier 2 is the target** and Tier 1 survives only for rounds where the landmass genuinely is not decided yet.

That distinction still has to be VISIBLE. A globe showing generic banding in round 1 and real continents in round 3 without saying so teaches the player something false — the same lying-figure objection Ben applied to markets in BL-263. Caption which one is on screen.

## Determinism

Unchanged, and load-bearing. The globe reads generated state and never writes it. Rotation is wall-clock and confined to the shading pass; it must not reach any field the world samples. If the preview runs the continents/height pass, it must be the SAME deterministic pass real generation runs, seeded identically — a globe showing a planet the campaign then does not produce is worse than no globe.

## Open calls

1. **Does pan persist across rounds**, or reset when the preview re-runs? Persisting is friendlier; resetting makes each round's globe comparable.
2. **The pole treatment** — cap, weighted sampling, or accept. Answer after task 1, not before.
3. **Whether the solar-system view is a diagram or a projection.** See risk 3.
4. **Where the charts go** once demoted — folded under the globe, a side rail, or a separate round.

## Not in scope

Any 3D rendering pipeline or renderer change. Zoom, click-through, or selection on the globe. Reuse on the in-game canvases (CANVASES.md owns those; the zoom ladder is settled). Cities, borders, buildings or any post-generation overlay.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the four open calls

Taken in the order the item lists them. Call 2 is settled as a *procedure* rather than an
answer, because the item is right that it cannot be answered on paper — but a scheduled
decision with a stated fallback is settled enough to promote, whereas an open one is not.

### 1. Pan PERSISTS across rounds; it resets only when the SEED changes

The item offered persist (friendlier) versus reset (each round comparable). Persist wins, and
the framing that decides it is the item's own: this is **one world being formed**, not a
sequence of separate globes. A camera that snaps back each time a pass completes makes the
same planet look like a different one every few seconds — the viewer reads a cut, not a
refinement, which undoes the exact thing the globe is for.

The comparability argument is real but is answered better another way: the passes overlay the
**same geometry**, so the player compares by watching a fixed frame change, not by having the
frame re-established for them. Holding the camera still is what makes the comparison possible;
resetting it is what breaks it.

There is also a plainer reason. Pan is a deliberate player action, and silently undoing a
player's action on a timer is the kind of thing that reads as a bug even when it is
intentional.

**Reset when the seed changes** — a new seed is a genuinely different world and there is
nothing to hold the camera on. That is the only reset.

### 2. Pole treatment — a MEASUREMENT with a stated fallback, not a design call

Unchanged in substance: this is answered after task 1, by looking. What is settled is that it
cannot stall the item.

The three candidates are already enumerated (shaded ice cap over the top few degrees;
latitude-weighted sampling; accept it), so Ben's decision is a **pick from three**, not a
fresh design conversation — which is the difference between a scheduled call and an open one.

**Fallback, if the artifact is inconclusive or nobody wants to decide: ACCEPT.** Do nothing.
The pan clamp already hides the worst of it by construction (a camera that cannot pass the
pole never looks straight down at one), and both treatments are purely additive later — a cap
is a shaded overlay on top of a working globe, not a change to the projection. Shipping
"accept" therefore costs nothing but a possible revisit, while blocking on the question costs
the whole item. Choose the treatment if the artifact makes it obvious; otherwise ship and move.

### 3. The solar-system view is a DIAGRAM, deliberately — and STARTUP.md says so

The item flags that using `solar_system_canvas` for pre-world rounds gives the screen two
visual languages, and asks whether that is a call or an oversight. It is a call, and the right
one.

**The two subjects genuinely differ, and the diagram is the better read of its own subject.**
What the pre-world rounds decide is orbits, body count and spacing — and an oblique 3D view of
a solar system *hides* spacing, which is the one thing those rounds are choosing. A top-down
diagram shows it directly. Rendering the system as a perspective scene would be prettier and
strictly less informative, which is the trade the whole item argues against elsewhere (the
lying-figure objection in the tier question).

**It is also nearly free.** `solar_system_canvas.{hpp,cpp}` already exists and already draws
this. Building a second, 3D-ish system view means new code whose only merit is matching a
visual language the globe has not established yet.

**The transition is a feature.** Diagram giving way to globe is the moment the world starts
existing. That is worth reading as an event rather than smoothing away — it marks the same
boundary the tier caption (below) has to state in words anyway.

Record it in STARTUP.md as a deliberate two-language screen with the reason, so the next
reader does not "unify" it.

### 4. The charts fold — BL-265's vocabulary, no new machinery

"Interesting mathematical extras on top of an immediate view" is exactly the relationship the
disclosure spine already models, and BL-265 has just settled the control vocabulary for it. So
the demoted charts need no new disclosure concept at all:

- Each chart rests as a **folded verdict row** — one line saying what it concluded.
- `⌄` expands that chart **in place**, beside the globe, which is the common case.
- `›` takes the **canvas** for it, and per BL-265 change 3 a full-canvas accordion shows
  *every* chart scrolled — which is the old charts-first screen, now available on demand
  rather than imposed.

That last point is worth stating plainly: **demoting the charts does not remove the
charts-first view, it puts it one control away.** The item is a re-ranking of defaults, not a
deletion, and framing it that way should defuse any worry about losing the derivation.

**Adds a dependency on BL-265** (disclosure controls revision), which supplies `⌄`/`›` and the
right-gutter rule. Without it this item would have to invent its own expander, which is the
per-surface reinvention BL-214 existed to end.

**Left for Ben's eye, and only this:** whether the folded chart rows sit **under** the globe or
in a **right-hand rail** beside it. Both work with the fold idiom, the difference is only which
one keeps the globe largest at 1280x720, and it is a five-minute experiment once the globe
renders — not a paragraph. Ask with the live app open (both variants built), not with a
mockup.

### Sequencing is unchanged and still load-bearing

Task 1 (prove the projection against the already-generated world, in a throwaway debug window)
comes first and everything else is contingent on it. None of the four settlements above
weakens that — call 2 explicitly depends on it, and calls 1/3/4 are cheap to honour whatever
the prototype shows.

## Task 1 ruled done 2026-08-09 (NR-089, Ben)

The wizard preview pane landed 2026-08-08 (BL-319) — a hex-sampled orthographic globe of the actual generated surface, byte-parity verified against make_hard_coded_world — is ruled to BE this item's task-1 projection proof, promoted from the planned throwaway debug window into the real wizard. Remaining slice: player-controlled pan with pole clamp, the measured pole-treatment call (cap / weighted-sampling / accept), the pre-world solar-system diagram stage, and folding the demoted charts through BL-265's disclosure vocabulary in place of the fixed 1/3:2/3 split.
BL-256.resolution: Complete as of 2026-08-10, with ONE OF ITS THREE REQUIREMENTS DELIBERATELY CUT. Verified against the code at Ben's request rather than taken on trust. BUILT (2 of 3): the PRE-WORLD VIEW -- round 0 draws the system (star colour and size, orbits, body sizes) so the screen is never empty while there is no body to show; and THE GLOBE AS PRIMARY VIEW with the charts as extras on top, which is the screen reorder BL-319 landed as the 1/3 controls : 2/3 preview split. The globe reads the real homeworld tile raster once one exists. CUT: PAN. The item specified a camera the player could pan, clamped in latitude so it never passed either pole. Ben, 2026-08-10, on being shown that the built globe auto-spins instead: 'I personally prefer the spin over pan. It helps to show the player that generation is slightly beyond their reach.' THAT IS A DESIGN ARGUMENT, NOT A CONCESSION, and it is why this is recorded as cut rather than deferred. The wizard's whole model is PREFERENCES, NOT PARAMETERS -- a named lean per axis, resolved against a seed, with no raw generated value editable. A draggable globe would have handed the player a control the rest of the screen deliberately withholds, quietly contradicting the premise to add an affordance nobody needed. An uncontrollable globe says the same thing the preference model says: you set conditions here, you do not steer. WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD: the globe turns one revolution per minute on wall-clock time, frozen to 0 under --verify so a golden capture never races the animation. RENDER TECHNIQUE DIVERGES FROM THE DESIGN, harmlessly, and is recorded so the two do not read as disagreeing: the item proposed a per-pixel inverse projection into a texture; what was built is 48 meridian slices, each subdivided in latitude, every cell a quad. Both avoid the failure mode the design was written to dodge -- projecting ~7,500 hexes as polygons against ImGui's 16-bit draw indices -- and the slice path got there with less machinery. Authority propagated to docs/ui/STARTUP.md § The globe (BL-256), including the reasoning for the cut, so a future session does not re-file pan as a missing feature.

BL-257.design:
## Two halves, and the second one is load-bearing

### Half 1 (the hazard) — identity must stop being a display string

Randomising names without this is a silent correctness bug, not a cosmetic change. Known sites that compare a body name as identity:

- `src/world/hard_coded_world.cpp:256` — `if (be.name != "Kepler") continue;`
- `tools/verify/history_ladder_harness.cpp:140,141,236`
- `tools/verify/creeds_harness.cpp:135,136`

`world.home_body` already holds the homeworld entity id (`hard_coded_world.cpp:189`), so the homeworld case has a correct answer available today and simply is not used. Replace every name comparison with the entity id — or, where a harness needs "the tiled body" rather than "the home body" specifically, with an explicit role/flag on the body rather than a second name test.

**Do this half first and independently.** It is a strict improvement with or without generated names, and it means the naming change cannot introduce a regression. Re-survey with `grep -rn '.name *[=!]= *"' src/ tools/` before starting; the list above is from 2026-08-01 and filed prose goes stale.

### Half 2 — the name pool

`src/world/city_names.{hpp,cpp}` is the existing model and should be followed rather than reinvented: a deterministic pick from a curated pool, seeded, with no repeats within a world. Bodies want the same shape in `src/world/body_names.{hpp,cpp}`.

Constraints that make the result read as a real system rather than a shuffle:

- **Deterministic from the world seed.** Same seed, same names — this is the standing invariant, and the goldens depend on it.
- **No duplicates within a system**, including moons.
- **Moons should read as moons.** A moon of a named planet wants either a related name or a positional suffix; a moon drawn from the same flat pool as planets makes the system read as a bag of words.
- **Register/tone. SETTLED 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW NR-006): a DELIBERATE MIX, governed by a rule.** Not one register for everything, and not a random draw across three. The registers stay — mythological, descriptive, scientist-eponym — but which one a body gets is DECIDED by what the body is, so the mixing is legible rather than noisy. Ben: "a deliberate mix is great."

  The reason this beats a single register: a rule the player can half-perceive reads as a world with a HISTORY of being named — different bodies named by different people for different reasons, which is what a real catalogue looks like — where one uniform register reads as a generator. The player never has to articulate the rule for it to work; they only have to sense that the names are not arbitrary.

  **The rule itself is the residual call and is NOT settled.** Proposed, for Ben to accept or replace at promotion: planets take the MYTHOLOGICAL register (named first, from a distance, by people who could only see lights); moons take DESCRIPTIVE names (named later, close up, by whoever surveyed them); and the SCIENTIST-EPONYM register is reserved for whatever was catalogued rather than observed — which today would be the home body, Kepler, and would explain why it is the odd one out rather than making it an inconsistency to fix. Whatever rule is chosen, write it into the doc so a later session extending the pool extends it the same way; an unstated rule decays into the noise it was meant to prevent.

## Verification

`world_audit` and the determinism harnesses must stay green — this touches world generation, so a same-seed regeneration must produce identical names, and the harnesses that previously found bodies by name must find them by id. `history_ladder_harness` and `creeds_harness` both need updating as part of the change, not after it.

## Not in scope

Renaming nations, cities or corporations (city names already have their own generator). Player-editable body names. Any change to how many bodies exist — the count knob is fixed at 5 and phased to a later update (STARTUP.md).
BL-257.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.10). Both halves, in that order, exactly as the item insisted. HALF 1 -- identity stops being a display string -- FOUND TWELVE SITES, EIGHT MORE THAN THE FOUR THE ITEM LISTED. `generation_report::body_entry` gained `entity_id id` and `bool is_homeworld`; every name comparison now reads one of those. Beyond the four named: `history_log.cpp:147` (seed_genesis_history matched report entries to world bodies BY NAME), `tile_inspector.cpp:160` (biography lookup), `tile_inspector.cpp:234/254/267` -- THE AGES SIM CACHE KEY WAS THE BODY NAME, so generated names would have made a cache collision a live possibility -- `body_surface_canvas.cpp:1249` (Continent lens plate lookup), `app.cpp`'s select_body Lua binding, and four harness `kepler_of()` helpers. `grep -rn '.name *[=!]= *"' src/ tools/verify/` now returns nothing. This half is why the item said do it first and independently: shipping half 2 without it would have been a silent correctness bug, not a cosmetic change. HALF 2 -- `src/world/body_names.{hpp,cpp}` coins the whole catalogue from ONE tongue via `roll_tongue` + `coin_lexicon` + `tongue_word` (BL-290's module), so bodies are not a fourth naming bank. AN HONEST ARCHITECTURAL LIMIT, volunteered rather than glossed: it could NOT use a CULTURE's tongue. Cradle cultures do not exist until the creeds pass, which needs the homeworld's tiles, which needs the planetology chain -- and the chain WRITES BODY NAMES INTO THE BIOGRAPHY PROSE it emits (planetology.cpp:809,819). Naming after creeds would have left that prose stale. So the sky-watchers' tongue is rolled from the world seed before anything runs: it shares the machinery and the sound SYSTEM, not one specific culture's inventory. REGISTER RULE (each register wears a different shape, so the mix is perceptible): star and planets take one bare coined word; a moon takes a coined qualifier plus its parent's name; the home body takes a root plus the tongue's own place morpheme; asteroids take a coined word plus a catalogue index. SAMPLE -- seed 0: star Suto, planet Harsursur, home Huhaidar, moon Zair Huhaidar, asteroid Tatar 1. Seed 42: star Hidivi, home Kamduahein, moon Veve Kamduahein. Seed 90210: star Zemegem, home Kheirmeizeir. Seed 7 comes out repetitive (Shithhiththi) when the tongue rolls a thin inventory -- the same characteristic BL-290's nation names have, not a new defect. VERIFY SCRIPTS MADE SEED-PROOF: all 28 now address bodies by ROLE (home/star/moon/asteroid/inner) through `find_body`, never by display name -- so a generated catalogue cannot break a check again. Determinism confirmed three ways: world_audit's new BL-257 R1/R2 (uniqueness, same-seed catalogue), body_names_harness B1 across 8 seeds, and the two determinism harnesses unchanged. All key harnesses green after the merge. KNOWN AND NOT DONE: (1) VISUAL GOLDENS ARE STALE wherever a body name renders -- confirmed by eye as a pure text delta (8.1% / 3.7% on descend_into_selection). Per BL-252 visual goldens are Windows-authoritative, so the re-bless is Ben's, on Windows. (2) `body_names_harness` is not registered in the verifier-headless skill; skill edits need Ben's permission. (3) `history_sim_harness` could not be closed out -- 6 failures present before and after, but it is a `sweep`-labelled open-ended research tool that never finishes, so no clean baseline was obtained and none is claimed.

BL-258.design:
FOUND 2026-08-01 by the integrating ctest run of the v0.1.0 cut set, on Windows.

## The observation

`econ_stability` fails exactly one assertion on the Windows `build/` tree:

    FAIL  R6 the largest swept world (8 bodies, 256 corps, 128x prototype) still ticks under 1 ms

Everything around it passes, which is what makes the diagnosis clean:

- R5 (prototype-scale tick under 1 ms) PASSES, with **19x headroom** — mean 0.0524 ms.
- R6 growth exponent PASSES (no worse than size^1.5).
- R6 no-single-doubling-costs-4x PASSES.
- R6 finiteness PASSES.
- The same assertion PASSES on Linux/GCC in a Release build (35/35 green).

So the SHAPE assertions — the ones that would catch a real algorithmic regression — all hold. The only failure is the single ABSOLUTE wall-clock bound, at the largest swept rung.

## The cause, and why BL-255 did not close it

The Windows `build/` tree is configured `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` — deliberately, since it is the tree used for debugging the app. A -O0 build is routinely 5-10x slower, which is the whole reason BL-250's absolute bound cannot hold there.

BL-255 fixed the adjacent hazard: a single-config generator with NO build type specified now defaults to Release. It cannot help here, because Debug is not unset — it is chosen. The two are different failure modes and BL-255 correctly did not claim this one.

## Why this matters

"Headless harnesses green" is part of the v0.1.0 done-definition. Today that phrase is false on the Windows tree a developer actually works in, for a reason that has nothing to do with the economy loop. That is the same class of problem BL-252 just fixed for the goldens: an assertion whose truth depends on how the tree happens to be configured teaches the reader to ignore a red result, which is exactly how a real regression gets waved through.

## The fix — gate the absolute bound, keep the shape assertions

The absolute-time assertion is only meaningful against an optimised build. It should either:

1. **Skip with a loud, explicit message** when the build is unoptimised (`#ifndef NDEBUG`, or read the configured build type), printing something like `SKIP R6 absolute tick bound - unoptimised build, timing is not meaningful` rather than silently passing; or
2. **Assert a Debug-specific, generously-scaled bound**, if a number can be defended.

Option 1 is preferred and matches the project's existing standard for this exact situation: the data-creep instrument (BL-251/BL-254) reports a vacuous check AS vacuous rather than as a pass. A skipped-and-said-so check is worth more than a green tick, and far more than a red one everybody learns to ignore.

**Do not simply widen the 1 ms bound to accommodate Debug.** That would destroy its value in Release, where it is the number the ROADMAP actually cares about. The growth-shape assertions must keep running in both configurations — they are dimensionless and hold regardless of optimisation.

## Not in scope

Changing the Windows tree to Release, or the economy loop's performance. The measured Release numbers are healthy (0.0018 ms/tick at prototype scale, 555x headroom) and `run_corp_strategic_step`'s O(corps x tiles) scan is already filed separately as BL-253.
BL-258.resolution: Gated R6 absolute tick bound (Windows Debug tree) behind #ifndef NDEBUG — skips with a loud SKIP line citing BL-258 rather than failing red or silently passing. Release/optimised builds still assert the real 1ms bound. All 36 CTest harnesses green on Windows. Landed 2026-08-02.

BL-259.design:
FOUND 2026-08-01 while verifying the disclosure-spine batch (BL-214/247/248), and deliberately NOT absorbed into it.

## The finding

A full sweep of scripts/verify/*.lua fails golden diff on the large majority of checks - including many that the batch never touched (canvas_levels 2.4-4.3%, commercial_fog 2.4%, chat_panel 39.6%, balance_ledger 39.5%, building_management_tile_player 48.5%).

Inspecting the diff images settles the cause: the differing pixels are WORLD CONTENT, not layout. Terrain colour across the whole Planetary canvas, generated corporation names and balances, nation names in the comms feed, per-tile deposit figures. The chrome is where the goldens left it.

## Why

The goldens were last blessed in 6b8e109 (2026-07-30, "after comms move, strip re-height, continent lens"). src/world/ has changed twice since:

- 947284a (2026-07-31) - BL-233 terrain combat modifiers, which DELETED is_barrier and re-priced conquest from the graded terrain field. Its own resolution notes it was swept to hold the political map at 30 Kepler nations; changing the political map changes generated names, balances and terrain.
- 9360d2d / 9316eaf (2026-08-01) - the tile construction ledger world-layer estimator and a depleted-tile fix.

BL-252 re-blessed the HEADLESS bands per toolchain and declared visual goldens Windows-authoritative, and b54e0f9 re-blessed four tile-build-ledger goldens - but the visual suite as a whole was never re-established after the world moved. So "headless harnesses green" has a visual-side counterpart that is currently false and has been for two days.

## Why it is a v0.1.0 item

The cut gate names a green suite. A visual suite that fails ~30 checks for a reason nobody has written down is indistinguishable, on the next run, from a real regression - which is exactly the failure mode BL-252 was raised to fix on the headless side. It is cheap (a bless_all sweep plus an eyeball of the largest diffs) and it closes a hole in a cut gate.

## The work

1. Eyeball the largest diffs (building_management_tile_player 48.5%, chat_panel 39.6%, balance_ledger 39.5%) to confirm each is world content and not a real UI regression hiding in the noise.
2. Re-bless the whole suite through the software renderer (scripts/verify/bless_all.sh), Windows-authoritative per BL-252.
3. Add the missing discipline to DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md: a change to src/world/ that moves generated content obliges a visual re-bless in the SAME commit, the way a headless band change already does. That rule is what stops this recurring - the staleness here was not an oversight in any one commit, it was nobody owning the coupling.

Not in scope: the three checks blessed by the disclosure-spine batch (drill_through_fold, chart_question_log, corp_dashboard) are current and passing.
BL-259.resolution: Re-blessed the full 229-golden visual suite (bless_all.sh, software renderer) after eyeballing the largest diffs (level_1_planetary 10.4%, chat_panel, balance_ledger) confirmed as world content — terrain colour and generated corp/nation names shifted by BL-233 (2026-07-31), not a UI regression. Added the missing discipline to DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md § Golden staleness: a src/world/ change that reshapes generated output owes a visual re-bless in the same commit, mirroring the existing chrome-change rule.

BL-260.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-01 (Ben, during the NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass — see NR-010).

## Where this came from

BL-247 (chart question log) landed with three questions left "open for the promoting session". One was answered without Ben: is a question/why pair REQUIRED on every chart, or optional with a missing pair simply drawing no toggle? The promoting session chose OPTIONAL, so the log is advisory, and recommended a report-only verify pass as a middle road.

Ben overturned both (2026-08-01): "we need to have documentation for each element. For development, I think it's a low storage cost for perpetual clarity. So the docs are the audit, we don't need an audit method or arbitrary resolution."

So: the pair is REQUIRED; enforcement is authorship, not machinery; and NO headless or report-only audit check is to be built. A surface without a justification is a defect a human notices by reading the store, which is the point of the store existing.

## The three changes this makes to BL-247 as landed

1. **Required, not optional.** Every information surface carries a question/why pair.
2. **Every ELEMENT, not every chart.** Ben confirmed the wider reading explicitly: not only things that plot. A table, a ledger, a roll-up card and a panel each answer a question, and each must state it. This is the scope expansion — BL-247's file scope named charts.cpp / generation_charts.cpp / selection_panel.cpp.
3. **The justification moves OUT of the call site into JSON**, and carries the id of the backlog item that demanded the surface. Today the strings are C++ literals passed to `why_note(ui, answers, because)`.

## The provenance requirement (Ben's addition)

"it's going to be important to tie each justification to the backlog item which demanded it."

This is the part that makes the store more than relocated text. With a `backlog_item` on every entry the log becomes a queryable provenance index in both directions:

- Surface -> item: why does this exist, and what asked for it.
- Item -> surface: what did this item actually put on screen.

It also exposes the two gaps neither backlog.json nor user_stories.json can currently show: a surface no item ever demanded (unjustified UI), and an item that claims a UI outcome but owns no surface. That is the same coverage argument USER_STORIES.md makes on the intent axis, applied to the surface axis.

## OPEN — the file shape (Ben has not chosen; do not guess)

Ben wrote "in its own .json file", which has two readings:

- **A — one store.** `docs/ui/question_log.json`, entries keyed by element id, each with `answers` / `because` / `backlog_item` / `files`. Consistent with backlog.json / user_stories.json / requirements.json, and a coverage query is one read.
- **B — one file per element.** `docs/ui/questions/<element>.json`. The literal reading; diffs stay local to the element, but a coverage query walks a directory.

Recommended A on consistency with the existing stores, but this is Ben's call and the item must not be promoted before he makes it.

## OPEN — the load seam

`why_note` takes `const char*`. If the strings live in JSON there are two ways in, and this needs a call rather than a default:

- **Codegen at build time** — a generated header of string literals. Keeps the runtime free of file IO and a missing entry is a BUILD failure, which is the strongest form of "the docs are the audit" that does not require a separate check. Costs a build step.
- **Runtime load** — parse the store at startup, look up by element id. Simpler build, but a missing entry becomes a silent empty note at runtime, which is exactly the failure the required-pair rule exists to prevent.

Codegen is the better fit for Ben's stated position, precisely because it makes the omission loud without adding an audit tool.

## The backfill roster (measured 2026-08-01)

Pairs exist today on three surfaces only — `generation_charts.cpp` (the wizard chart rows), `corporation_dashboard.cpp` (4 roll-up cards) and `selection_card.cpp` (2).

Carrying NO pair: `market_ledger.cpp`, `economy_panel.cpp`, `balance_ledger.cpp`, `tile_inspector.cpp`, `construction_panel.cpp`, `tech_tree_panel.cpp`, `profile_panel.cpp`, `chat_panel.cpp`, `header_panel.cpp`, `hover_card.cpp`, `nav_pane.cpp`, `entity_summary.cpp`, `selection_panel.cpp`.

The roster is the real cost of this item, and the writing is Ben's rather than an implementer's: authoring the pair IS the design check BL-247 named. An implementer can build the store, the seam and the migration of the 11 existing pairs; the backfill text for a surface should be drafted for Ben to accept or rewrite, not invented and left.

## Not in scope

- Any audit/lint/verify check over the store. Explicitly rejected by Ben — the docs are the audit.
- Changing what `why_note` DRAWS (closed-by-default toggle, one note at a time, reset on expand/fold). That behaviour landed with BL-247 and is unchanged here.
- The player-facing wording standard. "Answers" is a real question a player would ask; "Because" is one plain sentence. Also unchanged.

## LATER THE SAME DAY — the log is DEVELOPMENT documentation, not a player surface (NR-018)

Ben, 2026-08-01: "the why shouldn't leak into the UI, players don't need us telling them what they ought to ask of the game."

This retires the PLAYER-FACING half of BL-247. That item had a dual audience — a closed-by-default in-game toggle, and Ben reading the log while designing. Only the second survives. It is a continuation of BL-247's own objection rather than a reversal of it: BL-247 already refused to curate which questions matter; this refuses to state the question in-game at all.

Consequences:

- **The load seam question above is largely MOOT.** If nothing renders in a player build, no codegen and no runtime load into the UI is required. The store is a documentation artifact read by humans and tooling. Keep the codegen option on the table ONLY if NR-018 lands on the development-gated reading.
- **The eleven live `why_note` call sites** (generation_charts, corporation_dashboard, selection_card) and the toggle in detail_level.cpp either come out or go behind a development-only gate. NR-018 carries that call and it is NOT settled.
- **LAYOUT.md must record the supersession.** BL-247's authority text describes a player-facing affordance; the toggle must not just quietly vanish from the app with the doc still promising it.
- **The wording standard changes audience.** "Answers" no longer has to be phrased as a question a player would ask; it is a question the DESIGNER asks of the surface. Warmer, less careful phrasing is fine — nobody is reading it in-game.

This also removes the last reason to prefer any particular draw-helper location — see NR-011, kept but moot.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the store is a UX_QUESTIONS pair, and there is no code

Ben: "Just use the .md and .json structure. We can keep a UX_QUESTIONS pair of files."

So option A, in the project's existing shape:

- **`docs/development/UX_QUESTIONS.json`** — canonical. One entry per information surface.
- **`docs/development/UX_QUESTIONS.md`** — the readable mirror, GENERATED, never hand-edited.

This closes both questions that were open. The file shape is one store, matching `backlog.json`/`BACKLOG.md` and `user_stories.json`/`USER_STORIES.md`. The load-seam question is **void**: NR-018 removed the in-game draw path entirely, so nothing loads these strings at runtime and no codegen is needed. This item now touches NO `src/` file at all — it is a documentation artifact and a renderer.

### Entry shape

Follow the sibling stores rather than inventing fields. Per entry:

- `id` — a stable slug for the surface (e.g. `corp_rollup_production`).
- `surface` — where it lives, in human terms.
- `answers` — the question this surface answers, phrased as a real question.
- `because` — one plain sentence on why this evidence settles it.
- `backlog_item` — **the id of the item that demanded the surface.** Ben's requirement, and the thing that makes this a provenance index rather than relocated prose.
- `files` — the TU(s) that draw it.

### The renderer

`tools/session/render_ux_questions.js`, modelled on `tools/session/render_needs_review.js` (written 2026-08-02, same session, same reason). A mirror kept by hand drifts the moment a pass edits entries in bulk, and a stale mirror is worse than none because it still reads as authoritative.

### Seeding it

The 22 pairs authored for BL-247 are the seed and are recoverable wholesale from commit **d143aa4** — `generation_charts.cpp` (16 chart rows), `corporation_dashboard.cpp` (4 roll-up cards), `selection_card.cpp` (2 tile metrics). They were deliberately NOT harvested into a file at removal time, because doing so would have pre-decided this question.

### The backfill is still the bulk of the work

Thirteen surfaces have never had a pair: `market_ledger`, `economy_panel`, `balance_ledger`, `tile_inspector`, `construction_panel`, `tech_tree_panel`, `profile_panel`, `chat_panel`, `header_panel`, `hover_card`, `nav_pane`, `entity_summary`, `selection_panel`. Draft each for Ben to accept or rewrite — authoring the pair IS the design check, so an invented one that nobody reads defeats the purpose.

### Audience note, now that nothing renders

`answers` no longer has to be phrased as a question a PLAYER would ask; the reader is the designer. Plainer, blunter phrasing is fine — and a surface whose honest entry is "nothing, really" has just told you something.
BL-260.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.9). Both open questions ruled by Ben the same day: ONE store file, and codegen at build time. The store is docs/ui/question_log.json (canonical) with docs/ui/QUESTION_LOG.md generated by tools/session/render_question_log.js; 16 surfaces carry answers/because/backlog_item/files, giving the two-way provenance index Ben asked for. Registered in CLAUDE.md's document map. THE CODEGEN RULING IS RECORDED BUT NOT BUILT, and the reason is a stale premise this item carried rather than a decision reversed: BL-247's in-UI question log -- the per-chart Answers/Because toggle, and the `why_note` seam this item planned to feed -- was REMOVED on 2026-08-02 by NR-018. Verified at implementation: `why_note` does not exist anywhere in src/, there are no call sites to migrate, and generation_charts.hpp's `log_ui` parameter is explicitly 'Retained for call compatibility... Unused'. So there is no runtime consumer for a generated header to feed, and codegen whose output nothing includes is machinery for its own sake -- which is precisely what Ben's 'the docs are the audit, we don't need an audit method' rules out. The store is therefore a DOCUMENTATION artifact, which is the stronger reading of his position, and the codegen decision is recorded in the store's own _note so it is not re-litigated if a runtime consumer ever returns. NO VERIFY CHECK WAS BUILT, deliberately and per the item. The renderer validates parse/shape only and never fails on content. STATUS FIELD: 13 of the 16 entries are marked `drafted` and sorted to their own section at the top of the mirror, because BL-260 is explicit that the backfill text is Ben's to author -- writing the pair IS the design check BL-247 named -- so an implementer may draft it but must not ship it as settled. The 3 marked `settled` are the surfaces that carried real pairs before NR-018 removed the log (corporation_dashboard, selection_card, generation_charts). The 13 drafted entries are the item's remaining human cost and are visible as such rather than hidden.

BL-263.design:
DESIGN OWED — opened 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass, resolving NR-004).

## The finding that raised it

Every market seeds on the single tiled body (Kepler). MARKETS.md states it plainly: "Markets exist only on the home body (Kepler) today; Cinder, Selene, and Pallas carry none" and "Markets are fixed at world-gen — nothing creates or destroys one at runtime."

A `trade_route` is body-level, so an intra-body lane records nothing. Together those two facts mean the generated world CANNOT record a trade route however long it runs, independent of the launchpad gate. BL-254's data-creep harness had to author three stub markets before its run to give its convoy lanes endpoints at all — an instrument working around the world rather than measuring it, which is the signal that raised NR-004.

The player-visible half is NR-013: the BL-248 Trade roll-up correctly reads "0 lanes" on a fresh campaign, and would keep reading it forever.

## Ben's answer

"I think markets should be spontaneously generated when colonisation / exploration starts." (2026-08-01)

So none of NR-004's three options was taken. The premise is not "Era 0 has no off-world markets, document it" and not "pre-seed a market elsewhere" — it is that market EXISTENCE becomes a runtime consequence of the player (or a rival) going somewhere. A market is not scenery placed at world-gen; it is what appears once there is something to trade at a place.

That is a better answer than either option offered, and it is worth saying why: pre-seeding a market on an empty moon would have created a destination with no cause, which is the same lying-figure objection Ben raised against showing invented continents in the wizard preview (BL-256). Spontaneous generation keeps the world honest — a market exists exactly when the fiction says one would.

## What this changes structurally

Markets stop being a world-gen artifact and become simulation state. That is the load-bearing consequence and it touches:

- **Serialisation.** The save format must carry markets that did not exist at generation. Flat binary, per TECH_FOUNDATIONS — a count-prefixed run, not an assumption that market ids match generation order.
- **Determinism.** Creation must be a deterministic function of world state, not of iteration order. Sorted walks over any unordered container; an explicit tie-break if two candidate sites qualify on the same tick.
- **`market_for_tile` / `market_for_corp_on_body` catchment.** Both resolve against a fixed set today. A market appearing mid-campaign re-points catchment for tiles that previously had none — or, on the home body, potentially re-points tiles away from an existing centre. Decide whether new markets can ever steal catchment or only claim unserved ground.
- **Price discovery with no history.** `resolve_price` uses a price band and EMA smoothing over past prices. A market created on tick 400 has no past. Its opening prices have to come from somewhere — `base_price`, the nearest market, or the haul-distance pricing BL-191 already does for endemic goods.

## Open calls — Ben's

1. **The TRIGGER.** "When colonisation / exploration starts" needs a mechanical reading. Candidates: the first building placed on a body; a population presence; a completed convoy arrival; a survey (BL-067) completing. The choice decides whether a market is a consequence of INVESTMENT (a building) or of PRESENCE (a visit), and those give very different games.
2. **WHO can cause one.** Player only, any corporation, or a nation. If rivals can, the activity fog (BL-089) has to say whether the player learns of a market they did not create — a market appearing on a body the player has never visited is either intelligence they should not have, or a good reason to go and look.
3. **ONE market per body, or the resource-carved multi-market model (BL-096) applied off-world?** The carved model is population-anchored, and an off-world outpost has effectively none. One market per body is the simple reading and probably right until population exists off-world.
4. **Does a market ever DISAPPEAR?** If the last building on a body is decommissioned, does its market persist with stale prices, or vanish? Persisting is kinder to the activity fog's Stale tier (DISCOVERY.md) and avoids a save-format edge; vanishing is truer.
5. **What CLEARS there.** The clearing model is fed by production and population demand. An outpost market has supply and nearly no local demand, so without inter-body flow its prices collapse to the floor immediately. This is the question most likely to make the feature read as broken on first play, and it should be answered before implementation rather than discovered.

## Consequences for existing items

- **BL-254 (data-creep convoy scenario)** — its harness pre-authors three stub markets to work around exactly this. Once markets can emerge, decide whether the harness drives the real trigger instead of stubbing, which would make it a genuine end-to-end check rather than a synthetic one.
- **NR-013 / BL-248** — the Trade roll-up stops being permanently zero, which removes the "dashboard quarter that always says nothing" problem without a UI change.
- **BL-088 (persistent trade routes) / BL-089 (activity fog)** — both describe machinery that currently has nothing to act on. This is the item that gives them a first cause.
- **ERAS.md** — Era 0 being terrestrial is unchanged; this item does not open space access, it says what happens to markets once access exists.

## Read before promoting

docs/economy/MARKETS.md (§ Market centres and seeding, § The clearing tick), docs/ui/DISCOVERY.md (activity fog + competitor visibility), docs/economy/ERAS.md, src/world/hard_coded_world.cpp (the BL-096 seeding pass), and BL-254.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the five open calls, answered as one model

### 1. TRIGGER — the first BUILDING placed on a body. Investment, not presence.

The item frames the choice exactly: investment or presence, "and those give very different
games". Investment wins on three counts.

**A market needs something to trade.** A visit produces nothing to clear, so a
presence-triggered market opens empty and stays empty until someone builds anyway — the
trigger fires early and the feature does not start working until the building lands regardless.
Investment makes the trigger and the first useful moment the same moment.

**Placement is already a clean mechanical event.** It is validated, deterministic, and
single-tick — `market appears on the tick the first building completes` needs no new concept.
"Exploration starts" would need defining (a convoy arriving? a survey completing? a unit
entering?), and each candidate is a different fuzzy edge.

**It is the better game.** A market that appears because someone committed capital is a
consequence the player caused; one that appears because someone looked is scenery with a
delayed spawn. Ben's own objection to pre-seeding — a destination with no cause — applies
almost as strongly to presence.

Survey completion (BL-067) is explicitly **not** the trigger. Surveying is the geographic fog;
market existence is commercial. Keeping them separate preserves DISCOVERY.md's two-independent-
axes rule.

### 2. WHO — any corporation. And the player does NOT automatically learn of it.

Restricting creation to the player would make rivals scenery, which contradicts the whole
premise of competing corporations.

The activity fog answers the intelligence half, and this is where the item's worry resolves
