into a feature: **a market created by a rival on a body the player has never visited enters at
the fog's Unknown tier.** The player does not learn of it for free. They learn by going, by a
trade route reaching it, or not at all.

That is the same argument BL-262 (scoring) settles on: information the player is entitled to
is what the surfaces show, and anything else makes BL-089 decorative. It also gives the fog its
first genuinely consequential secret — a rival market you have not found is a real
disadvantage, not a greyed tile.

### 3. ONE market per body off-world

BL-096's resource-carved multi-market model is **population-anchored**, and an off-world outpost
has effectively no population to anchor to. Carving with no population is carving on an
arbitrary axis.

One market per body off-world; the home body keeps its carved multi-market seeding unchanged.
Revisit if and when off-world population exists — at which point the carved model applies for
the reason it was designed, rather than by analogy.

### 4. DISAPPEAR — no. It persists and goes dormant.

Three reasons, in increasing order of weight:

1. **The fog already has the concept.** DISCOVERY.md's **Stale** tier is exactly "this existed,
   my information is old". A dormant market is what Stale is for.
2. **It avoids a save-format edge.** Deleting markets means either id reuse (which will
   eventually alias two different markets across a save/load) or tombstones (which is
   persistence with extra steps). Count-prefixed runs of live markets is simpler than either.
3. **It is truer, not less true.** The item calls vanishing "truer"; it is not. An abandoned
   exchange does not become a place that never traded. Prices go stale, nobody clears, the
   record remains — which is what actually happens to a market town when the mine closes.

Surface it as **dormant**, not as an active market with frozen prices — a market showing last
quarter's prices as if current is a lying figure.

### 5. WHAT CLEARS — remote demand, and haul-distance opening prices

This is the call the item flags as most likely to make the feature read as broken, and it is
right: an outpost has supply and almost no local demand, so a market clearing only against
local population collapses to the floor on tick one.

**An outpost market clears primarily against INTER-BODY demand** — the pull of the home body's
markets through convoy routes — not against local population. That is not a special case bolted
on; it is what an outpost market *is*. Nobody builds a mine on a moon to sell to the moon.

**Opening prices come from BL-191's haul-distance pricing, not from `base_price` and not from
EMA.** The machinery already exists for endemic goods, and it is the right source for the same
reason: a price at a distant body should reflect what it costs to get the good to where demand
is. `base_price` would open every outpost at the same price regardless of distance;
EMA cannot run with no history.

So the price-discovery hole the item names has an answer that adds no new mechanism: **seed from
haul-distance, then let EMA take over once there is history to smooth.**

### Consequences, confirmed

- **BL-254's harness should drive the real trigger** once this lands — place a building, get a
  market — which converts it from a synthetic check into a genuine end-to-end one. That is the
  whole reason NR-004 was raised.
- **NR-013 / BL-248's Trade roll-up** stops being permanently zero with no UI change.
- **BL-088 / BL-089** get their first cause, as the item says.
- **ERAS.md** unchanged — this says what happens to markets once access exists, not when access
  arrives.

### Determinism

Creation is a function of world state, evaluated at one fixed point in the tick, with a sorted
walk over bodies and an explicit tie-break if two qualify simultaneously. Market ids must be
allocated from a monotonic counter carried in the save, **not** from container size — the latter
aliases after any removal and is the exact bug the persist-don't-delete rule above already
avoids.
BL-263.resolution: 2026-08-11 — complete. All five of Ben's settled calls implemented as specified: TRIGGER is the first building COMPLETING on a body with no market (maybe_spawn_market, called from both construct_building's instant-completion path and run_construction's pacing-loop completion, not placement) — survey completion is explicitly not the trigger, keeping the geographic/commercial fogs independent. ANY corporation can cause one (no player-only gate); a rival-created market on an unvisited body relies on the existing activity fog (BL-089) for its Unknown-tier gating — no new fog code needed, since fog visibility already reads presence/routes, not market existence directly. ONE market per body off-world (checked via a market_for_body scan before spawning); the home body's BL-096 carved seeding is untouched. Markets NEVER disappear — no deletion code exists or was added; dormancy falls out of the ordinary zero-supply/zero-demand clearing case. Opening prices seeded from the home market's own base_price marked up by a distance proxy (|orbital_radius_au difference|, moon-approximated at its parent — NOT the precise tick-pure angular distance supply_system.cpp's convoy routing uses, which only matters for real haul cost/speed, not a price curve). WHAT CLEARS: new inject_interbody_demand pulls a distance-discounted slice of the home body's own unmet demand onto every outpost market each tick (economy.market_emergence in Lua), preventing the price-floor collapse the design flagged as the likeliest failure mode; existing dispatch_convoys physical routing is untouched and independent. New market_emergence_harness (16/16 PASS): no market before any building, spawn on completion, correct centre_tile, exact opening-price and pulled-demand formulas, no second market on a second building, no self-pull on the home market, and a graceful all-zero-price degenerate fixture with no home market (no crash). Full ProjectIo build clean; econ_harness/econ_stability/resource_chain_harness/determinism_harness/construction_harness/world_audit/construction_gate_harness/buildings_rework_harness/multi_building_tile_harness/population_demand_harness/habitability_tranche_harness/supply_advance/trade_routes_harness/commercial_fog_harness all rerun clean. ai_skill_harness rebuilt fresh and rerun: identical 8 failures to the BL-366-only baseline, confirming BL-263 (and BL-368) do not move those bands further — corrected an earlier stale-exe misreading, see NR-169. No save-format work: no general serialisation system exists yet in this codebase to extend (no src/world/serialisation.cpp), so that half of the design is deferred until the general save seam lands, not part of this item's scope. docs/economy/MARKETS.md gains § Spontaneous market emergence.

BL-265.design:
DESIGN OWED — opened 2026-08-02 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW NR-016). This revises the disclosure model BL-214 landed, in Ben's own words, after seeing it running.

## Where this came from

NR-016 asked Ben to look at three changed surfaces in the live app. His answer went past the review: "I didn't notice this. I like it, but..." — and then four changes, three of them structural.

## Change 1 — ONE control becomes TWO: expand, and full screen

BL-214 shipped a BINARY model on Ben's own 2026-07-31 supersession: folded is a verdict line plus one chevron, expanded is a full-screen overlay, nothing in between. He now wants the two behaviours separated into two controls:

- **Expand** — "should just show a single graph in place, or an accordion of graphs for more complex menus." In place. The surface grows where it sits; the rest of the screen keeps working.
- **Full screen** — the overlay, but see change 2 for what "full" now means.

This is close to the three-level Glance/Read/Study stepper that the binary supersession replaced, and the item should say so plainly rather than pretend it is new: the middle rung is being restored, because a full-screen takeover turned out to be too big a step for "I want to see this one chart properly". What is NOT restored is the stepper's single cycling control — these are two distinct affordances with two distinct meanings, which is what makes it legible where the stepper was not.

## Change 2 — full screen takes the CANVAS, not the whole window

"Full screen should actually just take the place of a canvas, rather than the entire view. I would prefer to see consistency in the UI really."

Today `fold_overlay_begin` covers the entire window — nav rail, header, time column, Selection band and all. Ben wants it bounded to the canvas region instead, leaving the shell chrome in place.

The argument is consistency, and it is a good one: the canvas region is already the app's main stage, and the zoom ladder (CANVASES.md) already swaps what occupies it. A ledger going full screen would then be the same KIND of event as descending the ladder, using the same rectangle, instead of a second full-window mode with its own rules. It also means the player never loses the header, the clock or their selection — which today they do.

Consequence to design, not discover: the Esc ladder (BL-214 Decision 10, overridden per NR-009) and `any_expanded`/`fold` currently assume one window-wide overlay at a time. A canvas-bounded overlay may coexist with the fold-out ledger column, so "only one thing can be expanded" needs restating against the new geometry.

## Change 3 — a full-screened accordion must scroll ALL its items

"When we full screen an accordion, it turns into a vertical scroll of all items. Anything full screen deserves its full space."

Today expanding one stage of the History Chain gives that stage the screen and leaves its siblings folded behind the overlay. Ben wants the full-screen view of an accordion to be the WHOLE accordion, scrolled — every item open, top to bottom.

The principle he states is the general one and should govern the whole family: a surface that has taken the largest rectangle available has no excuse for showing a subset. Applies at least to the History Chain's stages, the wizard's per-round stages, and the corporation dashboard's four roll-ups.

## Change 4 — the controls live in ONE column, always

"Let's make sure that these buttons are right aligned, opposite to text, it is disorienting when a button is not in the same column, but does the same job."

The complaint is exact, and the code confirms it — placement is currently split across call sites:

- **LEFT of the label:** `generation_charts.cpp` (wizard stage rows) and `corporation_dashboard.cpp` (roll-up card rows) draw the chevron first, then the title.
- **RIGHT edge:** `tile_inspector.cpp` (History view-level) and `selection_panel.cpp` (Selection metric card) push the chevron to the far right with a `SameLine` offset.

So the same control does the same job in two different places on screen depending on which surface you are looking at. That is the disorientation, and it is a real defect rather than a taste question.

### RESOLVED — which column (see the settled vocabulary at the end of this item)

Ben appeared to give both answers in the same message — **left aligned** for the wizard chevrons (BL-264) and **right aligned, opposite to text** for the pair here. He then clarified that these were two different contexts rather than two rules, and the vocabulary at the end of this item is the settled result. Recorded because the apparent contradiction is instructive: the left-aligned control he had in mind was the RETURN control of a takeover view, not a row's expander.

Considerations for whoever asks him:

- **Left** wins on travel (the control is where the eye already is, next to the label it governs) and is what two of the four call sites already do.
- **Right** wins on separation (text and controls never interleave; the column reads as a gutter of affordances) and matches the two-button pair better, since two controls beside a label crowd it.
- With TWO buttons rather than one chevron, the right-hand gutter argument gets stronger — a pair of icons in front of every title is a lot of furniture before the words start.

## Not in scope

The fold state model itself (one thing expanded at a time) beyond what change 2 forces. The verdict-line content. Re-litigating whether the binary supersession was right — Ben has seen it running and asked for this; the item records the history so the next reader knows the stepper was tried, replaced, and partially restored on evidence.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the control vocabulary, in Ben's own terms

The apparent left-vs-right contradiction above was two different CONTEXTS, not two rules. Ben clarified, and the model is now closed:

### A foldable row

    Expandable item                                    ⌄  ›

The title reads from the left. Both controls sit at the row's right, **right-aligned to a fixed gutter** — not immediately after the label, because a gutter is what makes them line up in one vertical column across every row, which is the whole point ("it is disorienting when a button is not in the same column, but does the same job"). A title's length must never move its controls.

- **`⌄` expand in place.** Becomes **`⌃`** while expanded, and collapses on click. The surface grows where it sits: a single graph, or an accordion of graphs for a more complex menu.
- **`›` full canvas.** Opens the takeover view described next.

### The full-canvas view

    ‹ Example title for graphs
    <graphs below>

One control, **top left**, immediately before the title: **`‹`**, which returns. Nothing sits in a right gutter here — there is no list of rows to align with, and a return affordance belongs where a reader starts, not where they finish.

### Why this is consistent rather than a special case

The two placements answer two different questions. In a list, the controls act ON A ROW, so they belong in the row's own column of affordances. In a takeover, the control acts on the WHOLE VIEW and means "back" — and back is top-left everywhere in software, including this app's own zoom ladder.

So: **controls that operate on an item in a list are right-gutter-aligned; the control that leaves a view is top-left.** That sentence is the rule to carry into LAYOUT.md, and it is what any future disclosure surface should be checked against.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the consequences change 2 forces, closed

The item's own text flagged one thing as "to design, not discover": the fold state model
assumes a single window-wide overlay, and a canvas-bounded overlay breaks that assumption.
Closing it here, plus the three consequences that fell out of reading the code. This is the
last design owed; the item is promote-ready.

### 1. The single-target invariant belongs to the TAKEOVER only

Today `fold_state` is one `(surface, key)` and `detail_level.hpp` justifies it directly from
the binary model: "because expanded is an overlay, only ONE thing can be expanded at a
time". Splitting one control into two breaks that derivation, because the two controls have
genuinely different arities:

- **`›` full canvas** — a takeover of ONE rectangle. Stays a single global `(surface, key)`.
  Opening a second replaces the first. The existing invariant survives here unchanged, and
  for the original reason.
- **`⌄` expand in place** — NOT single-target. An accordion of graphs is by definition
  several rows open at once, so this must be a SET of `(surface, key)`, not a target. A
  single-target in-place expander would make change 1 unbuildable: opening the second graph
  would close the first, which is the accordion behaviour Ben is asking for the opposite of.

So the state becomes two fields, not one widened one: keep `fold_state expanded` for the
takeover, add a set for in-place. Do not try to unify them — they answer different questions
(which one view has the stage, versus which rows are unfolded) and collapsing them back into
one field is how the invariant got mis-stated in the first place.

### 2. Inside a takeover, the in-place set is IGNORED

Change 3 says a full-screened accordion shows every item, scrolled. That is only coherent if
the takeover does not consult the in-place set — otherwise the same accordion would render
differently depending on which rows the player happened to have unfolded before pressing `›`,
and "anything full screen deserves its full space" would hold only sometimes.

**Rule: the takeover renders every item of its surface open, top to bottom, in a scroll
region. In-place state is display state of the folded view and does not travel.** Returning
via `‹` restores the in-place set exactly as it was, so the takeover is non-destructive.

### 3. Esc does NOT collapse in-place expansions

The Esc ladder gains the takeover rung and nothing else. In-place expansion is not a mode the
player is *in* — it is a reading preference, the same kind of state as a disclosure triangle,
and Esc has never collapsed those. Putting it on the ladder would make Esc unpredictable
(sometimes it leaves a view, sometimes it re-folds four graphs you deliberately opened).

The ladder after this item and BL-266 (which removes the hide-selection rung):

    exit-confirm -> system menu -> pop card_stack -> pop corp_rollup_drill
      -> close full-canvas takeover -> system menu

Outermost first, unchanged in shape. The takeover rung replaces today's "fold overlay" rung
and does the same job under the new geometry.

### 4. Coexistence with the fold-out ledger column is intended, not tolerated

`foldout_column_rect()` is entirely LEFT of the canvas region, so a canvas-bounded takeover
and an open ledger occupy disjoint rectangles and can both be on screen. That is the point,
and it produces the case worth naming: a foldable row inside a ledger (History Chain stage,
corp dashboard roll-up) can open its takeover in the CANVAS while the row that opened it
stays visible in the left column.

This reads correctly rather than oddly, and for Ben's own stated reason — it is the same
event as clicking a body on the canvas: the source stays put, the stage changes. State it in
LAYOUT.md so the next reader does not "fix" it by dimming the ledger.

### 5. The canvas rectangle must become ONE function first — this is task 1

Change 2 is "full screen takes the canvas", and there is currently **no canvas rect in the
codebase to take**. The region is re-derived ad-hoc wherever it is needed: `app.cpp` composes
`shell_column_width(disp.x)` with `header_panel_height` for the frame HUD anchor,
`ledger_chrome.cpp` composes it with `profile_panel_height`, and the bottom edge comes from
`selection_band_height(disp.x, disp.y)` at a third site. Three derivations, no name.

**Add `ui::canvas_rect()` to `foldout_column.hpp`, beside the other screen-geometry
functions, and have the takeover use it.** This is the item's first task and everything else
depends on it, because "consistency in the UI" (Ben's stated reason for change 2) is exactly
what a single derivation buys and three drifting ones cannot. `foldout_column.hpp`'s own
header comment already records the cost of the alternative — the minimap and bottom strip
"silently drifted out of alignment" while they were independent numbers, which is the same
failure one step over.

Migrating the existing three call sites onto `canvas_rect()` is in scope (it is the whole
point). Migrating the zoom-ladder canvases onto it is NOT — they work, and CANVASES.md owns
them; note it as a follow-on rather than widening this item.

### 6. The four glyphs are DRAWN, not typed

The settled vocabulary is written as `⌄ ⌃ ‹ ›`, and none of those are in the font atlas.
BL-234 fixed a defect of exactly this shape (26 strings rendering "?" for missing
codepoints), and `detail_level.cpp` already sidesteps it deliberately — `draw_chevron` builds
a triangle through the draw list with a comment saying why.

**Both controls draw their own glyph through `ImDrawList`, as `draw_chevron` does today.**
The characters in this item are notation for the design, not string literals for the code.
Anyone implementing this from the prose alone would reintroduce BL-234, so it is recorded
here rather than left to be rediscovered at the atlas.

### What is still NOT settled, deliberately

The takeover's entry/exit transition (instant, or a brief grow from the row). Untouched
because it is a feel question that wants the live app, not a paragraph — and the current
overlay is instant, so shipping instant changes nothing and defers cleanly.
BL-265.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.9). All of Ben's 2026-08-02 changes implemented. CHANGE 1 -- expand and full screen are now two controls with two meanings, restoring the middle rung of the old Glance/Read/Study stepper (the item says to admit that plainly, and the code does) without restoring the stepper's single cycling control. CHANGE 2 -- the takeover is bounded to the CANVAS, not the window: `fold_overlay_begin` sizes to `ui::canvas_rect()` through a new `takeover_rect()`, so every caller migrated at once and the shell chrome, header, clock, comms dock, Selection band and minimap all survive a full-screen. ONE SURFACE DELIBERATELY LEFT WINDOW-WIDE: the New World wizard's chain stages, which run on their own screen before the shell exists -- there is no canvas to take and no chrome to preserve, so canvas_rect() would carve an arbitrary sub-rect out of a screen with no shell column. Recorded in takeover_rect's comment and LAYOUT.md. CHANGE 3 -- a full-screened accordion now shows the WHOLE accordion, scrolled: the History Chain and wizard stages open the whole ROUND, and the corporation dashboard shows all four roll-ups (its `expanded.key` no longer selects what is drawn, only what the drill scopes to; `rollup_body()` extracted so the column and the takeover share one builder). CHANGE 4 -- all four call sites unified on the right gutter via `disclosure_controls`/`disclosure_gutter_width`; a row offering only the takeover leaves the left slot EMPTY so the column never moves. `gutter_text` added after long verdicts were seen rendering straight through the controls in the 380px column. CHANGE 6 -- every glyph is DRAWN, not typed: `draw_caret` and `draw_open_arrow` build through ImDrawList, and no such string literal exists in src/. This is the BL-234 defect class the item explicitly warned would be reintroduced by anyone implementing from the prose alone. THE ONE-THING-EXPANDED INVARIANT WAS RESTATED rather than widened, which the item named as a consequence to design rather than discover: the TAKEOVER stays single-target because it owns one rectangle, while IN-PLACE became a SET (`fold_state::in_place`) because a single-target in-place expander makes an accordion unbuildable. Coexistence with the open ledger column is intended and documented as such (foldout_column_rect is entirely left of canvas_rect), with an explicit note not to 'fix' it by dimming the ledger. Esc gains only the takeover rung, so returning restores the folded view exactly. `SetNextWindowFocus` is now consumed once on open rather than every frame -- harmless window-wide, but it would have fought the ledger beside it. Signatures of any_expanded/expand/fold/fold_overlay_begin are unchanged, so app.cpp's Esc ladder and Lua verify hook were untouched. NOT VERIFIED without a GUI: in-place expansion itself, because app.cpp's `verify.fold` hook only drives the takeover -- the takeover paths, gutter alignment and glyph rendering are confirmed from captures, the in-place draw paths by inspection only. GOLDENS: all 10 in drill_through_fold now differ 19-30%, expected since the item changes appearance deliberately; re-baselining is Ben's call and, per BL-252, visual goldens are Windows-authoritative anyway. Merge note: the agent branched before BL-281 landed in the same batch, so its tile_inspector version paired Story with Tiles and referenced the removed `detail_surface::history_tiles` -- it would not have compiled. Resolved by keeping the unified gutter call and dropping the Tiles branch. Also corrected the stale binary-model comment in ui_state.hpp that this item's split invalidated.

BL-266.design:
DESIGN OWED — opened 2026-08-02 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW NR-017), as the consequence of his NR-009 answer.

## The call

Ben, resolving the Esc-ladder question: "the selection element should probably be always open. So esc drills up to the 'pause screen', when we implement that."

## Why now, when dismissal was right before

"At that point, the mini-map drew focus, and it would seem like the canvas was covered by a selection element. Currently, we basically fill the entire perimeter, meaning that it looks more awkward when the selection element disappears."

This is a layout change invalidating an interaction decision, not a reversal of a mistake. BL-194/195/196 designed a sticky card that FLOATED over an open canvas, where dismissing it genuinely gave the player their view back and the minimap was the anchor the eye returned to. BL-213 retired that for a fixed bottom band, and the shell now fills the perimeter — so hiding the band no longer frees the canvas, it opens a hole in a frame. Same affordance, opposite effect, because the thing around it moved.

BL-194/195/196 are annotated stale on their dismissal half rather than rewritten (DELIVERY.md § No retroactive refactor).

## The work

### 1. Remove the hide rung and the state behind it

`app.cpp`'s Esc ladder currently reads: exit-confirm -> system menu -> pop `card_stack` -> pop `corp_rollup_drill` -> fold overlay -> **hide selection** -> open menu. The hide rung sets `m_ui.selection_hidden_for = m_ui.selected_entity`; `selection_card.cpp` gates its draw on that field, and the ladder's `card_open` test reads it.

Removing the rung means Esc's terminal step becomes the system menu directly — which is what Ben means by "esc drills up to the pause screen". Delete `selection_hidden_for` rather than leaving it unread; a dead gate on a draw path is exactly the kind of thing a later session re-animates by accident.

### 2. Design the empty state — the real question

Today nothing draws when nothing is selected. "Always open" forces a choice that has never been made:

- **A resting band with no selection** — the element persists and shows something (a prompt, the player corporation, the last selection greyed). Needs authored content, and that content is on screen for the whole early game.
- **Selection is never empty** — something is always selected, so the band always has a subject. Cleanest visually, but it makes "deselect" unrepresentable and needs a rule for what is selected at campaign start.

The second is tempting and should be checked against real play before adopting: a game where you can never look at nothing is a game where the band always claims your attention. Ben's own framing — the perimeter is full, a gap looks wrong — argues for whichever option keeps the frame intact with the least invented content.

### 3. Align SELECTION.md

The doc describes three interaction states and assumes dismissal. It is the authority and must be updated as part of landing this, not after (standing rule: authority time-slices).

## The pause screen

Ben names a "pause screen" as Esc's terminal rung. One does not exist under that name; `show_system_menu` is the current terminus. Decide whether the pause screen IS the system menu renamed and expanded, or a new surface — and if it is new, it is its own item, not a rider on this one. Do not build a second full-screen surface inside a selection-band change.

## Verification

The Esc ladder is driven by verify scripts, and `selection_hidden_for` is observable state. Any script that presses Esc expecting the card to hide will change behaviour — re-run the drill/fold checks and re-bless rather than assuming only goldens move.

## Not in scope

The fold overlay rung (NR-009, settled and kept). The drill rungs (BL-196's `card_stack`, which stays). The band's content or layout beyond the empty state.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the empty state, and the two calls around it

### The empty state: the band rests on the PLAYER'S OWN CORPORATION

Of the two options the item posed, this is option A ("a resting band with no selection")
taking the branch that invents the least — and reading the code moves it from a preference to
the obvious answer.

**It is not authored content.** `selection_panel.cpp` already dispatches
`selection_kind::corporation` to a real builder (the shared per-entity content path, same one
the hover card and Tile Ledger use), and `selection_title` already resolves a corporation to
`w.corporations.at(id).name`. The resting band therefore draws a subject the app can already
render, with no new layout, no placeholder art, and no prose to write. Every other candidate
in the item — a prompt, the last selection greyed — requires inventing something that exists
nowhere else and then living with it on screen for the whole early game, which was the
item's own stated objection.

**It answers a question the player actually has.** "Select something" answers nothing. A
prompt is furniture. The player's own corporation is the one subject that is always relevant
and always changing, and resting there means the band is never dead space even when the
player is just watching the clock run.

**It keeps deselect representable, which option B could not.** This is the point that decides
it against "something is always selected". Under option B, deselection has no state to go to,
so the affordance stops existing. Here, deselecting has a clear and truthful meaning — *stop
looking at that, go back to looking at yourself* — which is a real navigational act rather
than a null. The band always has a subject AND the player can always let go of one.

**It is where BL-262 will want to live.** The scoring item is looking for a standing surface
(a measure the player reads continuously, not a verdict at the end). A band that rests on
your own corporation is the natural host for that, and choosing it now means BL-262 inherits
a home rather than having to argue for a new one. Not a reason on its own; recorded because
the two items are otherwise going to collide.

**Consequences.**
- `selection_kind::none` (`selection_title` -> "Nothing") becomes unreachable *for the band*.
  Keep the enumerator — other callers use it and a kind meaning "no subject" is legitimate —
  but the band never renders it, and that is a rule to state rather than an accident to
  leave.
- The resting subject needs a definition at campaign start, and it has a trivial one: the
  player corporation exists before the first frame, so there is no bootstrap gap. This is
  the rule option B would have needed and could not answer cleanly.

### The pause screen: it IS the system menu, and this item does not build one

Ben names "the pause screen" as Esc's terminal rung; the item correctly flags that nothing
exists under that name and that a new full-screen surface must not ride along on a
selection-band change.

**Settled: the pause screen is `show_system_menu` — the existing terminus, not a new
surface.** Esc's last rung already opens it; removing the hide rung makes it the last rung
*sooner*, which is exactly the behaviour Ben describes. Nothing needs building for his
sentence to become true.

Renaming it, or growing it into something richer (save/load, settings, quit-to-menu as a
designed screen rather than a menu), is a real and reasonable want — but it is a separate
item and nobody has asked for it yet. Not filed pre-emptively; if Ben wants the richer
surface he can say so and it gets its own id. What this item guarantees is only that Esc
lands somewhere sensible.

### Difficulty raised 2 -> 3

`selection_hidden_for` is not the one-line gate the original sizing assumed. It has **eleven
call sites**: the draw gate in `selection_card.cpp` (plus its dismiss-button writer), and nine
in `app.cpp` — three canvas click handlers that clear it on a new selection, the Esc-ladder
rung that sets it, the ladder's own `card_open` test that reads it, and two re-show paths.
Deleting the field means visiting all of them, and the item is right that leaving it as a
dead gate is the failure mode to avoid.

Still a small item, but it is a careful sweep rather than a deletion, and the three canvas
click handlers are the ones to check individually — each currently pairs "set selection" with
"clear hidden", and only the first half survives.

### Verification — the Esc scripts change behaviour, and that is the check

The item already flags this; making it concrete. Any verify script that presses Esc expecting
the band to disappear now expects it to stay, showing the player corporation. That is not a
golden-image drift to re-bless blindly — it is the requirement, and it is observable without
pixels (`selected_entity` and the absence of `selection_hidden_for`). Prefer asserting the
state over comparing the image where the script allows it, and re-bless the drill/fold
goldens after.
BL-266.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (build-heavy v0.1.1 batch, worktree agent). selection_hidden_for deleted — 18 sites (design counted 11; extra verify hooks + canvas files); Esc terminal rung is the system menu; band rests on the player corporation via swap-draw-restore (selected_entity stays null, deselect representable; selection_kind::none never rendered, rule in comment); SELECTION.md updated; sticky_card.lua + continents_terrain.lua re-asserted, dismiss_selection Lua hook -> clear_selection. requirements.json § selection-always-open R1-R3 complete, R4 pending golden re-bless (NR-104 — this box can't bless; Continent-lens-key overlap also flagged there).

BL-267.design:
FILED 2026-08-02 (Ben, immediately after confirming the BL-170 river render) — SSS priority, must design/build next. Design-owed: this entry scopes the problem and names the diagnostic + candidate directions; it does not commit to an architecture.

## The symptom, and why it is showing up now

Ben observed CPU lag this session, right after the BL-170 river render landed on top of BL-217 (checkpoint resolution), BL-208 (the history log + its generation-time genesis-chapter merge), and the Sprint 1 food-building pair. The river render in particular is a NEW always-on per-tile, per-frame cost (`src/ui/body_surface_canvas.cpp`, alongside the existing road/border/marker passes in the same per-tile loop) — every session that adds one more always-on canvas pass compounds onto the same single render thread, and world generation (six-pass tiles + nations + corporations + now the settlement-history chain BL-218/219 will extend) is a second, separate single-threaded cost paid at world-start.

## Measure before designing — do not guess where the time goes

BL-249 already built the instrument for exactly this (`src/ui/frame_stats.{hpp,cpp}`, F11 overlay, off by default): last/avg/max/1%-low frame time, broken into build/submit/present/other with ImGui vertex/draw-command counts. **NR-026 is already open asking Ben to run it** against the real app panning the full Kepler grid — that measurement is the first concrete step here, not a separate task, since it will say whether the lag is CPU-bound (sim/generation/draw-list-building) or GPU-bound (submit/present) before any architecture is chosen. BL-253 (`run_corp_strategic_step`'s O(corps x tiles) candidate scan) was already named as a growth-shape concern by the BL-250 sweep and judged "not a blocker at prototype scale" on 2026-07-31 — worth re-measuring now that the felt load is heavier and more systems are stacked on the same thread.

## Two directions, not yet chosen between

**GPU utilisation.** `docs/tech/TECH_FOUNDATIONS.md` already flags SDL3's GPU API as "available for future use ... without requiring a platform layer change" — chosen partly for this reason. Today rendering is ImGui immediate-mode plus a custom `ImDrawList` canvas (SDL3 + SDLRenderer3 backend) drawing on the order of 15,120 tiles (the full Kepler grid, per BL-249's own stated target) every frame, each with several passes (fill, landform relief, road, border, river, markers) computed on the CPU and submitted as vertex data. Open question: does "GPU utilisation" mean swapping the ImGui backend (SDLRenderer3 -> the SDL3 GPU API directly), or offloading specific per-tile computation (colour blends, river/border geometry) to a compute or vertex shader while keeping ImGui's own rendering path as-is? These are very different sizes of change.

**Multicore CPU threading.** The simulation core is explicitly deterministic (io-standing-rules.md) — no thread pool may be added to `world/*` logic without proving it cannot change iteration order or floating-point reduction order across runs. Candidate parallel-safe work, cheapest first: (a) the canvas tile loop itself is a read-only pass over `world` state per frame — computing each tile's fill/border/river geometry in parallel before a single-threaded submit to `ImDrawList` is a clean win with no simulation-determinism risk at all, since draw order can be fixed after the parallel compute; (b) per-body world generation passes are already logically independent of each other (each body's tile/nation/corp chain reads only that body's own state) and could run concurrently at world-start; (c) BL-253's per-corp strategic scan inside a tick — parallel-safe only if corp evaluation order never leaks into a shared reduction (market clearing, budget flows) in a way that changes float rounding; this one needs the most care and should be designed last, not first.

## Not yet settled

- Whether this item targets rendering only, generation only, or both — Ben's ask names both GPU and multicore, but they may resolve to different subsystems with different risk profiles, and BL-249's measurement should say which one is actually costing the frame budget before committing scope.
- Whether a thread pool / GPU compute dependency enters the build (CMakeLists.txt, FetchContent) — TECH_FOUNDATIONS.md's prototype-scope exclusions should be checked before adding one.
- Whether world-generation parallelism (per-body, at start) is in scope alongside per-frame render parallelism, or a separate follow-on — they have very different risk (once-at-startup vs every-frame) and could ship independently.

## Why design-owed rather than designed

The two directions above are real architectural forks (renderer-backend swap vs shader offload; render-loop parallelism vs generation parallelism vs simulation parallelism), each with different determinism risk and different build-system cost. Committing to one under lag pressure without the BL-249 measurement in hand would very likely solve the wrong bottleneck first.

## Measured (2026-08-02, in-session — the step this design asked for)

The BL-249 instrument gained a scripted tap (verify.frame_reset / verify.frame_csv + scripts/verify/pan_perf.lua). Nothing in src/ forces a dummy driver under --verify, so the numbers are real renderer + real vsync (this corrects NR-026's premise and frame_budget_hud.lua's stale header). 300-frame sustained pan, full Kepler grid, 1720x1080, Debug (the daily build/) vs Release (build_rel/, new Ninja tree, same pinned toolchain):

- Debug: 41-53 ms work/frame at every zoom — every frame over the 16.7 ms refresh, ~20 fps always. UI build owns 38-44 ms. /Od /RTC1 is the first cause.
- Release: 11.3-17.6 ms. Play zoom (11): ZERO frames over 16.7. Whole-grid zoom (0.9): 211/299 still over.
- Pan vs static: identical in both builds. There is no pan-specific cost; motion just exposes the constant per-frame cost.
- Sim + event pump: 0.01-0.04 ms. Submit/present: small. NEITHER fork this item posed is implicated.

VERDICT: both architectural forks declined at prototype scale. The real costs are (1) playing the unoptimised Debug binary, and (2) a flat O(all-tiles) per-frame overhead in body_surface_canvas.cpp — tile_at rebuilt per frame (logistics' body_tile_grid already caches exactly this on world, unused by the canvas), a 15k-id sort per frame, and full lens/colour work for every tile before any cull (no vertical cull exists). Both fixed by BL-268 (planetary canvas cull + cache) plus adopting build_rel/ for play. This item stays open only as the RE-MEASURE GATE: after BL-268 lands, re-run pan_perf; if the whole-grid Release residual (~155k verts of hex emission) still misses the ROADMAP budget, the follow-on is draw-list caching / coarse LOD for the zoomed-out grid — not a backend swap.

CLOSED 2026-08-07 (cut audit, Ben approved). The re-measure gate has been passed: the 2026-08-02 VERDICT declined both architectural forks, the executable half shipped as BL-268 (96712ec, complete), and the residual canvas-pass work is owned by BL-269. BL-268.design:
FILED 2026-08-02, designed by measurement (see BL-267's Measured section for the full numbers; the pan_perf CSVs are reproducible via scripts/verify/pan_perf.lua).

## The mechanism (all in body_surface_canvas.cpp's draw)

1. tile_at: an unordered_map<packed rc, entity_id> of the ACTIVE body's tiles is rebuilt per frame by iterating w.tiles (ALL bodies, ~34k entries) — pure waste: logistics.hpp's body_tile_grid(w, body) already builds and caches this exact raster (grid_y*gw + grid_x -> entity, null_entity absent) on world.body_tile_index, deterministically.
2. draw_order: the 15k active-body ids are collected and std::sort'ed per frame for deterministic draw order. Tile creation (tile_generation.cpp) is rows-outer with sequential create_entity ids, so ascending-id order IS raster row-major order — iterating the cached raster reproduces today's draw order exactly, no sort needed.
3. No vertical cull: every tile computes its screen centre, resolves built/owner/lens state (several hash lookups + colour math), THEN the horizontal wrap-window (k_min/k_max) decides whether any copy is drawn; rows never cull at all. At play zoom ~2% of tiles are visible but 100% pay the per-tile work.

## The fix

- app::render (mutable world in hand) ensures body_tile_grid(m_world, active_body) is built when the active body changes; the canvas (const world&) reads world.body_tile_index directly — no const_cast, no silent fallback (assert/skip if absent).
- Replace the tile_at build + sort with row-major iteration over the cached raster, restricted to the visible row range: rows don't wrap, sc.y = view_origin.y + (1.5*hex_size*row - grid_cy)*zoom, so [r0, r1] falls out of the clip rect ± hit_r in O(1). Column culling: hoist the existing k_min/k_max wrap-window test to the TOP of the per-tile body, before the built/owner/lens work — off-screen columns cost one multiply-compare.
- The border/neighbour passes that used tile_at.find(packed) read the raster by index arithmetic instead (same null_entity semantics).
- Lens pre-passes that are lens-gated (market catchment, industry field, scarcity) stay as they are — they don't run in the default path; only the always-on costs move.

## Why pixel-identical

Draw order is unchanged (row-major == ascending id, proven from generation loop order); culled tiles contributed nothing inside the clip rect (the ±hit_r margin matches the existing horizontal logic); no colour or geometry math changes. The existing golden suite is therefore the correctness check, un-blessed.

## Verification

R1: representative golden subset passes with no --bless. R2/R3: pan_perf A/B — Release play-zoom avg work < 8 ms (ROADMAP target; baseline 11.26), Debug play-zoom < 16.7 ms (playable dev build; baseline 41.21). R4: whole-grid numbers recorded; if Release z0.9 still misses 8 ms (it will remain vertex-emission-bound, ~155k verts), file the zoomed-out LOD/draw-cache follow-on named in BL-267 rather than stretching this item.

## Scope guard

No threading, no GPU-API change, no world/* contact beyond READING the existing body_tile_index cache (built by the same logistics call the dispatch loop already uses — determinism untouched). The measurement tap (frame_stats sample/reset accessors + verify frame_reset/frame_csv/window + pan_perf.lua) lands with this item as its verification instrument.
BL-268.resolution: LANDED 2026-08-02, same session as filing. planetary-pan-perf R1-R4 all met: six goldens pixel-identical un-blessed (against a baseline-blessed set — the pre-existing goldens were stale since BL-170's river generation shifted the world; re-blessed as routine policy); play-zoom pan 11.26 -> 4.98 ms work/frame Release, 41.21 -> 6.74 ms Debug; whole-grid Release 17.61 -> 12.10 ms (vertex-bound residual, filed as BL-269). PLANETARY.md § Draw-loop cost model records the shape; the pan_perf measurement tap landed with it.

BL-269.design: FILED 2026-08-02 from planetary-pan-perf R4 (BL-268's whole-grid residual). Design-owed: two candidate directions, not yet chosen — (a) zoom-LOD: below a zoom threshold draw tiles as flat quads or single AddRectFilled cells (no per-hex 6-vertex polys, no relief/road/marker detail that is sub-pixel at that scale anyway); (b) terrain draw cache: render the static layers (terrain fill + relief + lens tint) into an SDL texture once per (body, lens, survey-state) key and blit it, re-rendering only when one of those changes — dynamic chrome (markers, borders, beams, hover) stays immediate-mode on top. (b) is the bigger win and the bigger change (a texture target enters the renderer path); (a) is an afternoon. Measure first at the actual min zoom: BL-249's instrument + pan_perf z0.9 phase are the harness. NOT a backend swap — BL-267's verdict stands.
BL-269.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09. Direction (a), zoom-LOD, chosen by Ben after the measurement below; direction (b), the terrain draw cache, was NOT built -- (a) delivered enough that a texture render target could not be justified yet. WHY IT WAS PICKED UP NOW: Ben reported panning 'lags, but that manifests as occasional sharp jumps' and proposed a ~200ms delay before panning engages. Measuring first overturned the diagnosis. pan_perf on Kepler (15,120 tiles) showed the STATIC and PANNING phases at the same zoom are identical -- 157,084 vs 158,407 vertices, 14.25 vs 14.40 ms submit -- so panning costs nothing. The cost is the whole-grid ZOOM: 157k vertices against 6,172 one notch in, a 25x cliff, with submit alone (14.25 ms) blowing the 8 ms frame budget before the GPU does anything. The jumps are therefore a rendering symptom, not an input one: the pan is `pan += io.MouseDelta`, which is 1:1 and correct, so a frame taking 3x as long applies 3x the accumulated delta at once -- the right destination by a jumpy route. A delay would have ADDED latency to a 1:1 drag (world lags the cursor, then snaps) without touching frame cost. THE FIX: `AddConvexPolyFilled(verts, 6, ...)` costs ~10 vertices per tile once the AA fringe is counted; `AddRectFilled` costs 4 and emits no fringe. Below a threshold the canvas draws the terrain fill as a rect. THRESHOLD IS DERIVED, NOT PICKED: a hexagon differs from its inscribed rect by `draw_r * (1 - sqrt(3)/2)` = `draw_r * 0.134`, which falls under one pixel at draw_r < 7.46, so the bound is 7 px (corner cut 0.94 px there, and the per-tile landform icons at 0.42*draw_r are already unreadable). A first attempt used 5 px and did not fire at all -- at a 1080-tall window the whole-grid view sits at draw_r ~5.1-5.7 -- which is the argument for deriving the bound from geometry rather than eyeballing a constant that works at one window size. ONE REAL DEFECT FOUND BY LOOKING: the first working version sized the rect from the hex RADIUS and the terrain rendered as horizontal stripes. Rows step by 1.5*hex_size while a hex is 2*hex_size tall, so consecutive rows overlap; a radius-sized rect is shorter than the row pitch and leaves gaps. Sized to the grid step (col_step x row_step) the rects brick-lay and tile the plane exactly, because odd rows are offset half a column. Caught by capturing the canvas and looking at it, not by any assertion. MEASURED, whole-grid view: vertices 157,084 -> 63,004 (-60%), submit 14.25 ms -> 4.25 ms (-70%). Zoomed-in phases are byte-identical in vertex count (6,172 and 23,620), confirming the LOD does not fire where detail is readable. UNAFFECTED: terrain colour, relief shading, the survey mask and the fog wash are colour rather than geometry, so the analytic read the whole-grid view exists for is unchanged. The visible difference is that the far-zoom grid texture is brick-laid rather than hex-dotted. NOT DONE: BL-267's verdict stands, this is not a backend swap; and no attempt was made on `build_ms` (~9 ms), which is ImGui draw-list construction and the next thing to look at if the whole-grid view is still short of budget on low-spec hardware.

BL-270.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-02 (Ben, via the elicitation form in the pan-perf session).

## Ben's four settlements (verbatim answers)

1. **Scope: 'Every control including chrome.'** Not just the 8 gameplay verbs, not just verbs + reading controls — literally every press: canvas clicks (select / navigate / place), the keyboard binding table (pan/zoom/lens/speed/descend/ascend, app.cpp's canvas_command table), the nav rail, ledger tabs and sub-views, the lens strip, cross-cutting selectors (body/market/resource combos), time controls, the system menu, the construction panel flow, the Selection band affordances, the comms dock, and the New World wizard's controls.
2. **Entry fields: preconditions + typed arguments** on top of the fixed A/B pair (expected_output, reason_to_select). **Deliberately excluded** (offered, not selected): cost/spend and backlog provenance — the dictionary states what a press does and why you'd press it, not what it costs (that is world-state the blackboard reports) nor which item demanded it (that is UX_QUESTIONS' axis).
3. **Store home: docs/ai/** — 'since the consumer is the AI player'. ACTIONS.json canonical + ACTIONS.md generated mirror (sibling conventions: backlog.json/BACKLOG.md, user_stories.json/USER_STORIES.md), renderer tools/session/render_actions.js modelled on render_needs_review.js.
4. **Consumer: both, in sequence.** 'Dictionary now, generation and play consume it in sequence' — word-driven procedural generation (the New World wizard via words) consumes it first, word-driven gameplay after. Ben's milestone note: 'To consider what the difficulty level will be, we need this item. That is not really one item, it's the whole process of gameplay/development.' The dictionary is the substrate; the milestone is a process, not an item (NR-034 asks where it slots in ROADMAP).

## Entry shape

Per entry: `id` (stable slug), `surface` (where the control lives, human terms), `press` (what the player physically does — click/key/drag), `args` (typed arguments, named and typed as the code takes them — e.g. build: {type: building_type, tile: entity, target: resource_type}), `preconditions` (when the press is valid — for the 8 corp verbs these MUST mirror corp_command_result's rejection semantics exactly: no_corp/not_owner/invalid/placement/funds/state), `expected_output` (A — what observably happens, stated against world/ui state, honest about durative effects like pay-as-you-build), `reason_to_select` (B — why a player or AI would choose this press over alternatives; design intent in plain words).

## Why the seams make this cheap to keep honest

The 8 gameplay verbs already have a single validated entry point (apply_corp_command, 'the contract an out-of-process policy (stage C/D) would return' — corp_command.hpp's own words) with enumerated rejections; expected_output and preconditions for those entries are TRANSCRIBED from code, not invented. The UI chrome entries are authored prose, sourced from the authority docs (CANVASES/LENSES/LAYOUT/SELECTION/STARTUP) — where a doc and the dictionary disagree, that IS the finding.

## Relationship to the siblings

Third axis, companion not replacement: user_stories.json (intent — what the player is trying to do), UX_QUESTIONS.json/BL-260 (information — what question a readout answers), ACTIONS.json (action — what a press does and why). BL-260 stays docs-only per its own settlement; ACTIONS differs in kind because its consumer is a MACHINE player as well as the designer, which is why args and preconditions are typed rather than prose-only.

## Not in scope

- The text-play harness itself (prompt loop: blackboard + dictionary -> LLM -> corp_command). That is the next item in the milestone sequence, filed when the dictionary exists to feed it.
- Word-driven generation (the wizard via words) — consumes the dictionary later; not built here.
- Any in-game rendering of dictionary text (BL-260's NR-018 lesson stands: development documentation does not leak into the UI).
- Audit tooling beyond the mirror renderer's parse (the docs are the audit — Ben's standing position; the machine consumer will find gaps by failing to act, loudly).
BL-270.resolution: LANDED 2026-08-02, same session as filing and promotion. 114 entries across the five families (11 gameplay / 24 canvas / 15 lens / 36 ledger / 28 chrome) in docs/ai/ACTIONS.{json,md}, authored by five parallel family agents and merged with per-fragment validation; render_actions.js generates the mirror and doubles as the shape check. action-dictionary R1-R4 all met — the gameplay family is transcribed from corp_command.hpp (typed args + rejection semantics), and the sweep caught two doc-truth defects in passing: LENSES.md's stale supply-routes unreachability note (fixed) and the undocumented seventh rung of the Esc precedence ladder (transcribed in chrome.esc). AI_OPPONENT.md § 6a and CLAUDE.md § Documents carry the pointers. The next milestone items (the text-play harness; word-driven generation) now have their substrate.

BL-271.design:
## Settled at filing (2026-08-02 brainstorm)

- **Year tick, own loop.** The economy tick is a day; this needs a year (or campaign-season) tick with its own loop - a NEW loop, not a reuse of the economy tick. Seasonality (campaigning season vs winter / mare-clausum closure) is in from the start because it is half of pre-modern strategy, and it is cheap at this granularity (a season flag on the tick; doctrine and supply modifiers keyed to it).
- **The rupture transforms become recurring systems.** resolve_historical_ruptures' collapse/war/revolution logic is the seed: what fired once as a checkpoint fires each year as an evaluated decision by a nation actor. The checkpoint mechanism (BL-217) stays for one-shot branch points; the sim adds the continuous layer on top.
- **The record-burning rule carries over.** Wars in the sim erase and lacuna-ise the loser's record exactly as BL-218 landed it - 2000 years of that produces worlds whose written history is itself an artifact of who won, which is the philosophical-development payload.
- **Non-hegemony becomes emergent, not asserted.** Some seeds WILL produce a Rome; BL-224's invariant becomes a tuning target read off BL-275's sweep distributions (what parameter regions keep worlds multipolar), not a construction guarantee. The sweep is also the answer to 'what does an averted rupture need to look like' (BL-223).

## Open questions (for the design conversation, not blockers)

1. Determinism/runtime budget: 2000 ticks x ~40 nations x seed spread - integer arithmetic throughout per the standing rule, but what is the wall-clock budget per world? (Working target: a full 0-2000 CE run well under a second, so BL-275 can do hundreds.)
2. What state persists into the 1960 campaign when the sim replaces the pre-computed Stages 3-4 - the full province history, or the same summary the settlement pass produces today? (Cheapest honest answer: the sim RUNS at generation time and writes the same outputs BL-218 writes, plus a richer history log for BL-208's store.)
3. Does the player ever get a seat in the sandbox (crude feel-testing) or is it bot-only? Ben has not answered this; default is bot-only until he does.

## Naming constraint (Ben, 2026-08-03)

This item is filed off a real-history analogy ("use Rome as a sandbox"). Under the standing
rule added the same day (io-standing-rules § Terms & docs; GENERATION_STRATEGY § Real history
in, invented names out), that analogy is a **mechanism** reference only.

What this item takes from Rome: campaign-season structure, supply radii, how a frontier stalls,
how fast a hegemony forms, what makes a littoral power. What it must never take: a proper noun.
Every nation, province, city and commander the sim produces is named from the seeded sci-fi /
fantasy template banks, and the phoneme tables must not read as recognisably Latin — a name a
player can place as "the Roman one" has failed however good the mechanism under it.

Io's existing rule that Rome is *calibration reference, not content* already said this for the
mil-sim; it now applies to the whole Era −1 arc.

## Ruling (Ben, 2026-08-07): elimination and release are design intent

The first sweep (BL-275) found polity elimination and population collapse unreachable across 12 seeds - the no-elimination finding, filed in-session under pre-rebase id BL-308 and retired as a standalone item by this ruling. Its target stands here instead: **polity elimination must be possible, and so must release of subject nations** - death and breakaway are both required outcomes of the sim, not tuning accidents. The physical-constraint half is BL-316's (era -1 logistics) burden-of-breadth slice; the scorer half is the shared-currency redesign in the 2026-08-07 working tree (re-file if it stalls). Release of subject nations is NEW scope: the sim currently has no subject or breakaway mechanism at all.

BL-272.design:
## Settled at filing (2026-08-02 brainstorm)

**'Real tactics' means doctrine parameters, never battlefields.** This is the load-bearing constraint everything else prices off. 2000 years x ~40 nations x a seed spread is millions of engagements; if a battle is a tactical simulation, the sweep is dead on arrival. The workable shape:

- An **army is a stack of typed units** (unit_component grows a type; a stack is a vector of (type, count) pairs).
- A **battle is ONE deterministic evaluation**: unit-type matchup matrix x formation doctrine x BL-233's terrain scalars (terrain_defence / terrain_attrition / terrain_resistance, landed 2026-07-31 - and this is finally their intended consumer, per HISTORY.md's BL-224 note) x supply state x season.
- **Tactics are data, not manoeuvres**: a doctrine row reads like 'phalanx - devastating frontal, brittle flank, useless in mountain'. Rock-paper-scissors with historical teeth: a doctrine is a set of modifiers against the matchup matrix and the terrain scalars, nothing more.
- **Integer arithmetic with explicit tie-breaks** throughout - battle outcomes are gate-path decisions (they move borders), so the float ban applies.

**Engine parity contract:** the same resolve function serves the Era -1 sim and the 1960+ era; only the roster table (BL-274) and the doctrine table differ. No sandbox-only combat rules - anything the sandbox needs, the main era gets.

## Open questions

1. Matchup matrix size: per unit-type pair, or per class pair (infantry / cavalry / ranged / siege / naval) with type-level modifiers? (Lean: class pair + modifiers - the matrix stays readable and rosters stay cheap to extend.)
2. Naval combat: same engine with a sea 'terrain', or deferred? (Sea-cheap logistics makes navies strategically decisive before they are tactically interesting - lean: strategic-only naval presence first, engine extension later.)
3. Sieges/attrition vs field battles: the ancient norm is that attrition and supply kill more than battle does. Does the first cut model sieges as a doctrine ('assault' vs 'invest') or as a separate resolution path?
BL-272.resolution: Landed 2026-08-02 as Sprint 5's foundation wave. `resolve_battle` in src/world/combat.{hpp,cpp}: two army stacks (vector of {type_id, unit_class, count, type_power_mod}) + two doctrine_row values + terrain + season + supply -> battle_outcome (result, power tallies, integer per-mille losses, decisiveness). Lean taken on all three open questions: class-pair matchup matrix with per-type modifiers; naval entries contribute zero tactical power (strategic-only); sieges are a doctrine (siege_stance::assault/invest), not a separate resolution path. unit_component gained a type field (opaque roster index; BL-274 owns interpreting it). tools/verify/combat_harness.cpp 15/15 PASS (determinism, terrain flipping an outcome, tie-break, bounded losses, doctrine-drives-same-function, naval exclusion). Full CTest suite 41/41 green after merge to main.

BL-273.design:
## Settled at filing (2026-08-02 brainstorm)

- **Logistic growth per province**, integer fixed-point, carrying capacity derived from the province's farm endowment (the world-relative farm_q BL-218 already computes) - the ground feeds who it can feed. Growth modulated by war (drawdown at battles fought on or by the province) and by rare plague events (a checkpoint-class draw reusing BL-217's mechanism - eligibility-filtered, recorded, never a weight).
- **Manpower is the army budget**: a nation's recruitable stock is a fraction of its provinces' population, and units raised deplete it. This closes the loop that makes 2000-year wars self-limiting - the reason ancient hegemonies stall is manpower exhaustion, and the sim should reproduce that from the model rather than from a cap.
- **Feeds the existing surfaces on graduation**: at the 1960 handoff the province populations seed the population-centre scales (today drawn from a weighted distribution), so the demography the sim earned replaces a die roll - the same pattern as every other BL-210-era rewrite.

## Open questions

1. Granularity: population per province only, or with an urban/rural split? (Lean: province total first; the split is a refinement the 1960 agglomeration model can add.)
2. Plague as global events (Antonine-plague-shaped, hitting connected provinces harder - trade connectivity as the vector, which makes the sea lanes double-edged) or as local draws? The connectivity version is more interesting and reads straight off the logistics graph.
3. Does carrying capacity move when industrialisation arrives? Almost certainly yes - Stage 4's fossil-fuel escape from the organic economy IS a carrying-capacity jump - but the magnitude wants tuning against BL-275's sweep.
BL-273.resolution: Landed 2026-08-02 as Sprint 5's foundation wave. province gains population (int64_t), last_demography_year, manpower_stock; province_carrying_capacity(farm_q) is linear off the existing endowment field; advance_province_demography does integer fixed-point logistic growth + war drawdown; manpower_ceiling/replenish_manpower/raise_manpower give the bounded, self-limiting army budget; resolve_plague_event draws through resolve_checkpoint's eligibility mechanism. Leans taken on the open questions: province-total population (no urban/rural split); plague connectivity via grid (Chebyshev) proximity rather than the full logistics/trade graph, since that graph isn't reachable at this generation stage (noted in POPULATION.md); carrying-capacity response to industrialisation deferred, as scoped. tools/verify/demography_harness.cpp 20/20 PASS. settlement_harness re-verified clean against the extended province struct (21/21). Full CTest suite 41/41 green after merge to main.

BL-275.design:
## Settled at filing (2026-08-02 brainstorm)

- **Deterministic per seed, comparable across seeds**: same discipline as every harness - a sweep row is replayable from its seed alone.
- **Report, do not gate (at first)**: the sweep's first job is to SHOW Ben the distributions (the BL-219-sweep lesson: Ben asked to see failure cases). Assertions (e.g. 'hegemony rate stays under X%') come after he has seen the raw spread and said what he wants, not before.
- **Named metrics for the first cut**: per-seed final nation count; hegemony events (any nation crossing a territory-share threshold, with the year); wars per century and their average territorial transfer; lacunae per world (how much written history survived); ideology distribution at epoch; first/median/last industrialisation years; population at epoch vs peak.
- **Closes BL-210**: with this landed, the umbrella's last scope item (batch-sweep extension) is met and BL-210 closes after TILE_GENERATION.md's propagation share.

## Open questions

1. Sweep size vs runtime: hangs entirely on BL-271's per-world budget (its open question 1). 100 seeds at under a second each is the working target.
2. Output surface: printed table only, or a JSON the (future) generation ledger / wizard could read? (Lean: JSON + printed summary - the marginal cost is trivial, and the wizard's formed-vs-left chart shows there is appetite for generation evidence in the UI.)
BL-275.resolution: Landed 2026-08-05 ('The history sweep, and the answer it gives is no') as tools/verify/history_sweep.cpp - reports, does not gate; JSON + printed summary per the filed lean. Runtime target missed and said so (0.95-10 s per world, scaling with province count). First spread: hegemony 0/12, elimination 0/12 - the no-elimination finding, retired 2026-08-07 by Ben's ruling with its target recorded on BL-271. Requirements group history-sweep, all rows complete. Status flipped 2026-08-07 during the NR-079 rebase repair: the landing predates the rebase, which dropped the status change.

BL-276.design:
## Settled at filing (Ben, 2026-08-03 - hybrid, ~90%)

Two levers, per the sweep session's NR-041 options, landed together:

- **Mechanism (consequence, not dice)**: a rift-basin extension to run_continents. Where the boundary classifier finds a DIVERGENT pair of two CONTINENTAL plates, the boundary corridor founders: a strong negative height bias (distance-falloff from the boundary tiles) is stamped into height_bias, so Pass 2's percentile threshold floods it into an inland sea shaped by plate structure. Total ocean stays at water_fraction (the threshold is a percentile), so the basin RELOCATES ocean rather than adding it. Emits one biography line (chain_stage::engine) - the rift that became a sea is readable history. Worlds whose plate draw yields no continental divergent pair get no basin: those are the deliberately-hard ~10%.
- **Backstop gate (selection, reject-and-reroll)**: in hard_coded_world's Kepler wiring, an acceptance loop over the tile seed (attempt-folded XOR, attempt 0 = today's seed) regenerates into a scratch world until SOME enclosed sea >= 30 tiles exists (cap 6 attempts; on exhaustion keep attempt 0 honestly - no clamp, per the resolve_preferences idiom). This is the 'never impossible to try' floor: nearly every world has at least a small enclosed sea, even when the full Mediterranean arena is absent.

**Target numbers** (mediterranean_sweep is the measure): enclosed sea >= 300 tiles in ~88-92% of seeds; enclosed sea >= 30 tiles in ~100%. Do NOT overtune the basin toward 100% at 300 tiles - the hard-Rome tail is wanted.

**Determinism**: the basin pass draws no shared-stream RNG (distance field only; its history line uses the existing per-pair local rng shape), so it cannot perturb plate seeding or downstream passes beyond the intended bias. The gate is a pure function of (campaign seed).
BL-276.resolution: Landed 2026-08-03. Rift-basin mechanism (interior-segment corridor, adaptive width, rift-shoulder rim) + intracratonic sag fallback in run_continents; two-bar acceptance gate (arena >=300 x3 attempts, floor >=30 x6) on Kepler's tile seed in hard_coded_world. Measured over 500 seeds: floor 100%, arena 89.6% (target ~90%; the tail is the wanted hard-Rome set). mediterranean_sweep harness (new, asserted) + continents_harness, world_determinism, determinism_harness, world_audit all PASS. Docs: CONTINENTS.md section, TILE_GENERATION.md deferred note updated.

BL-278.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-03 (Ben's steer + the § 10 research sweep).

## Why MCP and not something bespoke

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol over stdio or HTTP: a SERVER exposes
`tools` (callable functions with typed args), `resources` (fetchable read-only data) and
`prompts` (reusable templates); a CLIENT is whatever agent runtime is driving. The field
converged on it independently — Vox Deorum, civ6-mcp, civStation and CivBench all wrap their
game as an MCP server over a fixed verb list. Adopting it costs no originality and buys every
existing client (Claude Code/Desktop, Gemini/Codex CLIs, Ollama-backed local loops, bespoke
harnesses) for free.

## The mapping — near-mechanical, because BL-206 and BL-270 already did the hard parts

| MCP primitive | Io asset |
|---|---|
| `tools` | `corp_command.hpp`'s verbs — already typed, already validated, rejections already enumerated in `corp_command_result` |
| `resources` | `--export-blackboard` JSONL (BL-206) — visibility-honest, deterministic ordering, schema-versioned |
| `prompts` | `reason_to_select` from `ACTIONS.json` (BL-270) — the design-intent prior |
| lookup tool | `actions_query.js` over `ACTIONS_INDEX.json` — hold the index, fetch entries on demand |

## Design calls settled by the research (§ 10c.5)

- **Push state, do not make the model pull it.** CivBench's "sensorium effect" — agents miss
  information they never think to query — is the dominant failure of a purely pull-shaped tool
  surface. The server must lead each turn with the blackboard slice rather than waiting to be
  asked for it. This is the single cheapest quality win available and it is an interface
  decision, not a model decision.
- **Mask to legal primitives.** Only `corp_command` verbs are exposed as tools; the validation
  path is the player's. Fairness is then a property of the seam, not of tuning — and a rejected
  command is a typed, loggable event rather than a silent no-op.
- **Never ask the model to carry world state across turns.** The observation-belief research
  (§ 10c.4, measured on exactly the open-weight class Io targets) shows belief accuracy degrading
  with multi-hop reasoning and drifting from coherence over long interactions. Hand it the state
  every turn.
- **Coarse cadence.** The model chooses strategy occasionally, not per-tick; the BL-202/203
  utility core executes tactically underneath. Unchanged from § 2C.

## Scope

In: the server process, the tool/resource/prompt surface over the three legs, the push-shaped
turn packet, a smoke path proving an attached client can read state and land a legal command.

Out: the trace/corpus format and the fine-tuning pipeline (BL-279); any in-process API call
(NR-039 settled that this never ships inside the exe); any change to `corp_command`'s verb set
— if a verb is missing, that is its own item.

## Determinism

Unaffected. The model is out-of-process, commands still apply at the tick boundary through
player-grade validation, and NR-039's proposed determinism carve-out stays reverted.

BL-281.design:

content builders are shared with the Tile Ledger and the hover card (SELECTION.md), so the

BL-281.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.9). It is work the design predates rather than work it judged, and it sits squarely inside the ledger's own premise of how this world came to be -- so Ages survives and only Tiles was retired.
