BL-340.design:
## Why this is not more Lua authoring

BL-323's S1 widened `k_extractable` from 4 to 15 targets with zero other code changes, because every consumer (placement, the build-mode target picker, the resource presentation table) was already generic over the list. The extraction half was therefore cheap. The processing half is not, and the reason is precise: the missing outputs are resources that **do not exist in the enum**.

Adding a `resource_type` value is not a Lua edit. It touches:

- **`components.hpp`** -- the enum itself, and any fixed-size per-resource array keyed off its cardinality.
- **`serialisation.cpp`** -- the save format. Resource ids are persisted; widening the enum is a save-format change, so BL-107 (save-format version) is adjacent and may want to land first or alongside.
- **market seeding and price bands** -- a new good with no seeded supply, demand or price band is a good that clears at a degenerate price. RESOURCES.md's tier model (raw -> refined -> product) says where each sits, but the seeding has to actually place it.
- **presentation** -- pip glyph and colour per ICONS.md, or the good renders as a hole in every readout.

## Scope

PRODUCTION.md designs 8 processing buildings; the registry loads 5 recipes after BL-323 added the Smelter's iron_nickel_ore -> steel. The gap is Chemical Plant, Electronics Lab, Fabricator, Assembly Plant and most Refinery outputs.

**Open question this item must settle first:** how many of RESOURCES.md's 31 resources actually need to exist for the prototype's chains to close, versus how many are Era 1 content that can stay unimplemented. The seven-resource prototype subset is the existing precedent for not building all 31 at once; the answer is probably a second small tranche, not the full set.

## Sequencing

After BL-323 (done). Wants a decision on BL-107 (save-format version) first, since this is the first deliberate save-format widening since that item was filed -- doing it blind is how a save-compat bug gets introduced with no version to gate on.

## 2026-08-10 - re-versioned by the Sprints 8-12 plan (v0.1.13 -> v0.1.14)

Moved v0.1.13 -> v0.1.14 (the new Procurement minor), per NR-120 ruling 3. The refocus says trade is coloured by military use and space equipment "initially" - so the processing roster stops being economic depth and becomes the goods the premise is made of. Without these resource types on the market, the colour is an assertion rather than a mechanic. Cut by Sprint 10 alongside the procurement/contract seam. Note this leaves v0.1.13 without its keystone; the five items remaining there stand on their own.

## 2026-08-10 - DESIGN PASS (settled; designed jointly with BL-350)

Designed together with BL-350 because they are mechanism and content for the same premise, and
each is incoherent alone. BL-094's rewrite says the militia "uses private companies to build
equipment for space": BL-350 is the buying, this item is the thing bought. Ship BL-350 alone and
the militia contracts for goods that do not exist; ship this alone and seven resources arrive with
no buyer that needs them - which is how BL-286's eight logistics goods landed inert and still are.

**The joint design's load-bearing decision:** `spacecraft_components` carries no background demand.
The militia's contracts are its only demand. That is what makes the coupling real rather than
thematic - the background economy does not want space equipment; a militia does.

### The admission rule (the durable half of the answer)

> A `resource_type` value must be consumed by an authored recipe, or be a terminal object some
> named actor contracts for or consumes. **No orphans.**

BL-286 is the cautionary precedent, named plainly: eight goods added with enum, serialisation and
base-price wiring, and no consumer. Two minors later grain, fodder, salt, transport_capacity,
charcoal, iron_blooms and bullion still have no mechanic that reads them. They cost save-format
width and readout space and return nothing.

Applying the rule: **IN** - silicon, refined_copper, ree_alloy (consumed by the Tier-3 recipes,
each also rescuing a dead raw); alloys, electronics (consumed by the Assembly Plant);
spacecraft_components (terminal - the militia's contract object); machinery (terminal, and the
Fabricator's *alternative* to alloys - it makes that building a choice rather than a forced path).
**OUT** - liquid oxygen (already folded into both Chemical Plant recipes by BL-308; nothing outside
the plant would hold it); clean water, building materials, consumer goods, medical supplies,
utilities (habitability goods whose consumer is deferred from the prototype).

### The real content is pricing, not the enum

The filed design above leads with the enum extension as the expensive part. **That is backwards.**
Every per-resource array is already sized off `resource_count` (components.hpp, world_gen_config.hpp,
recipe_registry.hpp, law.hpp, planetology.hpp) - there is no fixed-width `std::array<float, 32>`
anywhere in src/world/, which is why BL-286's eight-good extension needed no per-array edit.

The expensive half is that **three of the four raws the new recipes consume cannot be bought.**
silica, copper_ore and rare_earth_ore carry base_price 0, and clear_markets skips every resource
with no base price. A processing building auto-buys its input shortfall from the market, so a
Refinery pointed at silica draws against a market that will never supply it and the recipe is dead
on arrival. **This item's actual centre of gravity is closing the minable-but-unsellable
asymmetry;** the enum extension is a precondition, not the work.

### The authored tranche

Seven new enum values (32 -> 39), appended in tier order:

| Value | Tier | Recipe | Building |
|---|---|---|---|
| silicon | 2 | silica 2.0 -> 1.0 | Refinery |
| refined_copper | 2 | copper_ore 2.0 -> 1.0 | Smelter |
| ree_alloy | 2 | rare_earth_ore 2.0 -> 1.0 | Refinery |
| machinery | 3 | steel 1.0 + refined_copper 1.0 -> 1.0 | Fabricator |
| alloys | 3 | steel 1.0 + ree_alloy 1.0 -> 1.0 | Fabricator |
| electronics | 3 | silicon 1.0 + refined_copper 1.0 + ree_alloy 0.5 -> 1.0 | Electronics Lab |
| spacecraft_components | 3 | alloys 2.0 + electronics 1.0 -> 1.0 | Assembly Plant |

Six base prices on existing raws, closing the asymmetry: coal 2.0 (also the steel reagent - see the
correction below), silica 2.0, copper_ore 3.0, rare_earth_ore 6.0 ("low concentration, high base
price"), iron_nickel_ore 3.0 (recipe 6 already consumes it and it had no market),
platinum_group_metals 40.0 (terminal by design - RESOURCES.md calls it the belt's primary
high-value trade good; its job is to be sold).

Seven base prices for the new goods, on a deliberate ladder - silicon 5.0 (1.25x margin over input
cost), refined_copper 7.5 (1.25x), ree_alloy 16.0 (1.33x), machinery 22.0 (1.42x), alloys 34.0
(1.42x), electronics 29.0 (1.41x), spacecraft_components 140.0 (1.44x). The margin widens up the
tiers, which is the intended shape: Tier 3 is where RESOURCES.md promises "widest price divergence",
and spacecraft_components at 140.0 sits **56x iron ore**. That ladder is the value gradient the
whole space-equipment premise rests on.

These are first-cut authored constants in the existing style, not balanced figures. The shipped
table is not internally consistent either - food_rations at 6.0 from 2x3.0 of agricultural produce
is exactly break-even - so the tranche should not be held to a standard the existing seven do not
meet. Retune by playtest.

### Background demand - DELETED from this item (2026-08-10, sequencing change)

The design pass originally specified substrate `demand_basket` weights plus an abstract
refined-goods capacity in `inject_substrate_demand`, and named it the risk step. **That step is not
built here.** Ben's 2026-08-10 call put the living world (BL-365) first, and BL-365 removes
`inject_substrate_demand` outright - so building this would be building it twice.

Background production and consumption for the seven new goods is **BL-365's** responsibility. The
hazard transfers rather than disappearing: a good with demand and no supply pegs at 4x base
forever, and under real background industry that means no firm produces it. BL-365 carries it as an
explicit failure condition. The intended demand *shape* (machinery heaviest, then electronics,
refined_copper, silicon, alloys; spacecraft_components deliberately zero) is retained here as input
to BL-365's calibration.

### Scope explicitly excluded

Named `building_type` enum values (Refinery, Fabricator, Electronics Lab, Assembly Plant) - they
stay recipes on the generic processing_facility exactly as the shipped five do. Habitability goods
and their buildings. Retuning the shipped seven base prices. Deposit generation changes - every raw
this item prices already has authored deposits (BL-040).

### Corrections this pass owes elsewhere

- **This item's own `files` list named `src/world/serialisation.cpp`, which does not exist** -
  `find src -iname "*serial*"` returns nothing. Corrected on the item.
- **BL-107's "no flat-binary serialiser exists" is stale**, and the dependency it implies is live
  again rather than vacuous. As of BL-293 there are two such streams - history_log.{hpp,cpp} and
  order_book.{hpp,cpp} - both already carrying the magic + version header BL-107 specifies.
  `read_order_book` rejects a resource byte outside the known `resource_type` range, so widening
  the enum moves a validation boundary in shipped serialised state. Not a blocker, but the version
  bump is a real step.
- **PRODUCTION.md and recipes.lua disagree on the steel recipe.** The doc's Smelter table says iron
  ore + coal (reagent) -> steel; recipes.lua id 1 is `{ iron_ore = 2.0 }` with no coal. Pricing coal
  makes this worth reconciling in the same pass - recommend adding the reagent, since it gives coal
  a consumer that the admission rule would otherwise require.

### Requirement sketch (owed at promotion)

`headless`, extending econ_harness or a new resource_chain_harness: a rollout in which every one of
the seven new goods is produced, priced and cleared at least once, **and no priced good sits pegged
at the 4x band ceiling for the whole run**.
BL-340.resolution: 2026-08-11 — complete. Seven new resource_type values (silicon, refined_copper, ree_alloy, machinery, alloys, electronics, spacecraft_components) land: enum, base prices, recipes, UI presentation, docs. Six pre-existing raws gain base prices, closing the minable-but-unsellable asymmetry. Steel gains a coal reagent (closes NR-158). New resource_chain_harness verifies the chain; determinism/order-book/world-audit/construction/econ harnesses and the real build all confirmed green, ai_skill_harness bit-identical to baseline. requirements.json § processing-chain-roster (R0-R4, all complete). Background demand for the roster is BL-365's responsibility, not built here.

BL-341.design:
One command, on the Windows machine, from `DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md` § Dependency acquisition:

```
IO_DEPS_CACHE=/nonexistent cmake -S . -B <tmp>/build -DFETCHCONTENT_BASE_DIR=<tmp>/deps -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
```

`IO_DEPS_CACHE=/nonexistent` is load-bearing: without it the seeded cache satisfies the configure and the check proves nothing.

**Two outcomes, and they lead different ways.**

- **It fails with the schannel revocation error** -- the posture is vindicated: seed `_deps_cache` from a working tree once, and that machine never needs the network at configure time again. Confirm the seeded path then works there.
- **It succeeds** -- the original failure was transient or environmental (AV TLS interception, a cert-chain change since), and BL-302's machinery is insurance rather than a fix. Record that, because it changes how much the cache is worth carrying.

Either way the answer is cheap and the item is a verification, not a build. Blocked only on being at that machine.

## RUN 2026-08-13 on Windows 11 - it SUCCEEDS

The check was run from the repo root with IO_DEPS_CACHE=/nonexistent and a scratch
FETCHCONTENT_BASE_DIR: configure completed, exit 0, ~120 MB fetched cold. That is the second
of the two outcomes this item named.

So the schannel revocation failure that opened BL-302 was transient or environmental, not a
standing property of this machine, and the seeded _deps_cache is INSURANCE rather than a fix -
worth keeping for a fresh clone on a machine having a bad TLS day, but nothing depends on it.
Recorded in DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md § The from-cold check alongside the 2026-08-09 Linux run.

The parked blocker ("access to the Windows development machine") had dissolved - sessions now
run on Windows 11 directly.

BL-342.design:
## Why this is the unlock

Two minors (v0.1.3 Laws, v0.1.4 Techs) are stuck in design-forward limbo, and they are stuck on
the SAME missing object. BL-156 settled its shape on 2026-07-11 and BL-155 depends on it:

> `condition_set` = a flat AND-list of atomic conditions -- no nested OR-mesh (mirrors BL-087
> resolution 1: binary tree, no re-converging mesh). Keeps evaluation order deterministic and the
> predicate legible.

Nothing builds it. `tech_tree.hpp:49` still stores `condition` as a bare descriptive **string**
(`research | structure | stockpile | market | surplus | era`) -- a label, not something that can
resolve true or false. BL-156's own note names the promotion this forces: *"a law is read every
tick and must resolve true/false, so the label must become a structured predicate."*

Build it once, and both minors become buildable. That is the whole argument for this item existing
separately rather than inside either one.

## Scope -- deliberately just the predicate

**In:** the atomic-condition type, the AND-list container, a pure `evaluate(condition_set, const
world&) -> bool`, and a headless harness. **Out:** laws, techs, UI, persistence, any consumer. Those
are BL-343 and BL-344.

## Shape

An atomic condition is `{subject, comparator, operand}` over readable world state. The prototype
set follows tech_tree.hpp's existing six labels, promoted from strings to real subjects --
`research`, `structure`, `stockpile`, `market`, `surplus`, `era` -- because they were chosen
against real content and re-deriving them abstractly would be inventing where evidence exists.

Three properties are load-bearing:

1. **Pure and deterministic.** `evaluate` reads `const world&` and nothing else -- no RNG, no
   clock, no cached mutable state. It runs every tick for every enacted law, so it sits directly
   on the determinism invariant.
2. **Empty set means true.** BL-155: *"Most laws are unconditional once enacted (empty
   `condition_set` = always-on)"*. The degenerate case is the common case; it must be the cheap
   one, not a special case bolted on.
3. **A subject may be MILITARY, not only economic.** This is BL-094's design test applied at the
   foundation: *"Does this system reach military as well as economic outcomes?"* The prototype
   need not ship a military subject, but the type MUST NOT be shaped so that adding one later
   means changing the type. A `subject` enum that only enumerates economic quantities is exactly
   the failure the pivot is trying to avoid, and it is far cheaper to avoid now than to unpick.

## Verification

`tools/verify/condition_set_harness.cpp`: empty set is true; each subject resolves against a
hand-built world; comparator boundaries (>=, >, ==) are exact rather than epsilon-fuzzy on integer
subjects; evaluation is order-independent for an AND-list; the same world evaluates identically
twice (determinism).

## Sequencing

First. BL-343 (laws MVP) and BL-344 (techs MVP) both consume it and can then run in parallel.
BL-342.resolution: Complete 2026-08-10, and it did exactly what it was filed to do: two design-forward minors became shippable the day after it landed. src/world/condition_set.{hpp,cpp} ships the atomic condition ({subject, comparator, operand} plus the qualifier the subject reads), the flat AND-list, and a pure evaluate().  All three load-bearing properties are built and asserted by tools/verify/condition_set_harness.cpp (40 assertions): PURE AND DETERMINISTIC -- it reads a const world& and nothing else; where a measure sums over an unordered container (only the `market` subject does) it sums in ascending entity-id order, and the harness asserts two structurally-identical worlds measure bit-identically. EMPTY SET IS TRUE -- and true by falling out of the loop rather than by a special case in front of it, because BL-155's common case (most laws are unconditional once enacted) has to be the cheap path. A SUBJECT MAY BE MILITARY -- `military_units` and `military_strength` ship alongside the six promoted economic labels. Not because the prototype needs them, but because a shape is only proven by an instance; the harness asserts a mixed economic-AND-military predicate resolves.  Comparators are EXACT on integral subjects (llround on both sides, so `exactly 3` means three and not 'within an epsilon of three') and float on continuous ones (a stockpile of 3.5 units is real state, and rounding it would be a lie).  THREE DECISIONS TAKEN, all recorded in NEEDS_REVIEW.json rather than left as precedent: NR-112 -- evaluate() carries a SUBJECT CORP that the design sketch did not. Every consumer BL-343 and BL-344 name is per-corporation (a levy is charged to a corp; an earned tech is per-corp state), so a world-only predicate could not answer either question. Purity is unaffected. NR-113 -- the `era` subject measures launchpad ownership, because ERAS.md is designed-not-implemented and launchpad presence is the only space gate the code actually has. The honest measure rather than an invented one; every authored `era` condition keeps its meaning when the real Era system lands. NR-114 -- the `market` subject measures the mean resolved price across every market in the world, summed in id order. A law asking 'is this good expensive yet?' is asking a world-level question.  Authority propagated to docs/SYSTEMS.md § Conditions.

BL-343.design:
## The bar: one law you can turn on and see

Not the ten-law list, not a policy screen. **One law, enacted, changing a number the player can
already read.** A law the player cannot observe working is indistinguishable from an unimplemented
one, and that is the difference between v0.1.3 being cuttable and being another design document.

## Which law, and why that one

**The extraction tax** -- BL-155's law #1, family (a) margin modifiers: a per-unit levy on raw
extraction output.

It is the right first instance for reasons that are about the SEAM, not the fiction:

- Its effect family (scale a flow's price/cost) is the one the other three margin laws reuse, so
  building it builds a quarter of the taxonomy rather than a special case.
- Extraction output already flows through a single accounted path, so the seam is one place.
- The result lands in `apply_budget`'s existing five flows, which the budget ledger already
  itemises (BL-072/073/074). **The legibility is free** -- a new expenditure line, not a new
  surface.
- It is unconditional once enacted, so it exercises BL-342's empty-`condition_set` path, which is
  the common case.

## Scope

**In:** the `law` record (id, subject, `condition_set`, effect, enacted flag); ONE effect family
(margin modifier); the enforcement seam in `economy_system`; the enacted set on the world; a
budget-ledger line; a headless harness. **Out:** the other nine laws, the other three families,
enactment UI beyond a debug toggle, repeal politics, nation-negotiated rates (BL-280).

## The enforcement seam -- the one real design decision

BL-155 names it as open: *"where enforcement hooks into `economy_system` without breaking
determinism."* Settle it here, with one rule: **a law is a modifier OVER the market, never an
override OF it.** That is the principle already established when price clamps were vetoed
(2026-07-11) precisely because they would fight price resolution rather than shift a flow's cost.

So the levy applies where the flow is *accounted*, not where the price is *resolved*: extraction
output is priced by the market exactly as now, and the levy is a separate accounted cost. Two
consequences worth stating -- the market stays the only thing that sets prices, and the player can
see the tax as its own number rather than as an unexplained worse price.

Evaluation happens once per law per tick, before the economy step reads it, so ordering is fixed
and the determinism invariant holds.

## The design test, honestly applied

BL-094 asks: *does this reach military as well as economic outcomes?* An extraction tax does not,
and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. What this item owes instead is that **nothing in the
law record or the effect dispatch assumes an economic subject** -- the taxonomy must accept a
military effect when there is one to add (BL-315's conflict spine). Build the seam so the answer
can become yes; do not claim it already is.

## Verification

`tools/verify/law_harness.cpp`: an unenacted law changes nothing; an enacted levy reduces net
margin by exactly rate x units, with no other flow perturbed; two identical worlds with the same
enacted set produce identical balances (determinism); repeal restores the baseline exactly.
BL-343.resolution: Complete 2026-08-10. One law you can turn on and see, end to end.  src/world/law.{hpp,cpp} holds the record -- id, condition_set, effect, enacted flag, rate, resource scope -- on world::laws in authored order. seed_prototype_laws appends the Extraction Levy at world setup UN-ENACTED, so the shipped economy stays bit-identical until someone switches it on; a levy that charged from turn one would have been a balance change smuggled in as a feature.  THE ENFORCEMENT SEAM IS SETTLED, which was the item's one real open design question. The rule: A LAW IS A MODIFIER OVER THE MARKET, NEVER AN OVERRIDE OF IT -- the same principle that vetoed price clamps on 2026-07-11, because a clamp fights price resolution rather than shifting a flow's cost. So the levy applies where the flow is ACCOUNTED (apply_budget) and never where the price is RESOLVED (clear_markets). Two consequences worth stating: the market stays the only thing that sets prices, and the player sees the tax as its own number instead of an unexplained worse price. evaluate_laws resolves each enacted law once per corp per tick, before the money loop reads it, so evaluation order is fixed and determinism holds.  LEGIBILITY WAS FREE, exactly as the design predicted. A sixth Levies bar joins the Finance card's flow chart beside income / inputs / maintenance / wages / interest, and a Laws section in the Budget ledger puts its checkbox directly beneath the two policy-tier STUBS -- so the difference between a drawn lever and a working one is visible in one glance.  tools/verify/law_harness.cpp, 21 assertions: an un-enacted law charges nothing and leaves a balance bit-identical to a world with no laws at all; an enacted levy costs exactly rate x units; NO OTHER FLOW MOVES (the modifier-not-override rule, asserted directly); repeal restores the baseline bit-identically; two identical worlds charge identically; resource scoping works and multiple levies stack additively; a conditional law charges only once its condition_set is met, which is the BL-342 seam live; and a processor's output is not levied, because the ore was already levied once.  apply_budget's new `production` parameter defaults to null, so all ~14 existing callers keep the pre-BL-343 arithmetic untouched -- the reason the change landed with no economy regression anywhere in the gate.  BL-094's test, honestly applied: an extraction levy reaches economic outcomes and not military ones, and the item does not pretend otherwise. What it owed instead is that nothing in the record or the effect dispatch assumes an economic subject -- law_effect_kind is an open taxonomy a military effect joins without reshaping anything, and the predicate already carries military subjects. Build the seam so the answer can become yes; do not claim it already is.  NR-117 records the two composition calls (raw output only; additive stacking). Authority propagated to docs/SYSTEMS.md § Policy and docs/economy/FINANCE.md § Levies.

BL-344.design:
## What already exists, and the one thing missing

More of this is built than the minor's design-forward status suggests. `world/tech_tree.{hpp,cpp}`
holds a tree; BL-310 shipped a radial constellation viewer on F9. What is missing is that
`tech_tree.hpp:49` stores:

```
std::string condition; ///< research | structure | stockpile | market | surplus | era.
```

A label. It describes what the gate would be about; it cannot resolve. So the tree is a picture of
a system rather than the system, and no tech has ever been earned.

## The bar: one tech, earned by play, unlocking something real

Replace `std::string condition` with BL-342's `condition_set`, then make exactly one tech
satisfiable through ordinary play and have its unlock change what the player may do. End to end,
once. Everything else in the tree keeps its authored shape.

## Scope

**In:** the field promotion (string -> `condition_set`) with the existing tree re-authored onto it;
per-corp earned-tech state; the unlock check at ONE content gate; the F9 viewer showing
locked/earned honestly. **Out:** research points and their economy (BL-332), the constellation
grain and deeds (BL-087, v0.3.0), quest trees, the Era->Filter rename (v0.4.0).

## Which unlock, and the design test

Pick a **building or recipe** gate, because `can_place_in_world` and the recipe registry are
already the single choke points that placement and production both pass through -- so the unlock
is one condition in one place, not a new subsystem.

**And prefer a MILITARY unlock over an economic one.** This is BL-094's test -- *"does this system
reach military as well as economic outcomes? If a technology can only unlock a building, it is
being designed for the corporate player we are pivoting away from"* -- and v0.1.5 has just given
us something to point at: `building_type::military_base` landed with BL-325. Gating the military
base behind a tech is the same amount of work as gating a smelter, and it is the instance that
proves the pillar the pivot cares about. BL-332 (military points and research) is the natural
follow-on and should be sequenced against this rather than designed independently.

## Why the promotion is safe now

No serialisation layer exists yet (BL-107 is still open), so changing a stored field is a
compile-time change rather than a save-format break. This is a *cheap* window that closes the
moment saves land -- worth doing now for that reason alone.

## Verification

`tools/verify/tech_gate_harness.cpp`: a tech with an unmet gate is not earned and its content is
refused with the right reason; satisfying the condition earns it; the unlock then permits placement
at the same call site that refused it; earned state is per-corp, not global; two identical worlds
earn identically (determinism).
BL-344.resolution: Complete 2026-08-10. The loop is closed: one tech, earned by play, unlocking something real.  tech_node::condition was a descriptive STRING -- a label that described what a gate would be about but could not resolve -- so no tech had ever been earned and the F9 constellation viewer (BL-310) was a picture of a system rather than the system. It is now a condition_set, alongside two fields the promotion forced: `earnable` (false for the ~130 nodes with no authored gate, because an empty condition_set is TRUE by BL-342 property 2 and an un-authored tech defaulting to empty would earn itself on the first tick -- absence has to be modelled by absence, never by an empty predicate) and `condition_label` (the original descriptive word, preserved, and now honestly named a label).  THE UNLOCK IS MILITARY, per BL-094: E0-ML-01 'Standing Garrison Doctrine' gates building_type::military_base (BL-325) behind two extraction sites AND a Cr 2,000 balance -- an AND-list doing real work, with the harness asserting each leg binds independently. Gating a smelter would have cost the same and proved nothing the pivot cares about.  Earned state is PER-CORP (world::earned_techs), never global -- a world-wide set would unlock a rival's research for the player, and the harness asserts a rival earning it leaves the player locked. advance_tech_gates runs once per economy tick after the money loop (so a surplus gate reads this quarter's balance), and is monotonic and idempotent: a tech is not un-earned by a later dip below its threshold.  The refusal TEACHES rather than just refuses (BL-071's rule, applied to the gate): a new placement_reason::tech_locked and construction_result::tech_locked carry the reason to the build ledger, which shows the locked row with its explanation instead of an enabled Build button the front door would then refuse. The F9 viewer now reports EARNED, LOCKED with its unmet conditions itemised, or -- honestly -- 'no gate authored'.  STRUCTURAL NOTE (NR-116): the PREDICATE lives in the Lua-free src/world/tech_gate.cpp, not in scripts/tech_tree.lua. tech_tree.cpp pulls in sol2 and is excluded from IO_WORLD_SOURCES, so a gate that gates construction.cpp could not live there and could not be linked by a headless harness. BL-346.design:
## Why this is worth its own item rather than a footnote

The estimate is not display-only. Three consumers read it, and two of them ACT on it:

- the per-building profitability readout (cosmetic, but it is what the player trusts);
- **BL-079's loss-streak reflex** — a background corp idles a persistently loss-making building. An over-estimate hides a real loss, so a stacked marginal site that should be idled keeps running;
- **BL-181's workforce auto-solve** — it maximises a building's profit using this estimate. Solving against an inflated curve puts the workforce dial in the wrong place.

So the defect propagates from a number on a panel into two of the three sanctioned auto-actions on corps. That is what makes it a bug rather than a rounding issue.

## The fix

Mirror what `run_extraction` now does, using the helpers BL-193 already added rather than
re-deriving them:

1. Scale nominal by `placement_rules::stack_output_scalar(placement_rules::stack_rank(w, id))`.
2. Taper against the stack's combined nominal, not the site's own — `stack_members()` gives the
   group and `extraction_nominal()` the per-member figure, so the sum is three lines.

Both already exist and are harness-covered, so this is re-use, not new economics.

## Verification

Extend `stack_capacity_harness`: for a 3-stack, the estimator's revenue for each member must match
what `run_economy_step` actually credits that member over the same tick, and its remaining-life
figure must match the tick on which the shared taper exhausts them. Today rank 2 and 3 diverge on
both. Asserting estimate-against-actual rather than estimate-against-a-constant is what stops this
re-diverging the next time extraction changes.
BL-346.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.10). THIS ITEM'S OWN DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG IN ONE HALF AND RIGHT IN THE OTHER, and the correction matters more than the fix. WRONG: `estimate_building_profit` is NOT the buggy function. Its revenue is `br->output_quantity x price` -- the REALISED credit, carrying no nominal and no taper -- so it was never inflated by stacking. It follows that **BL-079's loss-streak reflex never saw an inflated number**, contrary to this item's stated reasoning when filed; it reads realised output. That claim is retracted. RIGHT, and the actual site: `estimate_prospective_profit`, the PRE-BUILD candidate estimator behind the construction ledger. It applied no rank decay and tapered against a single site's own nominal. Fixed -- rank = existing members + 1 via `stack_members()`, `stack_output_scalar(rank)` on its nominal, taper sized against the stack's combined draw with the candidate included. `extraction_nominal` is now exported from economy_system.hpp so members are priced by the figure the tick actually draws rather than a re-derivation. The stale 'no deposit sharing with existing sites' contract in the header is rewritten. ALSO RIGHT, by a different route: BL-181 WAS acting on an inflated curve -- through its own inline model in `solve_workforce_target`, not through the estimator. It now takes a stack_rank and applies stack_output_scalar. Supplying the rank without a circular dependency split the pre-pass: Pass 2 groups and ranks (rank is build order, independent of the solver), Pass 3 solves, Pass 4 sizes the shared taper. MEASURED ERROR of the old estimator (fixture: lone nominal 20, price 2.5): rank 2 ample reserve +25%; rank 3 ample reserve +56%; rank 3 mid-band reserve +213% (3.1x). The third is both halves compounding -- it missed the 0.64 decay AND tapered against 8x20=160 instead of 8x48.8=390.4, reading taper 1.0 where the true shared taper is 0.5. HARNESS: stack_capacity_harness gained section S.R7, 20 assertions -- 43 -> 63 PASS. All are estimate-against-ACTUAL, never against a constant: estimate, then build, then tick, then compare that site's credited output x price, at ranks 1/2/3; plus a 5-level reserve sweep across a 3-stack's taper band asserting both estimate == credited revenue AND that the estimate reads zero on exactly the reserves the tick reports exhausted (the remaining-life claim, checked pointwise); plus 'the stack-aware estimate is BELOW the lone-site model it replaced' and 'an unstacked tile estimates exactly what it always did' -- so the fix is a correction for stacked sites, not a haircut on every estimate. RESIDUAL, out of scope and flagged: corp_ai.cpp:536's call to solve_workforce_target still passes no rank (defaults to 1). corp_ai.cpp was outside the slice and already carries a documented deliberate divergence there.

BL-347.design:
## The measurement

Same machine, same Release build settings, `min` compared rather than `mean` because min is the
load-insensitive statistic.

| bodies x corps | pre-BL-193 min | post-BL-193 min | factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 x 8    | 0.0106 ms | 0.0181 ms | 1.71x |
| 2 x 32   | 0.0462 ms | 0.0931 ms | 2.02x |
| 4 x 128  | 0.2489 ms | 0.6552 ms | 2.63x |
| 8 x 256  | **0.9581 ms** | **2.0449 ms** | 2.13x |

End-to-end exponent moved 1.30 -> 1.36 (tolerance 1.50, so the SHAPE assertions still pass). The
one that fails is the absolute bound: `R6 the largest swept world still ticks under 1 ms`.

The cost is present at EVERY rung, including the 1x8 baseline. That is the signature of per-tick
fixed work added to every world, not of a scaling term that only bites at size.

## What the prototype actually sees — read this before prioritising

At **prototype scale the game is unaffected**: 0.2015 ms mean, R5 passes with 5x headroom against
the 1 ms target. The failing rung is a **128x synthetic sweep**, not a world anyone plays. So this
is lost GROWTH HEADROOM, not a live frame-rate problem — the same category as BL-253, which BL-250
filed rather than treated as a cut blocker.

## Probable cause, in order of suspicion

BL-193 turned `run_economy_step`'s production phase into four ordered passes. Two of them were
HOISTED out of the per-corp loop for a correct reason -- a stack's members may belong to a corp the
loop has not reached yet -- but hoisting changed what they cost:

1. **Pass 1 contention now runs for EVERY `(corp, body)` pair**, unconditionally. At 8 bodies x 256
   corps that is 2048 evaluations per tick whether or not any stack exists.
2. **Pass 2 (BL-181 workforce auto-solve) likewise runs for every building** before production
   rather than within it.
3. **Pass 3 sorts** the extraction sites by id to establish stored order -- O(n log n) per tick.

## The fix direction

Make the pre-pass proportional to the stacks that actually exist, not to the world:

- Most tiles carry ONE extraction site. Group first and only sort/aggregate groups of size > 1; a
  lone site needs no combined nominal and no rank lookup.
- Restrict the hoisted passes to the corps that own a stacked site, falling back to the old
  in-loop path for everyone else. The correctness argument for hoisting only applies to stacks.
- Consider caching the `(tile, target) -> members` grouping and invalidating it where
  `invalidate_logistics_caches` already fires -- placement, demolish, completion, decommission.

## Verification

`econ_stability` R6 must pass again on an idle machine, and the per-rung mins should return to
within ~10% of the pre-BL-193 column above. Add the baseline rung (1x8) as its own assertion: the
1.71x there is what proves the cost is fixed-per-tick rather than scale-dependent, and no current
assertion would catch it re-appearing.
BL-347.resolution: Landed 2026-08-09 (v0.1.10). R6 passes again -- verified 3/3 on a loaded box; the fixed 8x256 min is 0.87 ms against the 1.0 ms bound, which is also BETTER than the 0.958 ms pre-BL-193 baseline. NONE OF THE THREE SUSPECTS THIS ITEM NAMED WAS THE CAUSE, which is the finding. Per-pass instrumentation at 8 bodies x 256 corps (128 extraction sites, none stacked) measured: Pass 2's BL-181 workforce auto-solve 0.10 us/tick (negligible); Pass 3's sort of extraction ids 7.1 us -- the O(n log n) term the item flagged as a prime suspect was 3% of the added cost; Pass 1 contention 102 us but mostly PRE-EXISTING work merely relocated. THE REAL COST WAS std::map NODE ALLOCATION, per tick, in worlds containing no stack at all: a map node per extraction site (`stack_by_building`, 45.6 us), a heap vector per tile (`stacks`, 18.3 us), a node per building (`corp_of_building`, ~60-89 us -- a map BL-193 added SOLELY to serve the pre-pass), and a duplicate contention map alongside the one already in `report.workforce_contention`. The lesson is that the expensive thing was allocation the restructure introduced incidentally, not the algorithmic term anyone would flag by reading. FIX: one flat `vector<site_slot>` sorted by (tile, target, id) and scanned for runs; only runs of length > 1 get an entry. A lone site's shared taper IS its self taper (combined == own nominal, a bit-identical expression), so it takes run_extraction's own-nominal path and `stack_draw*` became nullable. `corp_of_building` is built only when a stack exists; the duplicate contention map is gone; Pass 1's per-corp demand map became one reused vector. No caching was needed -- the sort costs 7 us. PER-RUNG min, A/B against base 65041ca, alternated over two rounds: 1x8 0.0119 -> 0.0102; 2x32 0.0484 -> 0.0397; 4x128 0.3027 -> 0.2246; 8x256 1.0657 -> 0.8625. FAIL in both base arms, PASS in both fix arms. DETERMINISM NOTE worth knowing: Pass 1's per-corp demand now walks in first-touch order over cc.assets (stored order) rather than ascending body id. The result is a keyed map either way and each body's accumulation sequence is unchanged, so it stays deterministic -- but it is an ordering change, recorded rather than buried.

BL-348.design:
## Why this is now worse than before BL-290

Before BL-290 the whole name was Earth-flavoured, so it was at least *consistent*. Now the culture
half is coined from the province's own phonology and the region half is not, which reads as a bug
rather than a style -- "MelethWorirUlael Reach" puts the two systems side by side in one string.

## The fix is already built

BL-290 added `coin_lexicon`, which coins a tongue's own words for *realm*, *town* and *epithet* as a
**pure function of the tongue** -- seeded by hashing the phoneme inventory, not by a caller's RNG.
Adding a *region* morpheme to that lexicon is the same shape as the three that exist, and it
inherits the property that matters: two passes coin the identical word for a culture without
sharing a stream.

So this is consumption again, not a new mechanism: `region_word` stops returning a literal and
starts asking the province's tongue.

## The one real decision

`region_word(col, row, gw, gh)` currently selects on POSITION -- a coastal province gets "Coast", an
interior one gets "Reach". That mapping is worth keeping: it means the name carries a fact about the
ground rather than being decorative. So the tongue needs a small *set* of region morphemes keyed by
the same geographic categories, not a single word -- coin N of them per tongue and index with the
existing positional logic.

Check what the current categories actually are before coining; if there are five, coin five.

## Verification

`settlement_harness` (21 assertions today) plus a determinism re-run: same seed, same province
names, and no English morpheme left in the generated set. Print a sample of ~15 province names in
the landing note the way BL-290 did -- that is what let its result be judged rather than trusted.
BL-348.resolution: Complete 2026-08-10. Consumption again, not a new mechanism: region_word stopped returning a literal and started asking the province's tongue.  coin_lexicon now coins NINE region words per tongue, sized to settlement.cpp's existing positional mapping -- a 5-band north-to-south axis and a 4-sector dawnward-to-outer axis. Nine rather than one because the item's one real decision was to KEEP the positional rule: naming a province for where it sits means the name carries a fact about the ground, and a single coined word per culture would have made it decorative. The rule was split out as region_slot() so the geography and the language it is spoken in stay independent.  The nine words are drawn LAST in coin_lexicon, after polity/settlement/qualifier, so those three keep their exact draws and every nation and city name generated before this change is byte-identical after it. Confirmed: creeds, settlement, history_ladder, era_world, determinism_harness and world_determinism all pass unchanged.  SAMPLE (default seed, as BL-290 did so the result can be judged rather than trusted): Dothkua Shethdeith, Rekmaik Taikme, Rairuath Rairith, Shuahualmi Beduas, Kuakuam Ruatem, Nuathorsho Ruvor, Kuakuam Muamem, Nuathorsho Rove, Tatadith Hezo. No English morpheme survives, and the kinship is emergent on this axis too -- Nuathorsho Rove / Nuathorsho Ruvor and Kuakuam Ruatem / Kuakuam Muamem draw their region words from one sound system, because coin_lexicon is a pure function of the tongue.  The English table is kept as the fallback for a culture whose tongue cannot coin at all (no onsets or no vowels): a province with no name would be worse than one with an out-of-register name, and that branch is unreachable for any culture the creeds pass actually produces.  OBSERVED AND NOT FIXED, because it predates this item: duplicate province names occur where two provinces share a culture AND a region slot (four 'Rekmaik Taikme' on the default seed). The positional mapping has nine outcomes and a large culture can hold more than nine provinces, so it was always possible; BL-290 and this item only made it legible. Not filed as work -- it may read as a plausible repetition of place names rather than a defect, and that is Ben's call to make when he sees the map.  Authority propagated to docs/generation/NATION_GENERATION.md § Pass 5 -- Naming.

BL-349.design:
## The test asserts something the generator explicitly declines to promise

`corporation_generation.cpp` says an unmet diversity floor is **honest** — it is a preference, not
a guarantee. `settlement_harness` S7d asserts it as **hard**. That gap is the defect; the knife-edge
behaviour is a symptom of it.

The mechanism, traced during BL-338: the floor's reroll only re-picks provinces **inside a corp's
home nation**, so it is simply unmeetable when no corp's nation holds a processing-capable
province. In the observed case energy provinces actually went UP (5 -> 6) while the assertion
failed — the count moved in the right direction and the test still flipped, because what it really
depends on is which nation happens to own which province after an unrelated generation change.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than tolerating

**A knife-edge test steers tuning silently.** BL-338 picked `lowland_share = 0.15` on a drainage
argument, and that value is also the one that keeps S7d green. The implementer said so explicitly,
which is the only reason it is visible at all — a less careful pass would have produced the same
number with only the drainage argument attached, and nobody would know the test had a vote.

That is the real cost: not a red suite, but a test quietly acquiring influence over parameters it
was never meant to constrain.

## The fix — pick one, they are different claims

1. **Assert what the generator promises.** Soften S7d to the preference it actually is: check the
   floor is *attempted*, or assert a much weaker diversity property that does not depend on
   province ownership. Cheapest, and most honest to the code as written.
2. **Make the generator meet the floor.** Widen the reroll beyond the home nation so the floor
   becomes meetable, then keep the hard assertion. This changes generated worlds, so it is a
   design decision about whether corp diversity is a guarantee — that belongs to Ben, not to a
   test.

**Do not simply retune until it is green.** That is what it has been getting.

## Verification

Whichever way it goes, the check is the same: sweep `lowland_share` across 0.15 / 0.20 / 0.25 and
confirm S7d's verdict no longer moves with it. If it still flips, the fix did not address the
mechanism.
BL-349.resolution: Complete 2026-08-10, taking the item's OPTION 1: assert what the generator promises.  corporation_generation.cpp says an unmet diversity floor is HONEST -- 'the last attempt's emergent set stands rather than being patched'. settlement_harness S7d asserted it as HARD. That gap was the defect; the knife-edge behaviour was only its symptom. The mechanism, traced under BL-338: the reroll re-picks provinces only INSIDE a corp's home nation, so the floor is unmeetable when no corp's nation holds a processing-capable province -- which is a fact about who owns what after an unrelated generation change, not about corporations at all.  S7d now asserts the property that does NOT depend on province ownership: the corporation set is not a MONOCULTURE (at least two of the three focus classes represented, with two or more corps). An all-one-focus world is a real defect in the derivation; a world missing one of three classes is the generator being honest about the ground it was given. The three-way split is PRINTED rather than asserted, so a genuine regression is still visible to a reader instead of being traded away for a green light.  VERIFIED BY THE SWEEP THE ITEM SPECIFIED. lowland_share across 0.15 / 0.20 / 0.25: S7d now PASSES at all three, where it previously passed / failed / failed. The underlying variation is unchanged and still reported -- 6/1/1, 5/0/3, 6/0/2 -- so the fix removed the test's vote without hiding the movement it was reacting to. lowland_share was restored to 0.15 afterwards; no generated world changed.  OPTION 2 WAS NOT TAKEN AND IS NOT DEAD. Widening the reroll beyond the home nation would make the floor meetable and justify keeping a hard assertion -- but it changes generated worlds, and it is a design claim about whether corporate diversity is a GUARANTEE or a preference. The item itself says that belongs to Ben rather than to a test. Recorded as NR-118 so it can be decided rather than defaulted.  The disclosure that produced this item is worth restating: BL-338's lowland_share pick was defensible on the drainage argument AND happened to be the green value, and the implementer said so. A less careful pass would have produced the same number with only the drainage argument attached, and nobody would have known the test had a vote.

BL-350.design:
**Status:** designed 2026-08-10, jointly with BL-340. Filed at BL-094's rewrite (NR-120).

### What this item owns

The mechanic BL-094's 2026-08-10 rewrite introduces and nothing existing covers: the militia
contracts a private company to build it equipment, rather than the equipment simply existing on a
market it can always afford, or being produced by an economic arm it owns outright (the 2026-07-04
chartered-corp/shared-treasury design, retracted by the rewrite).

### The spine

> **A procurement contract is a build order placed with someone else.**

BL-095 already ships the whole pacing model: commit on affordability, draw materials per tick as
real market demand, progress at the rate the market can supply, stretch up to ~10x or pause, pay
across the build rather than up front. A contract is that same object with two changes - the
materials are drawn against the **supplier's** market, and the output is delivered to the
**buyer's** pool.

This is the design's main claim to legibility. It reuses a shipped, understood, already-tuned
mechanism instead of inventing a second payment-and-pacing shape, and it means a stalled contract
stalls for a reason the player already understands from construction.

### The four filed questions, answered

**Q1 - Does the treasury debit on order, on delivery, or split?**
**Split: a deposit on order, the remainder drawn per tick across the lead time** - mirroring BL-095
exactly. Deposit fraction is a Lua constant (`economy.procurement.deposit_fraction`, first cut
0.25). Both alternatives fail concretely: on-delivery-only makes ordering free, so the dominant
strategy is to order from every supplier and cancel all but the fastest; on-order-only makes the
contract a spot purchase with a delay, where the counterparty's price and refusal do no work and it
collapses back into the order book.

**Q2 - Is refusal a hard block or a payable penalty?**
**A hard decline at quote time, with a stated reason. Not payable-through.** Refusal is not a wall:
it is priced information. A declining supplier states why, and other suppliers may still quote, so
the player routes around a refusal rather than buying through it. A payable override would collapse
refusal into a surcharge, making the counterparty a vending machine with a markup - precisely what
BL-094's rewrite retracted the shared treasury to avoid. **If everything is buyable, there is no
counterparty.**

Four decline conditions: **no capacity** (supplier holds no completed building that can produce the
good); **no input access** (supplier's market cannot supply the recipe inputs - reuses BL-095's
paused test); **law/embargo** (a `condition_set` (BL-342, shipped v0.1.3) evaluates false); and
**reputation floor** (pair standing below a threshold). The third is the useful one: condition_set
is shipped generic predicate machinery, so the law layer reaches procurement for free. That is
BL-315's "what the militia must answer to" axis arriving without new machinery, and it is the
strongest single argument that this seam sits in the right place.

**Q3 - Does reputation persist?**
**Yes, minimally: one scalar per (buyer, supplier) pair, moved by completed and cancelled contracts
only.** Effects are deliberately narrow - it shifts the quoted price within a band and breaks ties
in quote ordering. It does not unlock exclusive goods and does not by itself gate access beyond the
Q2 floor. The reasoning both ways: a persistent scalar is what makes a *sequence* of contracts a
strategy rather than each one an isolated purchase; but the moment it gates access to goods it is a
tech tree wearing a relationship's clothes, and BL-087 already owns that job. **Read alongside
BL-345** (politics MVP relationship axis, v0.1.6) - if BL-345 lands first, this reads its axis
instead of storing a second one.

**Q4 - Parallel to, or an extension of, BL-037's preferred-seller routing?**
**A parallel object on the same seam - not an order-book entry.** Written against BL-293 (landed),
which made the order book world state, had clear_markets read it directly, and joined three verbs
to corp_command (enum 11 wide, append-only). A contract cannot be a book entry: the book is
price-time priority over anonymous asks, with no representation for a named counterparty or a lead
time. But procurement joins the **same command seam**, for the reason BL-293 gives - so the
player's press and the AI's command are one implementation rather than two that agree.

Three new verbs, appended (enum 11 -> 14, append-only per BL-293's convention): `request_quote`
(ask a named supplier for price + lead time on a quantity), `accept_quote` (convert a live quote
into a contract; debits the deposit), `cancel_contract` (terminate in flight; forfeits the deposit,
moves reputation). Plus a **fourth flat-binary stream** after history_log and order_book, following
both exactly - magic IOPC, a version, count-prefixed records, rejection rather than
reinterpretation.

The composition, stated once: the contract's per-tick material draw enters market demand exactly as
BL-095's construction draw does, so the supplier's own inputs clear through the existing order book
at market prices. **Procurement is a layer over the market, not a second market.**

### Lead time is derived, not authored

`lead_time_ticks = base_ticks x ceil(quantity / supplier_throughput_per_tick)`, where throughput is
what the supplier's relevant buildings actually produce. A bigger order takes longer; a supplier
with real capacity is faster.

This gives the mechanic a second job worth having: **the quote is an intelligence channel.** You
learn something about a rival's industrial capacity by asking it for a price. That is legitimate
under BL-068 (competitor internals private, markets public), because the supplier volunteers the
figure in its own quote rather than the player reading its internals. It is a new, diegetic route
through the activity fog, and DISCOVERY.md should pick it up when this lands.

### The buyer is not the militia yet - and does not need to be

This item was filed `blocked_on: [BL-094]`. **That block is dropped**, and the reason is a version
inversion worth stating: this item targets v0.1.14, BL-094 targets v0.3.0. An item cannot be
blocked on one that lands three minors later without being silently unbuildable.

The block dissolves on inspection, because **the seam is buyer-agnostic.** A contract is between two
corp-like entities holding a treasury and a pool. Today both are `corporation`. When BL-094's
militia entity lands it becomes the natural buyer with no change to the seam. `requires: [BL-094]`
stays as a read-alongside; what BL-094 supplies is the *narrative* - why the buyer does not simply
build the thing itself - and narrative does not block a mechanism.

### Relationship to BL-280 (negotiated tax rate)

The shared shape is real: quote -> accept/decline -> standing term, pointed at different
counterparties. But BL-280's actual blocker is untouched by this design - its open question is what
the nation wants in return for a lower rate, the counterparty cost without which the tax dial is
free money. This item answers the analogous question structurally (the supplier wants price, lead
time and standing), which does not transfer to a sovereign granting a tax concession.
**Recommendation: this item does not wait for BL-280.** Extract a shared negotiation primitive when
the second user actually exists - not speculatively, on one user, against an item that is still
design-owed and difficulty 5.

### Scope explicitly excluded

The militia entity itself (BL-094, v0.3.0). Unit materiel consumption - what a fielded unit draws
per tick; BL-332's military points are a separate currency and stay separate. A negotiation dialogue
(BL-334, Stage C) - the quote is a number with a reason string, not a conversation. Tax bargaining
(BL-280). Multi-round haggling - a quote is take-it-or-leave-it in this cut; counter-offers are a
later item if the seam proves worth deepening.

### 2026-08-10 - sequencing: this lands AFTER the living world

Ben's call the same day put BL-365 (background industry) first, cutting v0.1.13 in Sprint 10; this
pair moves to Sprint 11 / v0.1.14. The reason is specific to this item: the counterparty model above
- a supplier that can refuse, with the player routing around the refusal to another quote - needs
suppliers to choose between. Against the pre-BL-365 world (8 lean corps, ~24 buildings on 15,120
tiles) "another supplier may still quote" is frequently false, and the mechanic would ship correct
but unexercised. That is the shape of Sprint 9's `hire_unit`, which shipped correct and was never
once observed firing across five harness seeds (NR-121).

### Requirement sketch (owed at promotion)

`headless`, a new procurement_harness: one contract quoted, accepted, paced and delivered end to end
with the treasury debited in the split shape; plus one decline observed for **each** of the four
refusal conditions. Sprint 9 shipped a done-definition that honestly recorded a path never observed
firing; this requirement is written so that does not recur.
BL-350.resolution: 2026-08-11 — complete (mechanism only, matching the item's own excluded scope). Three new corp_verbs (request_quote/accept_quote/cancel_contract) on the shared command seam; split-payment contracts (deposit + paced remainder); four distinguishable decline reasons (capacity, input access, embargo via condition_set, reputation floor); a standing (buyer,supplier) reputation scalar; a fourth flat-binary stream (procurement.{hpp,cpp}, magic IOPC) modelled on order_book. One named simplification: fixed-schedule pacing rather than BL-095's market-gated rate. New procurement_harness (18/18 PASS); eight pre-existing harnesses plus the real build confirmed no regression. requirements.json § procurement-contract-seam (R0-R4, all complete).

BL-351.design:
Evidence: market_clearing.cpp:329-336 computes available = min(order.quantity, pool) per order without decrementing a running remainder, so N duplicate orders each see the full pool. BL-365.design:
**Status:** design-owed - the shape below is settled; the calibration and the perf model are not.

### What exists today, stated exactly

`inject_substrate_demand` (market_clearing.cpp, step 2 of the clearing tick) writes:

- **demand** = `population_weight x demand_basket[r] x elasticity(price)` - a per-capita basket over
  seven authored resources.
- **supply** = `min(capacity[r] x capacity_scale, demand x clearing_fraction)` - an abstract nation
  capacity that tracks demand and clears it only to 90%, leaving the margin by construction.

No building produces any of it. The saturation is an assertion made once per tick.

### The measurement that motivated this

`pregame_balance_harness 80`, run 2026-08-10 against the real generated world: the player corp's
balance grows linearly (~5,530 cr/tick) to tick 23, decelerates through a knee at ~tick 24, and
**plateaus from ~tick 47 at ~185k cr**, oscillating +/-60 and drifting slightly down.

**The economy has a carrying capacity and reaches it.** That is the empirical case for this pivot:
the player corp saturates not because it has run out of ambition but because the abstract substrate
clears a fixed fraction and there is nothing further to trade against. A market made of real actors
is what turns that ceiling into a contested one.

Two incidental findings from the same run:

- **A resource sits pegged at exactly 4.00x base in every run** - food_rations at 12 ticks, steel at
  80. The harness reports that peg as a PASS for "the fillable gap is lucrative", so the assertion
  currently passes *because* a price is jammed against the band ceiling. A vacuous green this item
  must not inherit.
- **Per-tick cost on the real world is ~3.5 ms**, rising to ~4.9 ms by tick 160, against BL-250's
  0.0018 ms/tick on the small synthetic sweep world.

### The premise this reverses

GENERATION_STRATEGY.md's economic premise states a saturated base whose broad industry **the Nation
AI owns**, with the player and rivals as *specialist* corporations. Corp holdings are lean *because
of* that premise - `holdings_range` gives 3-4 / 2-3 / 1-2 buildings by focus, so eight corps plus
the player put **~16-32 buildings on Kepler's 15,120 tiles** (~0.2% of the map). Rewriting that doc
is part of this work, not a follow-on.

### Who owns the background industry - settled, and constrained

**More background corporations. Not a nation actor.**

This is not a preference; it is what the standing rules allow. `.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md`
prohibits nation behaviour (BL-054 stays deferred) while explicitly sanctioning background
**corporations** running a deterministic scored-utility layer over the corp-command seam
(BL-202/BL-203, widened by BL-324). Filling the world with nation-owned industry would need the one
actor class the rules forbid; filling it with firms needs no new exception at all.

### The count is calibrated, not authored

The load-bearing design decision. Do **not** author "place 800 buildings".

Generate background firms and their holdings until the body's real production meets a **target
fraction of its real demand** - first cut 0.90, deliberately the same figure as today's
`clearing_fraction`, so the opportunity gap is preserved *by construction* rather than *by
injection*. Generation stops on a measured condition, so the world stays saturated when tuning moves
recipes, deposits or population.

This is what keeps BL-078's and BL-112's requirements meaningful under a new mechanism: the same
assertions (differentiated demand, a live margin, a lucrative fillable gap) still hold, but they are
now *emergent* rather than *arranged*. **And the 4x peg above must be an explicit failure**, not a
pass - a good pegged at the band ceiling means supply is absent, which under this model is a
generation bug rather than a lucrative opportunity.

### It also inherits BL-340's background-demand step

BL-340's design pass originally specified substrate basket weights and an abstract refined-goods
capacity for its seven new goods. That step was deleted from BL-340 when this item was sequenced
first, because it would have extended a function this item removes. Background production and
consumption for silicon, refined_copper, ree_alloy, machinery, alloys, electronics and
spacecraft_components is therefore **this item's** responsibility - with the one deliberate
exception BL-340's design turns on: `spacecraft_components` gets no background demand, because the
militia's contracts are meant to be its only buyer.

### Open questions the design pass must settle

1. **Do background firms use corp_ai or a cheaper path?** Running the full scored-utility layer for
   ~80 corps is the perf risk above. A reduced per-tick model for background firms - produce, sell,
   maintain, but no build/demolish scoring - may be the honest answer, with corp_ai reserved for the
   handful of *rival* corps that actually contest the player. Probably the most important question
   here.
2. **Does the player see 80 corporations in every corp-facing surface?** The Corporation lens, the
   dashboard, and the market's preferred-seller list all enumerate corps today. A background/rival
   distinction may need to exist in the UI even if it does not exist in the data model.
3. **What happens to `nation.resource_abundance` and the substrate capacity arrays?** They become
   dead state if the substrate goes. Removing them is a components change; leaving them is a
   different kind of debt.
4. **Does BL-130 (real market inventory) become a prerequisite?** "No stored inventory" is a much
   larger simplification once supply is real - a market that conjures any shortfall undercuts the
   whole point of modelling real producers.

### Sequencing

**BL-253 is a hard prerequisite** and has been re-goaled A/v0.1.13 for it - see that item's
2026-08-10 note for the arithmetic. BL-366 (multi-building tiles) and BL-368 (real population
demand) land before this item within the same minor.

### 2026-08-11 update - Q1 resolved

Ben: full corp_ai scored-utility layer for ALL background firms, not a reduced model. Rejects the reduced-model recommendation above; the perf risk (NR-160) stands and BL-253 becomes load-bearing rather than a hedge - the O(corps x tiles) scan must be fixed before ~80 corps can run corp_ai every tick. Questions 2-4 remain open.

### 2026-08-11 third update - Q2-Q4 resolved

**Q2 (Ben): surfaces distinguish background firms from rivals, rather than showing ~80 uniformly.**
Data-model consequence: `corporation_component` gains `bool is_background` alongside the existing
`is_player` — a corp is exactly one of player / rival / background, no fourth state. Generation
(BL-365's own firm-generation pass) sets it true for every firm it creates; the handful of corps
generated by the existing CORPORATION_GENERATION.md pipeline (today's 8) stay `is_background =
false`, i.e. rivals. Surface consequence, left to BL-367-adjacent UI work rather than specified
here: the Corporation lens and dashboard group background firms into a single aggregate entry
("Independent Producers" or similar) with named rivals listed individually; the market's
preferred-seller list may still route trades through individual background firms internally
(BL-037's routing is unaffected) without exposing all 80 in the picker. `export_corp_blackboard`
(BL-206) should also carry the flag, so the AI-player word interface can distinguish "a rival is
doing X" from "background noise."

**Q3: dead substrate state is deleted, not kept.** `nation.resource_abundance` and the substrate
capacity arrays (`inject_substrate_demand`'s capacity/capacity_scale fields) are removed outright
once real firms replace them - per standing practice (no backwards-compatibility shims for
intentionally-removed mechanisms). This is a deletion this item makes directly, not a follow-on.

> **Amended at landing, 2026-08-11 (NR-172): `nation.resource_abundance` was KEPT.** The blanket
> claim above does not survive checking the actual read sites. What T1 deleted is the substrate
> injection state proper - `nation_substrate`, `nation_substrates`, `substrate_params`.
> `nation_component::resource_abundance` is a *different* thing that the substrate merely happened
> to sit next to: a per-nation sum of the resource deposits on its owned tiles, built in
> `nation_generation.cpp` (~519-543) and scaled in `settlement.cpp` (~770). Its two readers -
> `src/ui/entity_summary.cpp`'s ranked top-resources display and `hard_coded_world.cpp` - are
> general nation information and neither is substrate-specific, so deleting the field would have
> removed a working UI surface to satisfy a sentence rather than a dependency. It stays, and it
> earns its keep independently of this item.

**Q4: BL-130 (real market inventory) is now a hard prerequisite, not a neighbour.** The design
draft's own reasoning settles this: "a market that conjures any shortfall undercuts the whole point
of modelling real producers." Without real stored inventory, a background firm's sale and a
player's purchase both read/write a fiction, and the saturation this item exists to create would be
unverifiable. `requires` updated to include BL-130.

### Correcting the premise first

Ben's framing was "pivot on the design philosophy that a tile is one building". **That is already
not the rule**, and this item should not be written as though it were. `placement_rules.cpp`
§ `stack_capacity`:

```
if (type != building_type::extraction_site)
    return 1;
const float richness = tc.resource_deposit[target];
return max(1, richness / k_richness_per_site);   // 1-5 by richness
```

and `buildings_on_tile` counts per `(tile, type, target)`. So one tile **already** takes several
iron sites plus several coal sites plus one processor plus one port plus one hub. What is
capacity-1 is every **non-extraction** type - which is the exact half BL-193 deferred: "Whether
processors stack on land, workforce or road tier is a separate question, deferred by BL-193 rather
than answered by it."

**So this item answers BL-193's deferred question. It is a completion, not a pivot.**

### Why it matters to BL-365, beyond Ben asking for it

Saturation needs a lot of buildings, and Kepler's land is a fraction of its 15,120 tiles.
One-building-per-tile would spread industry as a uniform carpet. Multi-building tiles let it
**cluster** around population and deposits - an industrial district rather than a lawn. Clustering
is what makes a saturated world legible instead of noisy, so this is a legibility item as much as a
capacity one.

### The design question BL-193 actually left open

What bounds a non-extraction stack? Extraction has a natural bound (deposit richness). A processor
has none. The three candidates BL-193 named:

- **Land** - a flat per-tile ceiling. Simplest; says nothing interesting.
- **Workforce** - the stack is bounded by what the body's population can staff. Ties into a shipped
  system (workforce contention already throttles an over-built corp uniformly) and makes the bound
  diegetic.
- **Road tier** - the tile's logistics capacity bounds what can sit on it. Ties into roads
  (BL-146-149) and makes infrastructure investment raise the ceiling.

**Recommendation: workforce, with road tier as a modifier.** It reuses two shipped systems, gives
the player a lever (build population / build roads to raise the cap), and produces the clustering
BL-365 wants without a magic number. **Not settled - Ben's call.**

### The output-decay question

Extraction stacks pay `0.8^(k-1)` per site, because they share one deposit. Processors do not share
a deposit, so the same decay has no physical justification. Whether a processor stack decays at all
is part of this design.

### 2026-08-11 update - stack bound resolved

Ben: capped by terrain type, and a tile that accumulates enough buildings TRANSFORMS to a new "urban" terrain type. This is a new mechanic, not a simple numeric bound - it introduces a tile-composition transition at runtime (today's terrain is set once at generation) and a new `terrain_composition` value. Follow-on design work needed before this is buildable: the building-count threshold per starting terrain type, whether the transform is reversible (a tile that loses buildings ever reverts?), what "urban" terrain does to deposits/ambient-resource guarantee (TILES.md), and whether it changes tile stat/movement rules the way other composition values do. Files gain docs/economy/TILES.md and the terrain_composition enum (likely src/world/components.hpp or tile-adjacent header).

### 2026-08-11 second update - the urban-transform mechanic, designed

Ben's answer widened the question: the bound is **terrain-type capacity**, and a tile that fills
its capacity **transforms** to a new `urban` terrain-composition value. This is consistent with
TILES.md's own framing — "a fixed character set at world generation... does not change during play
except through deliberate player development" — the transform IS that deliberate-development
exception, not a violation of the fixed-at-generation rule.

**Scope note:** this only bounds *non-extraction* stacking (processors, ports, hubs, admin,
amenity, military base — the half BL-193 deferred and this item answers). Extraction stacking stays
richness-bound as shipped; it is a separate axis and untouched here.

**The cap table (authored, per starting composition — first cut, tunable data not a hardcoded rule):**

| Composition | Non-extraction cap | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Grassland, Forest, Wetland | 6 | Habitable; already the settlement-favoured compositions (POPULATION.md) |
| Tundra | 3 | Marginal habitability |
| Barren, Rocky, Regolith, Metallic | 4 | Industrial-friendly, low habitability ceiling |
| Volcanic, Icy | 2 | Hostile; TILES.md already gives these the lowest habitability ceiling |
| Ocean | n/a, exempt | Already capacity-1/no-buildings; this item does not touch water tiles |

**The transform, once capacity is reached:**

- Composition flips to a new **`urban`** value in `terrain_composition` (12th value). One-way,
  never reverts — matches TILES.md's "fixed... except through deliberate development" framing, and
  keeps the mechanic simple (no decay/abandonment modelling, which is out of scope here).
- Urban's own non-extraction cap is high (first cut: 12) — soft-bounded in practice by workforce
  contention (the shipped system), not by this cap.
- **No new extraction or ambient-resource placement on an urban tile** — the ground is built over.
  Extraction sites already standing when the transform fires are grandfathered and keep operating
  (deliberately not retconning existing player investment).
- Urban gets the **High** habitability ceiling (matches the settlement-favoured compositions it
  supersedes) and a build-cost/logistics discount reflecting established infrastructure — reuses
  the existing `landform_logistics_cost` multiplier mechanism rather than inventing a second cost
  axis; exact multiplier is an implementation-time tuning value, not a design commitment.
- Fires identically for player, rival and background corps — deterministic, no new exception to the
  standing rules (the transform is a mechanical consequence of building count, not an agency grant).

**Implementation shape (for the promoted task, not committed yet):**
- New `terrain_composition::urban` enum value, `src/world/components.hpp`.
- `stack_capacity` (`placement_rules.cpp`) reads a per-composition cap table for non-extraction
  types instead of the flat `return 1`.
- A transform check (e.g. `maybe_transform_to_urban(tile)`) runs after non-extraction placement,
  flips `terrain_composition` when the cap is hit. Determinism: pure function of tile state, no RNG.
- TILES.md gains the urban row (composition table, ambient-resource table exclusion, habitability)
  and the cap table above **once this lands**, per the standing authority time-slice rule — not
  before.

**Still open, left for the promoted task rather than blocking design:** whether the player gets an
explicit notification/log line when a tile transforms (a UI polish question, not a mechanic one),
and the exact urban logistics-cost discount value (a tuning number, set at implementation and
measured, not authored here).

Follows BL-366. Once the capacity-1 rule is lifted for non-extraction types, a tile can hold a
heterogeneous set - several extraction stacks against different deposits, several processors, plus

BL-368.design:
### Why it is separate from BL-365

Removing the substrate removes two things at once: fake supply (which BL-365 replaces with real
firms) and per-capita demand (which has no replacement unless population centres actually consume).
Splitting them keeps each independently verifiable, and the demand half is the one with a known bug
already attached.

### The known bug it must fix

MARKETS.md § Known limitations records it: the population agri demand stub never reaches clearing.
`run_economy_step`'s population pass writes `agricultural_produce` demand directly into markets, but
`clear_markets` zero-resets demand before accumulating - so the write is erased the same tick. The
real pull today is the substrate basket.

**Take the substrate away without fixing this and population demand is zero, not restored.** That is
the failure mode this item exists to prevent, and it is why this lands before BL-365 rather than
after.

### Scope

Generalise the erased agri stub into a real per-centre basket across the tradeable set, written at
the right point in the clearing order (after the reset, alongside the other demand sources), with
the price elasticity the substrate basket already models moved onto it.

### Open question

Habitability goods (clean water, consumer goods, medical supplies) are what a population *should*
consume, and none of them exist as `resource_type` values. Either population demand is restricted to
the goods that do exist (food_rations, agricultural_produce, water, refined_fuel), or this item
grows a resource tranche of its own - which would then want reading against BL-340's admission rule
(a resource must have a consumer or be a terminal object; no orphans).

### 2026-08-11 update - resource-tranche question resolved: grow it now

**Ben: add the habitability-goods tranche now**, rather than restricting population demand to the
four resources that already exist. Scope, drawn from RESOURCES.md's already-authored (but
un-modelled) habitability table:

- **Three new `resource_type` values land: Clean Water, Consumer Goods, Medical Supplies.**
  Building Materials and Utilities are explicitly OUT of this item's scope - Building Materials
  feeds construction cost (a different consumption path, PRODUCTION.md's concern, not population
  demand), and Utilities is already modelled as an abstracted budget cost with no resource
  identity of its own (RESOURCES.md is explicit on this). Only the three that population centres
  actually consume as tradeable goods are in scope.
- **Each gets a producing building** (Water Treatment Plant, Consumer Goods Factory,
  Pharmaceutical Lab per RESOURCES.md's table), satisfying BL-340's admission rule (a resource
  must have a consumer AND a producer, no orphans) on both ends: population centres are the
  consumer, the new building is the producer. Recipe inputs per the existing table - water for
  Clean Water; food_rations + refined goods for Consumer Goods; chemical + agricultural outputs
  for Medical Supplies - exact recipe quantities are an implementation-time tuning value, not
  authored here, matching how every other recipe in the prototype is handled.
- **Supply comes from BL-365's generation-till-target-fraction model, same as any other good** -
  this item does not hand-place these three buildings; BL-365's background-firm generation builds
  them like any other production building once the recipe/building types exist. This item's own
  scope is the resource_type values, the three building_type values + recipes, and the population
  demand basket read; BL-365 supplies the firms that produce them.
- **Save-format consequence**: three new resource_type enum values grow every per-resource array
  (sized by resource_count, already the additive pattern the enum has followed - see BL-107's
  version-header note on this being a live, not hypothetical, step now). No format-breaking
  change, purely additive.
- Files gain `docs/economy/PRODUCTION.md` (building/recipe tables), `docs/economy/RESOURCES.md`
  (flip the "None of this table exists" banner for the three landing values), and
  `src/world/components.hpp` (enum growth) alongside the item's existing file scope.
