BL-369.design:
### The question

`app::start_new_game` runs `pre_game_ticks` and then **rebases the clock**, so the warm start
consumes no in-game time and play still opens at `epoch_year` (1960). The world is generated *at*
1960 state and then ticked forward 20 years, with the result relabelled as the 1960 opening
position.

Is the warm start:

**(a)** a settling pass on a 1960 world, with the calendar correctly untouched, or
**(b)** genuinely the years 1940-1960, in which case generation should produce a **1940** world and
the clock should advance to 1960 during it?

(b) is the more coherent story and much the larger change - it would interact with BL-271's Era -1
history sim, which already runs 0->1960 and would need to stop at 1940 and hand over. (a) is what is
built and is defensible: the pre-game history is a fiction that produces a plausible opening
position, not a simulated two decades.

### Recommendation

**(a), documented.** Say plainly in ERAS.md that the warm start is a settling pass with no calendar
meaning. Revisit only if the opening year becomes player-visible or configurable - which the New
World wizard (STARTUP.md) could plausibly make it.

### 2026-08-11 - settled

Ben: (a) - the warm start is a settling pass with no calendar meaning; play still opens at epoch_year (1960). Action: add a short note to docs/economy/ERAS.md stating the warm start consumes no in-game time and is not a simulated 1940->1960 history. Light-mode doc change, no code change needed.

## CLOSED 2026-08-13 - already satisfied, no code change

warm start is a settling pass with no calendar meaning) is ALREADY PRESENT at ERAS.md lines
35-41, landed by commit 835ff70 (the Sprint 10 design pass), and src/core/app.cpp carries the
matching NOTE comment above pre_game_ticks. Nothing was owed - the item outlived its own
completion, which is the class of drift the retire sweep exists to catch.

BL-377.design:
**Status:** designed 2026-08-12, at Ben's request, as the first design work of the 0 CE refocus
(NR-177). This is the item NR-177 names as *"the mercenary SELL side (who contracts you, on what
terms, win/lose consequences) has no item at all, where procurement.cpp is only the buy side."*

### What this item owns

The player's **income**. Under the refocus the player is a mercenary company — the militia ancestor
— and a mercenary company's core loop is not extraction and it is not trade. It is: **be
contracted, field force, be paid.** Every other system in the game is either what you spend that
money on or what makes fielding force expensive.

That makes this the item the refocused product stands on. BL-350 shipped the seam by which the
player **buys**; nothing yet describes the seam by which it **earns**.

### The claim to reuse — stated precisely, because the loose version is wrong

The tempting one-liner is *"a mercenary contract is BL-350's procurement contract with the player as
the supplier."* **That is wrong in the part that matters**, and stating why is what shapes the
design.

`procurement_contract` (components.hpp:499, a 40-byte save-format record) carries
`resource + quantity` as its deliverable and completes when `ticks_elapsed` reaches
`lead_time_ticks`. Both are wrong here:

- **The deliverable is not fungible.** `resource + quantity` cannot express *"hold the river
  province through the campaign season"*. There is no resource whose quantity means that.
- **Completion is not a countdown.** A procurement contract finishes when enough ticks pass. A
  mercenary contract finishes when a **fact about the world** becomes true — or fails when the
  deadline passes and it is still false.
- **Failure is a distinct outcome from cancellation.** BL-350 has cancel (you walked away, you
  forfeit the deposit). This needs *lost* (you fought, you were beaten) — the same money outcome,
  a very different reputation and narrative outcome, and the one that makes contracts risky.

So: **a sibling record, not the same record.** What genuinely transfers is three shipped things,
and they are worth having:

1. **The command seam.** Three more `corp_verb`s appended to the same enum BL-350 extended to 14
   (append-only, BL-293's convention), so the player's press and an AI's command stay one
   implementation.
2. **The split-payment pacing.** Deposit on acceptance, remainder across the term — BL-350's Q1
   answer, already tuned, already legible, already reusing BL-095's construction model.
3. **The reputation scalar.** `world::corp_reputation`, a (buyer, supplier) map, already
   serialised. A mercenary's standing with a client is exactly that object.

### The spine

> **A contract is a condition_set the client will pay to have become true, by a deadline.**

That is the design, and it is short because `condition_set` (BL-342, shipped v0.1.3) is already
generic, pure, deterministic predicate machinery — and BL-350 already evaluates one for its
embargo decline, so the precedent for using it as *contract terms* is set rather than invented.

A contract record therefore carries: the client, the company, a **success `condition_set`**, a
**deadline in ticks**, a fee, a deposit fraction, and the accrued state (`ticks_elapsed`,
`deposit_paid`). The whole variety of contract types — take this province, hold that one, break a
siege, escort a convoy, deny a road — is **authored data in the predicate**, not a type enum in
C++. Adding a contract kind is a Lua change.

This is the design's main claim to legibility and it is the same claim BL-350 made: reuse a shipped,
understood mechanism rather than invent a parallel one.

### Where offers come from — the second reuse, and the stronger one

Contracts must be *offered* by someone, and the offers must be deterministic (io-standing-rules
§ Determinism). The answer is already in the tree.

`history_sim.cpp` scores four verbs per polity per year, and one of them is **campaign** — a pure,
integer, argmax-over-bounded-candidates scorer that already decides *which neighbouring province a
polity wants and how badly* (`w_farm`, `w_ore`, `w_port`, `w_ring`, `w_dist`, `w_def`,
`w_cult`). It also already computes the **stall**: a campaign whose arriving force falls under
`stalled_supply_q` because the objective is too far or the defender too strong.

> **A contract offer is a campaign the polity wants and cannot win alone.**

Take the existing candidate scoring; where the polity's own projected force is insufficient but the
objective's value is high, it does not launch — it **offers the objective as a contract**, at a fee
derived from the value it scored. Where it can win alone, it campaigns and offers nothing.

Three things this buys, none of which needs new machinery:
- **Offers are deterministic and replayable**, because the scorer already is.
- **Offers are legible**, because the fee tracks a value the sim actually computed rather than a
  designer's table.
- **The contract market has a natural rhythm** — offers appear when the political map is under
  tension and dry up when it is settled, which is a *reason* for boom and drought rather than a
  spawn timer.

The architecture transfers; the constants do not. That is BL-271's own transfer contract, applied.

### The four questions this design has to answer

**Q1 — Does the player choose the force, or does the contract specify it?**
**The player chooses.** The contract names the *outcome* and the *fee*, never the force. This is the
single decision that keeps the item a strategy game rather than a mission list: the whole skill is
reading whether the fee covers the force the objective actually needs, and a contract that specifies
its own force has pre-solved that.

It also makes underbidding a real failure mode — take a cheap contract, send too little, lose the
fight, lose the fee *and* the standing. That is the loop's teeth.

**Q2 — What happens on failure?**
Three distinct terminal states, deliberately, against BL-350's two:
- **completed** — the predicate held before the deadline. Balance of fee paid, reputation up.
- **failed** — the deadline passed with the predicate false. Deposit forfeit, no balance, reputation
  down *harder* than cancellation. You are not paid for trying.
- **cancelled** — the player withdrew before the deadline. Deposit forfeit, reputation down, but
  less than failure. An honest early exit costs less than a rout.

Failure must be survivable, per CONCEPT.md § Stagnation as loss: there is no lose screen, and losing
a contract is a *progressive* setback. The loss vector is the spiral — reputation falls, fees on
offer fall with it, and the company can no longer afford the force that would win the contracts that
would restore it. That is bankruptcy-by-reputation, and it is the mercenary reading of CONCEPT.md's
two existing loss vectors rather than a third one.

**Q3 — Can the player hold contracts from opposed clients?**
**Yes, and nothing prevents it mechanically — but standing prices it.** Accepting a contract against
a client you also serve is legal, resolves normally, and costs reputation with the injured party on
completion. Making it *illegal* would need a faction-alignment model the game does not have and the
refocus does not want; making it *free* would delete the only interesting thing about being a
mercenary.

This is the one answer here taken on design judgement rather than derived from a shipped mechanism.
It is recorded in NR-177's family as reversible.

**Q4 — Is the contract offer public or private?**
**Private per client, visible to the player only where the activity fog already reaches** — the
existing `body_activity_visibility` tiers (BL-089, DISCOVERY.md). A polity you have never dealt
with and cannot see does not offer you work. This gives the discovery layer a second job for free
and gives reputation a *reach* dimension: standing opens the map, not just the price.

### Serialisation

A **fifth flat-binary stream** after history_log, order_book and procurement, following procurement
exactly: leading magic (`IOMC`) + version, count-prefixed records, rejection rather than
reinterpretation, a `static_assert` on the record size as the tripwire. See procurement.hpp; this
item does not restate the rationale.

The `condition_set` in the record is the one novel serialisation question — it is a structured
predicate, not a scalar. Two options at promotion: store the predicate inline, or store an index
into an authored contract-template table and keep the predicate in Lua. **Recommend the template
index**: it keeps the binary record fixed-size, it makes contract kinds data, and a save that
outlives a template-table change should reject rather than reinterpret, which the version bump
already gives.

### Scope explicitly excluded

The combat that resolves a contract (**BL-315**, conflict spine — this item states what is *at
stake*, never how a fight resolves). Unit materiel draw per tick. Multi-round fee haggling — a
contract is take-it-or-leave-it in this cut, matching BL-350's Q4 exclusion. Contracts between the
player and *another corporation* rather than a polity. Any narrative or dialogue layer.

### Requirement sketch (owed at promotion)

`headless`, a new contract_harness: one contract offered by the objective scorer, accepted, paced
and completed with the fee paid in the split shape; plus one observed instance of **each** of the
three terminal states, and one determinism assertion (same seed, same offers). Written this way
because Sprint 9's `hire_unit` shipped correct and was never observed firing across five seeds
(NR-121), and BL-350's own requirement was written to stop that recurring.

BL-378.design:
**Status:** designed 2026-08-12, from Ben's steer the same day. **Corrected mid-session** — the
first cut of this item read his *"change the canvas to a mini-map"* as *the minimap becomes a world
overview with a viewport rect and click-to-pan*. That was wrong. His actual meaning:

> *"I meant the circumplanetary mini-map to a max zoom canvas render, fixed on the player's starting
> base."*

Not an overview. A **fixed close-up of home**. The rest of this design is written against that.

### The problem

`canvas_level` (ui_state.hpp:16) has three rungs — `solar`, `circumplanetary`, `planetary` —
and MINIMAP.md's model is *the minimap always shows the rung one step out*. With the primary canvas
on Planetary, the minimap therefore shows **Circumplanetary**: a planet with its moons and local
space.

Under the refocus that view is dead weight. There is one body, space is unreachable, and the inset
spends 336 x 252 px of prime screen real estate showing somewhere the player can never go.

### The replacement

> The inset becomes the **Planetary canvas rendered at maximum zoom, camera locked to the player's
> starting base.**

It is not a navigation control and not an overview. It is a **standing readout of home** — what your
camp looks like right now, at full detail, while the primary canvas is somewhere else entirely.

**Why that is the right object for this game specifically.** A mercenary company is structurally
always away from home: the contracts (BL-377) are fought on someone else's ground, and the primary
canvas follows the fighting. The one thing the player has that is *theirs* is the base. Giving it
permanent screen presence makes the company feel like a company rather than a cursor, and it costs
no new interaction vocabulary at all.

It also quietly answers "what do I own" without a ledger round-trip, which is the same argument
BL-194's Selection-band neighbourhood view already won.

### Cheap by reuse — this is mostly wiring

Three shipped pieces do the work:

1. **BL-194's zoomed tile-neighbourhood view** already renders a small hex neighbourhood into an
   inset rect in the Selection band. That is this feature, pointed somewhere else.
2. **`hex_render.hpp`** is already the shared source of truth for the terrain palette
   (`terrain_colour`), the landform relief channel (`landform_relief`) and hex geometry —
   extracted precisely so the band inset and the main canvas do not diverge. A third consumer is
   what it was built for.
3. **BL-331 (landed)** seeds the player corp with one `military_base` on a home-province tile, so
   the camera target is a real entity from turn one rather than something this item must invent.

Zoom bounds are already defined: `kMaxZoom = 20.0f`, `kMinZoom ~= 0.877`
(body_surface_canvas.cpp:44-45). "Max zoom" is therefore a value, not a judgement call.

### The layout constraint — the minimap box keeps its rect

`selection_band_height = minimap_height + chrome_margin` (foldout_column.cpp:44-49), where
`minimap_width = max(336, 0.28 x min(disp_x, disp_y))` and `minimap_height = 0.75 x width`.
That is **336 x 252 px at 1920x1080** and 403 x 302 at 2560x1440.

The Selection band's height is derived from the minimap's so the bottom strip's top edge lands
exactly on the minimap's — the alignment BL-216 and BL-312 were written to fix. **Changing the
inset's contents is free; changing its rect is not.** If a later item wants it resized, the
derivation must be re-anchored first, as its own change.

### The ladder collapses with it — by GATING, not deleting

With the inset no longer showing the rung above, nothing reaches `solar` or `circumplanetary`
and the asymmetric descend-by-body / ascend-by-minimap model has no referent.

**Do not delete them.** Ben's ruling (NR-177) is *stash the space work and merge it back for DLC*,
which makes deletion the expensive path — resurrecting reverted code across months of divergence.
`canvas_level` keeps all three enumerators behind a world-level capability flag (era, or an
explicit `space_reachable`). The ancient product ships with it false; the DLC merge is a flag flip
plus content. SOLAR.md and CIRCUMPLANETARY.md then document a gated feature rather than rotting.

### The three open calls

**Q1 — Is the inset interactive at all?**
"Fixed" is explicit, so **no pan and no zoom inside it**. But a single click is nearly free and
obviously wanted: **recommend click-to-centre** — clicking the inset moves the *primary* canvas to
the base. That keeps the inset itself fixed (Ben's word) while giving "go home" a one-click home,
which a player will otherwise want within about ten minutes.

**Q2 — What is the target if the starting base is gone?**
Bases can be demolished, and a mercenary company plausibly relocates. `corporation_component`
already carries an **HQ** (BL-182 — the holding nearest the corp's holdings centroid, designated at
generation), which is defined for every corp and survives any single building's loss.
**Recommend: the starting base, falling back to the corp HQ**, so the inset always has a subject and
never renders empty.

**Q3 — Does it show live activity, or just terrain?**
**Recommend live** — units garrisoned, the building's own state, construction in progress. A static
terrain thumbnail is a screenshot; the reason to give a readout permanent screen space is that it
*changes*. This is the difference between the feature being loved and being ignored.

All three are recorded here as reversible rather than assumed settled.

### The action dictionary must move with it

Entries in the `canvas` family of ACTIONS.json are invalidated, and a stale entry misleads a
text-driven player exactly as a stale golden misleads a visual check (ACTIONS.md's own standing
rule): `canvas.ascend_key`, `canvas.descend_key`, `canvas.minimap_ascend` retire while gated;
`canvas.navigate`, `canvas.body_next`, `canvas.body_prev` lose their referent with one body.
Add the click-to-centre verb if Q1 is accepted. Re-render with
`node tools/session/render_actions.js`.

### Scope explicitly excluded

Any change to the Planetary canvas's own draw pass, hit-testing or lens rendering. Resizing the
minimap rect or re-anchoring `selection_band_height`. A second inset. Whether the base view earns
its own lens treatment.

### Requirement sketch (owed at promotion)

`visual`, a new scripts/verify/minimap_base_render.lua: the inset renders the player's starting
base at max zoom, stays fixed while the primary canvas pans and zooms away from it, and survives the
base being demolished (Q2 fallback). Plus `headless`: with the gate false, no code path reaches
`canvas_level::solar` or `canvas_level::circumplanetary`.

BL-379.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, from the NR-129 investigation.

## What is wrong

`corp_ai.cpp`'s muster-base candidate calls `can_place_in_world(w, tid, military_base, iron_ore, -1.0f, corp)`. The `-1.0f` disables the BL-323 logistics-reach rule. `construct_building` — the seam that actually applies the resulting command — passes `reg.construction().max_logistics_reach` instead. So enumeration is checking a strictly weaker precondition than application, and can select a tile the seam will refuse.

The tech gate in the same call is handled CORRECTLY (the `corp` argument is passed explicitly, and defaults to `null_entity` which would disable it) — this item is only about the reach argument sitting beside it.

## Why it is hygiene rather than a bug

The greedy loop increments its budget counters only after `apply_corp_command` returns `applied`. A refused candidate therefore consumes no build slot, mutates nothing, writes no decision-log entry, and does not stop the next-best economic build being tried in the same evaluation. The cost is one wasted seam call per evaluation while the corp holds no military base. That ordering is now commented at the increment site, because it is what makes this whole class of mismatch benign and nothing asserted it.

## The catch, which is why this is not filed as a one-liner

Passing the registry's reach budget is not obviously sufficient. `tile_reach_cost` returns -1 for 'unknown' when the body's reach field has not been built, and the reach rule treats unknown as a pass — so if the field is not warm at enumeration time the check is a no-op and the change buys nothing. Enumeration also holds a `const world&` while building the field needs a mutable one. So the real work is establishing whether the field is reliably warm at that point in the tick, and if it is not, deciding whether enumeration should skip the reach check honestly (documenting that the seam owns it) rather than appear to perform one.

## Done when

Either enumeration and the seam agree on the reach budget, or the enumeration site carries a comment stating why it deliberately does not and what absorbs the difference. Both are acceptable outcomes; what is not acceptable is the current state, where the argument looks deliberate and is unexplained.

BL-382.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, from the NR-180 investigation. Two independent findings, filed together because they are the same class: a write that looks like a mechanism and is not.

**1. `supply_system.cpp`'s convoy injection is unpriced — and asymmetrically visible, which is the real finding.** The line adds arrived convoy cargo to `market.supply` and its comment says 'Inject into market supply so the next clearing pass prices it'. But `credit_arrived_convoys` runs AFTER `clear_markets` in the tick, and `clear_markets` zeroes both arrays at its top — so the value written is erased before any clearing pass ever reads it. The pool credit beside it IS live and does real work; only the supply write is inert. So far, so harmless. But it is NOT unread. `run_corp_strategic_step` is the last thing `run_economy_step` does, and `run_economy_step` runs BEFORE `clear_markets` in the tick — so the scorer reads the inflated `supply` that the clearing pass will shortly zero without ever pricing. The convoy write is therefore invisible to price resolution, to the ledgers and to the player, and visible to exactly one consumer: `forecast_glut_multiplier`'s numerator. A write that only the AI can see is a worse defect than a dead one, because it gives the rival a private and arbitrary signal that nothing else in the game agrees with.

Either move the call, or delete the write and correct the comment. Deleting is probably right: the cargo lands in the pool, and the pool's surplus reaches supply through the ordinary auto-surplus path next tick anyway. Note the interaction with BL-381 — while the glut gate stays non-discriminating this costs little, but it must not survive the fix that makes the numerator mean something.

**2. `inject_interbody_demand` can never fire in the generated world.** It gates on `home_shortfall = home.demand[r] - home.supply[r]; if (home_shortfall <= 0.0f) continue;`. Home supply exceeds home demand by two to three orders of magnitude for essentially every resource (see BL-381), so the shortfall is always negative and outpost markets receive zero pull. The mechanism is sound and the world simply never satisfies its precondition — so this is NOT a delete: it is a note in MARKETS.md saying the pull is dormant until demand means something, and a natural thing to re-check when BL-381 lands.

Neither is urgent. Both are the kind of thing that costs an hour of confusion to the next person who reads the file believing the comment.

BL-386.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found by AI play (two independent players, same conclusion).

## The defect

In the auto-clear pass for unmatched standing sell supply: `const float clearing = std::max(rp, se.floor_price);` followed by `flows[se.corp].income += se.rem * clearing;`. Nothing debits a buyer, nothing caps the floor, and nothing checks the floor against the market's own price band. Income is exactly linear in the floor the seller names.

Measured by a player: baseline 5,535/tick; floor 2.0 gave 17,829/tick; floor 5 gave 44,654/tick; floor 1e6 gave 8.94 BILLION per tick; floor 1e12 reached cash 1.587e17 by tick 26. The market price of the good never moved off 0.625 in any run and no other corporation's balance was debited.

## AND IT IS ALREADY FIRING, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MATTERS

This is not only an exploit a player could reach for. **The rival AI is doing it every time it trades**, and it resolves NR-144's open question about why rival trading tripled AI net worth.

The chain: a glutted good's price is pegged at `0.25 x base_price` (the band floor). `corp_ai` lists at `floor = base_price * trade_floor_multiple`, default 1.0, i.e. AT base_price. So `clearing = max(0.25*base, base) = base` — **every unit the AI lists earns four times the market rate, funded from nothing**. NR-144 recorded the tripling and reasoned it was 'corps converting idle stock to cash rather than a broken scorer'. It was a broken market, and the scorer was innocent.

## THE CODEBASE ALREADY KNOWS HOW TO DO THIS, ONE LOOP AWAY

Independent triage found the detail that makes the fix unarguable: the MATCHED-trade loop immediately above this one DOES debit the buyer — `flows[t.buyer].expenditure` — because a matched trade has a real counterparty. The auto-clear pass beneath it credits `flows[se.corp].income` and debits nobody. So the correct shape is present in the same function, twelve lines earlier, and the defect is that one path was written as a market and the other as a wish.

## Why the auto-surplus path is fine and this one is not

The auto-surplus path clears at `ref_price` — the price the market actually resolved — so 'the market is a perfect counterparty' costs the world goods at a fair price. That is a deliberate prototype simplification (MARKETS.md) and it is defensible. The order book path lets the SELLER name the price the perfect counterparty pays, which is a different thing entirely: it is not a simplification of a market, it is the absence of one.

## PROPOSED FIX

A floor price should DECLINE a sale, not raise its price. That is what a floor means and what the dictionary entry for `place_sell_order` already tells an agent it means ('minimum acceptable unit price'). Concretely, in the auto-clear pass:

```
if (se.floor_price > rp) continue;   // held back: the market will not meet the floor
flows[se.corp].income += se.rem * rp;
```

so an order above the market clears NOTHING and the stock stays in the pool, and an order at or below the market clears at the market price. That makes a floor a genuine reservation price, makes `trade_floor_multiple` a real strategic dial rather than a money multiplier, and removes the free income without removing the buyer of last resort.

**Expect this to move every economy golden and to CUT AI net worth by roughly the tripling NR-144 recorded.** That drop is the fix working, not a regression — re-bless with a note pointing here.

## THE SPEC SAYS TO DO IT, WHICH IS WHY NOBODY CAUGHT IT

Found in triage and it changes what this item has to touch. The behaviour is not code drifting from a
specification — it IS the specification:

* `docs/development/req/requirements.json`, group `player-sell-orders`, row **R2**, status **complete**:
  "A standing player sell order sells up to its quantity from the (corp, body) pool, **valued at
  max(resolved_price, floor_price)**."
* `docs/economy/MARKETS.md` step 11 states the same thing and calls it a **prototype invariant**.
* `ACTIONS.json`'s own entry contradicted ITSELF — asserting `max(price, floor)` in one clause and
  "a floor above what the resolution supports means less or nothing sells" in the next.

So the requirement certifies the defect, the authority doc blesses it, the dictionary states both the
behaviour and its opposite, and every downstream check confirmed the code against the wrong spec. The
requirement must be REWRITTEN, not re-verified; MARKETS.md's step 11 restated; the dictionary entry
corrected (done 2026-08-13).

## AND THE AI's DEFAULT STOPS WORKING WHEN THIS LANDS

`corp_ai` lists at `floor = base_price * trade_floor_multiple`, default **1.0**, while a glutted good's
resolved price sits at the band floor **0.25 x base**. Under the fixed rule — a floor above the market
clears nothing — a rival at the default would sell **nothing at all**, having previously sold everything
at 4x. So `trade_floor_multiple` must be re-tuned in the same change, or the fix silently converts an
overpowered trader into one that never trades. It becomes a genuine reservation dial for the first time,
which is what BL-380 wants it to be.

## Guard it with a test that could have caught it

`order_book_harness` must gain an assertion that no corporation's income from a clearing exceeds its cleared quantity times the market's resolved price. That is the invariant, it is one line to check, and it is the thing no existing assertion states.

Note the fix direction the triage explicitly rules OUT: do not cap `floor_price` in `corp_command`'s validation. An arbitrarily high floor is a legitimate thing for a seller to name — it means 'hold' — and the defect is in the payer, not the validator. Capping the input would hide the bug and remove a real strategic option at once.

## Independently verified 2026-08-13

Triaged as a real defect at high confidence by an agent with no authoring context, which reproduced it end-to-end against the live seam and concurred with the proposed fix.
BL-386.resolution: Landed 2026-08-14 (seam batch, commit 62e7951 + integration fixes). The floor is a reservation price: auto-clear holds above the resolved price, pays rem*rp otherwise; trade_floor_multiple 1.0->0.25 so rivals keep trading. Full evidence in requirements.json § sell-order-floor. Follow-on: BL-422 (held orders still credit market inventory at listing time).

BL-387.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found by AI play.

## The defect

`apply_corp_command` begins with `if (w.corporations.find(cmd.corp) == w.corporations.end()) return rejected_no_corp;` and that is the whole of its actor validation. Per-verb checks use `owns(w, cmd.corp, cmd.subject)` to confirm the corp owns the BUILDING it names — but nothing confirms the CALLER may act as that corp.

In play: a player issued `COMMAND corp=<rival> verb=9 ...` and it returned `applied`. Rival balances moved by +57.9M, +50.1M, +25.7M over six ticks. The inverse is an attack rather than a gift — a 0.001-unit order placed in a rival's name permanently suppresses that rival's auto-surplus path for the triple (BL-380), throttling a competitor's entire income on that good.

## Why this was never a defect before, and is now

In-process, `cmd.corp` is set by the scorer itself, so the field was never attacker-controlled and the missing check cost nothing. `--serve` turned the seam into an EXTERNAL input surface and the same field became caller-supplied. Nothing about apply_corp_command changed; its threat model did.

**This is the second instance in one session of exactly that pattern** — the NaN float guard (NR-184) was the first. The AI-facing seam is an untrusted input boundary in a way the internal caller never was, and validation written for a trusted caller does not transfer. Two instances is enough to call it a rule rather than an incident, and it should go in the standing rules.

## PROPOSED FIX

Authority belongs at the PROTOCOL layer, not in apply_corp_command — the in-process scorer legitimately commands every rival corp and must keep doing so. So:

* `run_serve` gains a session actor: `--serve --as <corp>` (default: the player corp), and the `COMMAND` opcode refuses any `corp=` that is not the session actor, with a new `rejected_not_owner` at the opcode level.
* For the research use where an agent legitimately drives several corps (bot-vs-bot, the BL-279 corpus), an explicit `--as any` opt-in, so the permissive mode exists but must be ASKED for and is visible in the invocation.
* `tools/mcp/server.js` pins its actor at startup and never forwards a caller-supplied `corp` for writes.
* `smoke.js` asserts that a command naming a corp other than the session actor is refused — replacing the assertion that currently only checks the reply is well-formed, which this session already flagged as overclaiming.

Note the interaction with BL-386: with the floor-price fix in, driving a rival is no longer a route to printing money, but it is still a route to sabotaging one.

## The read side is worse, and is filed as BL-397

Adversarial play found the same hole on the READ path: the BLACKBOARD opcode takes a corp id from the request line and returns that corp's OWN-ASSET facts — cash, pools, recipes, workforce. So BL-068's competitor-visibility model is enforced within a blackboard and not between them. Fix both together under one session-actor model; stopping the writes while the reads still hand over the private view would be half a fix.
BL-387.resolution: Landed 2026-08-14 (seam batch, commit 93abadb). Session actor at the protocol layer: --as <corp|any>, default player corp; COMMAND refuses non-actor corps; server.js pins its actor. Standing rules gained the untrusted-boundary invariant (NR-234). Evidence: requirements.json § seam-actor-authority.

BL-388.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found by AI play.

## The defect

`apply_corp_command`'s build case calls `construct_building(w, reg, cmd.corp, cmd.tile, cmd.type, cmd.target, built)`. `corp_command` carries a `recipe` field, documented in its own header as 'set_recipe (and build seed)', and the ACTIONS dictionary tells an agent that `build` takes a recipe. It is never passed.

A player ordered a Food Processor with `recipe=2`, got `result=applied building=34631`, and the blackboard then reported `building_recipe = 0` — a steel smelter. Success reported; different building delivered.

## Why it is worse than a dropped argument

It is silent, and it defeats the seam's whole self-correction story. A typed rejection teaches an agent what it did wrong; a success that builds something else teaches it something false. The player only noticed by reading the blackboard back and comparing — a check most callers will not make, because `applied` is supposed to mean applied.

It also compounds: because every seam-built processor runs recipe 0 (steel) and steel's coal reagent is unpriced in the served world (BL-389), no seam-built processor has ever produced a single unit. A player ran five campaigns and roughly eighty building-ticks of processing without one unit of output, and could not tell why.

## PROPOSED FIX

Forward `cmd.recipe` to `construct_building`, and REJECT rather than silently coerce when the recipe is invalid for the type: a recipe on a non-processing type, or an id `get_recipe` does not resolve, should be `rejected_invalid`. Note `set_recipe` has the adjacent hole — it validates that the recipe resolves but not that it belongs to `processing_facility` — and both should be closed together, since a caller that can name a recipe at build time will name one at set time too.

Add an assertion that a building constructed through the seam carries the recipe it was asked for. Nothing currently checks that the command's arguments survive into the world it creates.

## Independently verified 2026-08-13

Triaged as a real defect at high confidence, reproduced end-to-end. The triage adds the mechanism precisely: `construct_building`'s eighth parameter defaults to `no_recipe`, and the function then COERCES it — `bc.recipe = (recipe != no_recipe) ? recipe : reg.recipe_id("steel")`. So the argument is not merely dropped; the callee substitutes steel by design when none is supplied, which is reasonable for a caller that has no opinion and wrong for one that stated it. Forwarding `cmd.recipe` is the one-line core.

BL-394.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found in play.

## The gap

`debit_hire_cost` charges a roster row's gate. Row 0's gate is `{0,0,0,0}`, so nothing is tested and nothing is debited. There is no cash cost anywhere in `hire_unit`'s path, and no per-tick upkeep is applied to a raised unit by anything in `apply_budget`. A player raised ten units in a single tick, for nothing, and could have raised a thousand.

The reason this has never shown up is that the only actor exercising the verb until now was `corp_ai`, which caps itself at one hire per evaluation and three units held. That is a SCORER POLICY, expressed in `corp_ai_params`, not a rule of the game — so it binds the AI and does not bind a player, and the seam has just acquired players.

**Same shape as BL-387 and NR-184 — the third instance this session.** A constraint that lived in the only caller looked like a rule until a second caller appeared.

## PROPOSED FIX

Give the roster a real cost floor: no row should hire for nothing, and the classical rows in particular should cost SOMETHING even if the gate is meant to be permissive. Author it in `economy.lua` beside the other roster data so it is a tuning change.

Then decide whether standing forces cost upkeep. They currently do not, which means an army is a one-off purchase with no carrying cost — a strange shape for a game whose player is about to become a MERCENARY COMPANY (NR-177), where the tension between force size and payroll is close to the whole point. Flagged rather than decided here; it belongs with BL-377's contract loop.

BL-396.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found by an agent whose whole agenda was to break the seam. It is the most severe finding of the session and it is one root cause with many faces.

## The root cause

Every field in the COMMAND opcode is parsed with `atol` and then `static_cast` directly into its destination — `corp_verb` (uint8_t), `building_type`, `resource_type`, `road_tier` (uint8_t), `workforce` (int). Nothing checks that the parsed value is in range for the type it is about to become.

## What that produces, measured

**A rejection that mutates, which is the invariant this seam must never break.** `verb=256` truncates to 0 and BUILDS A BUILDING, answering `applied building=34630`. `verb=512`, `verb=1024` and `verb=-256` all build. `verb=265` places a sell order. So a caller naming a verb that does not exist gets a completely different action performed in its name, reported as success.

**A segfault.** `type=200` casts to `building_type` and indexes the economics array out of bounds: exit 139, no RESULT line, no BYE, the process gone and the session's whole world with it. One line from any caller.

**Phantom buildings.** `type` 8..20 pass placement and construct a building of a type not in the enum, which then persists in the corp's asset list, ticks through `run_economy_step` forever, and is priced off whatever memory follows the economics array.

**Silent wrapping.** `workforce=-5` and `workforce=201` are correctly refused, but `workforce=4294967396` wraps to 100 and applies — the guard is real and the parser lets values around it. Same shape on `recipe` and `unit_type`.

**`road_tier=255`** is priced as a Highway (the economics lookup clamps) and then written RAW into `tile.road_level`, which feeds `road_traversal_multiplier` — so one command creates a road tier the game has no concept of, with a movement bonus nothing intended.

## AND IT DEFEATS THE GUARD ADDED EARLIER TODAY — recorded honestly

`kv_getf` was given an `isfinite` check this session, after review found NaN reaching the order book. That guard tests the DOUBLE. `quantity=1e300` is a finite double, passes, and then overflows to +infinity when narrowed to `float` on assignment. So the NaN hole is closed and the infinity hole beside it was not, in the same function, by the same author, in the same session. The lesson is the one BL-387 and BL-394 also carry: validate at the boundary means validate the value that actually lands in the field, not the one you parsed.

## PROPOSED FIX

One helper, used everywhere: parse into a wide type, RANGE-CHECK against the destination's real domain, and fail the whole command with `rejected_invalid` on any violation — never truncate, never wrap, never clamp silently.

* `verb` must be `< corp_verb_count`; add that constant beside the enum so it cannot drift.
* `type` must be a declared `building_type`; same for `resource_type` and `road_tier`.
* Narrow floats through a checked conversion that rejects anything not finite AS A FLOAT, not merely as a double.
* Reject a malformed COMMAND wholesale rather than applying it with defaults — the same call this session already made for non-finite floats, generalised to every field.

`smoke.js` must then assert the whole class: an out-of-range verb, type, resource, road tier, workforce and quantity each refused, and — the load-bearing one — that the world is UNCHANGED after each refusal.

## Note on severity

None of this is reachable from the GUI, which cannot emit an out-of-range enum. It is reachable from the first day the seam took external input, which is the fourth instance this session of that same pattern.
BL-396.resolution: Landed 2026-08-14 (seam batch, commit ff46f3f + review-barrier tightening). Checked wide parse + real-domain range check on every COMMAND field; corp_verb_count/building_type_count beside their enums; float fields validated as the float that lands (strtod, full-token, isfinite-as-float). Evidence: requirements.json § wire-parser-validation.

BL-397.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found by adversarial play. The sibling of BL-387 on the READ side, and it is the more serious half.

## The leak

`export_corp_blackboard` is carefully visibility-honest about what corp X may learn about corp Y — rival buildings yes, rival cash and pools and recipes no (BL-068). That model is correct and it is undermined completely by the transport: the BLACKBOARD opcode takes `corp=` from the request line and exports THAT corp's own-asset section. A player read every rival's cash, pools, and per-building recipe and workforce simply by asking for them.

So the fog is enforced within a blackboard and not between blackboards. BL-068's whole competitor-visibility rule, and the commercial-sphere activity fog with it, are decoration on a seam that will hand over the private view for the asking.

## The oracle

Smaller but the same family: `remove_sell_order` returns `rejected_invalid` for an id that does not exist and `rejected_not_owner` for one that belongs to someone else. The two are perfectly distinguishable, so sweeping the id space reveals exactly how many orders stand globally and which are whose — without placing a single order. This is the cost of the typed-rejection discipline, and it is worth paying, but it should be a deliberate choice rather than an accident.

## PROPOSED FIX

Both fall out of BL-387's session-actor model, which is why this requires it: once `--serve` knows which corp the session IS, BLACKBOARD serves that corp and refuses any other (except under the explicit `--as any` research opt-in), and the order-book oracle narrows to the caller's own book — an id outside it answers one code, not two.

Do them together. Fixing the write path alone would leave the read path handing out exactly the intelligence the write path was just stopped from acting on.
BL-397.resolution: Landed 2026-08-14 (seam batch, commit 0e0f12f). BLACKBOARD serves the session actor only; the remove_sell_order oracle is closed (foreign == nonexistent == rejected_invalid); JS clients' line framing fixed to END-alone termination. Evidence: requirements.json § seam-read-privacy.

BL-407.design:
## Why this one first

Of the six spectator items this is the only one that adds no simulation state and
changes no rule. It is a reader over two stores that are already populated on every
tick of every existing session. It also pays outside spectator mode: it is the
instrument AI_OPPONENT.md § 10h asks for - *"a harness asserts what its author
already suspected; a player discovers what nobody thought to assert"* - and the
idle/resume oscillation that § 10h records as the AI's dominant behaviour for an
unknown number of sprints was invisible for exactly this reason.

## The surface

A ledger window on the nav rail, following the standing toggle rule (clicking the
rail icon while active closes it; re-clicking the active sub-view tab closes it).
Rows newest-first, one per decision:

| column | source |
|---|---|
| tick / date | `corp_decision.tick`, rendered through the campaign calendar |
| corp | `corp_decision.corp` -> name, in the corp identity colour (`palette::corp_identity_colour`) |
| verb + target | `corp_decision.command` rendered through the ACTIONS.json gloss for that verb |
| reason | `corp_decision.reason` -> the reason code's human phrase |
| margin | `winning_score` vs `runner_up` - the number that says whether it was a close call or a walkover |

**The margin column is the point.** A decision taken at 0.81 against a runner-up of
0.79 is a coin-flip the tuning could have gone either way on; one taken at 0.9
against 0.1 is a conviction. Nothing currently distinguishes them, and the
difference is most of what "what strategy is it running" means.

## Two stores, one view

`world::ai_decisions` is a 256-entry ring - live, cheap, and it wraps. The history
log is permanent but stores prose (`event` / `consequence` strings), not scores.
The feed reads the RING for the live tail (with margins) and falls back to the LOG
for anything older than the ring's window (without margins, and say so in the row
rather than faking a number). Do not widen the ring to avoid this: its 256-cap is
deliberate ("derived observability, not save-format state - bounded so the log can
run forever", corp_command.hpp).

## Filters

By corp, by reason code, and a verb filter. The reason-code filter is what turns the
feed from a river into an answer: "show me every `best_build` this run" is a
different question from "show me every solvency-defence idle".

## Out of scope here

Clicking a row to select the subject and move the canvas is BL-410 (attention
director) - it needs the camera work, not the feed. The per-run aggregate is BL-411.
This item is the raw log, legibly rendered.

## Obligations

New surface, so it owes a `question_log.json` entry (BL-260 - the question it answers,
why it earns its space, the item that demanded it). New controls, so the ledger family
in `ACTIONS.json` gains its entries; a stale dictionary misleads the AI player.

## Amendment, 2026-08-14 housekeeping (NR-229)

Shipped with two filters, corp and reason, not three. The design above named a verb filter alongside them; it was dropped rather than built. The reason filter already partitions the verb families well enough in practice (best_build implies build, dial_* imply the dials) that a third control would mostly duplicate the second one. If a verb filter is wanted later it is a small addition (one ui_state int, one combo, one predicate).

BL-409.design:
## Ben's reframe, and why it is the better item

The question was drafted as *may the scorer drive the player's corp under a spectate
flag* - an exception carved into the standing rule that the player's own corp is never
auto-acted on strategically. Ben, 2026-08-14: *"In spectator mode, there is no need to
mark a corp as played by a human. 'Who plays your corp' collapses as a question."*

That is a cleaner formulation and a smaller change. The standing rule protects a corp
**because a human owns it**. Spectator mode has no human owner, so the rule is not
being excepted - its precondition is absent. `player_entity` stops meaning *the corp the
rules protect* and means only *the corp the camera and the ledgers are currently pointed
at*: a **viewpoint**.

## What changes

- A spectator flag on the session (set from `--spectate`, and from the main menu).
- Under it, `corp_strategic_eval_due` and `run_corp_strategic_step` stop special-casing
  `world::player_entity` / `corporation_component::is_player`. Every corp evaluates on
  the same staggered cadence. The two guards are corp_ai.cpp:465 and :499.
- `player_entity` remains set - the UI needs an anchor - but nothing reads it as an
  ownership claim. The `(Player)` tag in `draw_corporation_summary` becomes a viewpoint
  marker or is dropped under spectate.
- Player-press affordances (construction placement, order entry, workforce dials) are
  disabled under spectate. Not hidden - **disabled and legible**, so it stays obvious
  that the mode is a window, not a broken game.

## Determinism

This must not perturb the seeded run. The cadence is `sorted-corp-id index % cadence_k
== tick % cadence_k`, so admitting one more corp shifts nothing for the others - the
index is over the sorted corp set, which does not change. The player's corp simply
stops being skipped at its own slot. A spectated run and a played-but-idle run will
diverge (correctly - one has an extra actor), but each stays replayable from its seed.
Verify with a headless harness: same seed, spectate on, run N ticks twice, assert an
identical `world::state_hash`.

## The standing rule

`.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md` § Determinism & data model carries the
player-corp prohibition and its BL-181 workforce-dial exception. It gains the
no-seat clause **when this work lands**, not before - the authority time-slices
(DELIVERY.md § Design state). Ben's grant is dated 2026-08-14 and recorded in
NEEDS_REVIEW.

## Deliberately NOT in scope

Reassigning the viewpoint to an arbitrary rival mid-session. That is 42 `player_entity`
references across 14 UI files and it is a separate item if it is ever wanted; the
no-seat framing makes it much less necessary, since under spectate every corp is
already symmetric and the Selection element already inspects any of them.
